(I later find out that the generators are never supposed to run on day with such poor air quality, but an emergency circuit issue required them to kick in temporarily.)

It doesn’t always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise, nearby residents like Lindsay Shaw tell me. We meet while she’s out for a walk with her dog, and she describes the way the sound permeates into her home. Constant light from the data center shines right into her bedroom at night unless the bathroom door is fully closed. Her fiancé has taken to wearing an eye mask.

Piedmont Environmental Council land use director Julie Bolthouse worries about how Loudoun will keep up with the energy demands imposed by data center expansion.

Nobody wanted it this way. In an ideal world, Vantage would have done what hundreds of other data centers in the area have done and connected to the Dominion energy grid by the time the site went online last year. But after Vantage had already signed agreements with customers leasing space in the new data center, Dominion informed Vantage it didn’t have enough capacity to get the 800,000-square-foot data center on the grid. Rather than let the building sit dormant until Dominion built up capacity, Vantage decided to create its own energy source using gas turbines. This is becoming more and more common in other parts of the country, as the new AI-motivated data centers require vastly more energy than the old cloud servers.

Residents and local politicians acknowledge that the Vantage site is an outlier because of its unusual reliance on on-site generated power from natural gas — albeit a very annoying one. Before it was built, Shaw tells me she thought a data center would be among the best options that could come to the lot across the street, in part because it wouldn’t be something that would drive a lot of traffic near what she says is an already dangerous intersection. But now she says the data center has caused plenty of other problems and feels the operators have not been proactive enough in engaging neighbors. Vantage’s senior vice president of global public policy, John Stephenson, says he “would respectfully disagree” that they haven’t proactively engaged nearby residents. He notes that they held a community meeting at a nearby brewery to field questions early on, but admits that “in retrospect, we probably could have done more.” The company has taken different approaches to mitigate the noise, including installing insulation and repositioning the turbines to lower their tone.

But residents who live near other data centers throughout Loudoun — even those that don’t have to generate their own power on-site — also complain of noise. Jason Mello says he hears a constant “low-frequency drone” he attributes to the HVAC systems of nearby data centers from his Ashburn home. Living near Dulles Airport, many Ashburn residents are used to the sound of planes overhead, “but planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.”

Mello shows me videos of the noise from his deck outside a town hall meeting where we meet. He says he’s already spent $2,600 getting two new window inserts, with three more to go in his bedroom. He was quoted at least $15,000 for new siding that would further mitigate the noise. “As a homeowner, if I want to live in peace at night, that addresses the inside,” he says, “but if I’m sitting on my deck, I can constantly hear that humming. And I think that’s why you got to fix the problem also at the source.”

“You’re thinking, ‘You work your whole life, you own something.’ But you actually don’t own it, because a power company can say, ‘I like your house. I want to take it.’”

Data centers have become next-door neighbors for many Loudoun County residents.

Several residents tell me that the boom in infrastructure needed to support the data centers has impacted their ability to enjoy the natural resources of Loudoun that once attracted them. “You can barely hear the birds anymore,” says Jessica Medeiros, another resident who lives across the street from the Vantage data center. Even when she tries to retreat from the noise near her home, she’s regularly reminded of the data centers’ presence. As a regular runner on the famed Washington and Old Dominion trail for the past 20 years, Medeiros says the “constant construction,” towering power lines, and reduced shade because of cleared trees “ruins the experience with nature.” She often says that when she dies, “I want my ashes scattered along the trail. But I think that trail’s going to look a lot different in another 10 years.”

“The greenery is gone. The sense of community is gone. It feels very stale,” says Jenny Marza, another Loudoun County resident. “There’s no more trees left and every inch is taken up by greed.”

While fighting new development near her own home, Marza has already felt pressure from the data center explosion on her small export logistics business. For years she’s been looking at buying office and warehouse space in the area to be near the airport, but prices have been so astronomical that she’s been forced to continue leasing. Now, even her current office rent has skyrocketed — she suspects because every landlord knows that data centers are willing to pay an average of $3.76 million per acre.

It doesn’t always sound like a lawn mower, though. Other days, the gas turbines that power the data center make an even more annoying high-pitched squealing noise.

Marza says “I’m kicking myself” over a warehouse she came close to buying last year for around $5 million, but held off because it was more space than she needed at the time. “And then we put a pause on the search for two years and when we returned, it was like, ‘Holy crap, there’s nothing left.’” Anything that was selling at $5 million was now $10 million. To Marza, the residential property tax savings and increased home values mean little when compared to the quality-of-life concerns she has and the ability to help her small business survive. “I feel like it’s a drop in the ocean of what they’re getting in return,” she says. “I feel like nobody protected our interests as a community.”

“Done the right way, you can be good neighbors,” Shaw says, reflecting on the Vantage site near her home. “But this one was done like that shady neighbor next door that has people coming in and out all hours of the night. And then the FBI raids them and you’re like, ‘Well, I knew something shady was going on.’”

When I arrive at the Loudoun government building on a July evening shortly before 6:30PM, I’m handed a red flyer outside by a group advocating for local government control of utilities used to power data centers. Inside, the nearly full room is prominently speckled with light blue shirts that read “I support data centers.” The shirts list the reasons: “Because I like: lower taxes, excellent schools, better job opportunities.” They also include caveats: “When they are: in the right location, well-designed, quiet, environmentally sensitive.” The slogan doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue.

I comfortably score a seat, but later hear complaints from some attendees who say they arrived shortly after me and were relegated to the overflow room. Though it’s a first-come-first-served event, those critical of data centers grumble that industry supporters seem suspiciously well organized in their early arrivals.

Still, it doesn’t have the kind of fireworks or soundbites that have made community meetings about data centers around the country into national news. While some residents voice strong frustration, the two-and-a-half-hour forum is cordial and respectful of Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall’s request of no cheering nor jeering.

“Planes come and go. The data center hum never stops.”

Tippett’s Hill Cemetery, one of the oldest African American cemeteries in the area, is surrounded by data centers.

Randall is in a tough spot. As head of the elected nine-member panel tasked with adopting local ordinances, appropriating funds, and rezoning land, Randall has just enough power for her constituents to lay responsibility for their criticism at her feet, yet not enough to change some of the things she says she wishes she could. At the meeting, she listens to residents’ concerns, promising to follow up with phone calls for some while repeatedly acknowledging and lamenting the quality-of-life frustrations many of her neighbors have about living near data centers. But she also declines to give ground on topics she said are unfounded or detached from political reality.

Randall walks residents through the history of data centers in Loudoun, including what they are and how they came to be zoned the same way as office parks. Before getting to the audience participation portion, she clicks to a slide that says “4 Things That Are Unpopular But True” with a grimace emoji. The first: At one point in time, residents actually preferred data centers over new housing developments. She references opposition to a 2021 proposal to build up to 779 residential housing units in Ashburn, called Hyde Park. Across about 125 comments, residents reportedly worried about increased traffic and infrastructure strain. Nearly two years after submitting the application, the developer withdrew and decided to establish a by-right data center there instead. “One of my worst days was January 5th, 2023, when the applicant called me and said, ‘Forget it. I’m going to go build a data center,’” Randall says. “And I pretty much begged them not to.”

“So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?”

The second unpopular truth: It’s not legal for Loudoun to enact a moratorium on development without the state’s permission.

Third: Both the Biden and Trump administrations have indicated AI infrastructure buildout will be a national priority, so that’s unlikely to change anytime soon.

And fourth: Despite resident backlash to certain data center land use exceptions the board has granted, the alternative would have been that those data centers could take the land by right anyway, with much less in return. The lesson being, if data centers can break ground whether government officials want them to or not, the county might as well get something out of it.

Residents who speak at the hearing do not dispute her account of the county’s history. Many express frustration about the buildings encroaching on greenery or creating annoying and near-constant noise issues. But many others, including several in the blue shirts, argue in support of data centers as stewards of the community they are proud to be known for. One Ashburn resident describes a peaceful experience living across from a data center. “When the weather is good, I’ll open my bedroom windows, from which I can see it directly. It is silent, it is clean. It is a good neighbor,” he says. Another resident, who leads the nonprofit Northern Virginia Science Center Foundation, credits data centers with generating revenue that can help fund such endeavors to a greater degree than it sees in nearby Fairfax. The organization lists Loudoun County, Dominion Energy, and data center company QTS among its partners.

Randall affirms residents’ data center complaints, but also fact-checks several claims about supposed data center projects she says never existed in the first place. One Ashburn resident, for example, bemoans what he calls the “Ashburn Commons proposal” that would create a blight next to existing housing, greenery, and other community institutions. Randall asks him to clarify if he is thinking about a proposal near the Harris Teeter grocery store.

“Yes!” he answers.

“That’s not real,” Randall says. Her colleague adds the would-be developer hasn’t even submitted a formal application for it, and the government had denied an initial request.

“Well,” the resident cries out, “praise the Lord on that!”

“I don’t want to be the example of what not to do.”

For all the gripes, I’ve still yet to meet anyone in Loudoun County who actually says they oppose data centers entirely. Whether they’re currently living next to gas turbines or their backyard could potentially be seized to build a transmission tower, Loudoun residents still recognize that data centers help power the technology we use every day. After all, they need to go somewhere. Why not there?

But even if Loudoun residents have accepted the economic benefits as a tradeoff for the loud eyesores near their homes, it doesn’t mean they’re open to an expansion of that deal.

“It’s not about trying to get rid of the existing data centers. These data centers are here. They’re running. I don’t want them to go anywhere,” Bolthouse says. “The question isn’t, ‘Do we need data centers?’ The question is, ‘Is it worth threatening our air quality, threatening our water supply, and throwing our communities into chaos, and taking people’s private land for transmission lines to get it?’”

I spoke with over half a dozen Loudoun residents, and universally, this is what they want communities considering data centers to understand: Know what you’re getting into. That means making sure existing laws and ordinances will apply to data centers, that local utilities have a plan to ensure enough capacity for the expected buildout, and that neither data centers nor the infrastructure needed to power them can be built too close to homes or schools.

Even Rizer says the buildout in Loudoun has, in some places, gone beyond what he’d have hoped. “There’s no data centers here that aren’t where they’re allowed to be, but I think sometimes there’s a difference between what you’re allowed to do and what is probably best for the community,” he says. “And that’s what we’ve had to clean up a little bit.” At the town hall, Randall showed aerial images of several residential communities that were directly bordered by data centers. Those arrangements are not what any Loudoun official or resident considers ideal — but even so, she said, property values in those communities have only gone up.

There are limits. Loudoun hasn’t had a strategic focus on bringing in more data centers since 2019, Rizer says. More recently, the local government is pursuing a plan to pump the brakes further — doing away with the ability for data centers to use office-zoned land by right, and considering pausing new permit reviews while contemplating zoning changes that could better address community impacts.

When peers around the country contact him about whether they should invite data centers into their communities, Rizer says, “It’s not right for every place. So do you want them? And if you do, where do you want them? How many do you want? And under what conditions would you take them?”

For Loudoun, unlike many yet-to-be-developed areas in the US, there is a definitive end in sight. The county has an ever-diminishing amount of space left to develop data centers, after which point it will continue to collect tax revenue when the companies update equipment within their walls.

Loudoun residents hope that by the time it gets to that point, the things that they love about the area are still there. For many, it’s the convenience of living near DC, but still close to nature. It’s also often about the quality public schools, funded in part with the revenue raised by the colossal energy-guzzling slabs in their backyards.

HVAC units on top of data centers can contribute to the loud noise many residents complain about.

AOL’s roots helped make Loudoun the first major data center capital, and that came with both advantages and challenges. For communities starting to consider their first data center today, Bolthouse says they’re in a much better position than Loudoun was because the industry isn’t yet “embedded” in layers of government. She still thinks their story could become a beacon of hope for others, rather than a warning — but it’s an uphill battle to get there.

“I don’t want to be the example of what not to do,” she says. “I want to be the example of what to do. I want to bring journalists out to see how we fixed problems, how we are doing much better, and how communities are happy with these facilities because they’ve done something better.” Hearing Bolthouse’s frustration with the ever-expanding energy demands imposed by data centers, it’s surprising to hear her embrace the ones that are already here. But for all the friction they’ve caused in her community recently, it’s also clear from my visits and conversations that data centers have played a central role in supporting many positive aspects of life in Loudoun. The question, now, is whether Loudoun can manage its existing demand and successfully serve community needs as the data center footprint continues to grow.

If Bolthouse sounds optimistic, she is certain that something has to give. In the past, Loudoun’s data center buildout was quiet and steady. Today’s is anything but. “I don’t see how that happens with the scale and speed to market that the industry is pursuing.”
excerpt:
In 2007, the US was on the cusp of an economic recession, and Buddy Rizer was tasked with finding Loudoun County, Virginia, a new way to make money. Rizer’s earlier career as a radio DJ didn’t exactly make him an obvious candidate to find a solution, but he was looking for what he called a “real job” and stumbled into a role at Loudoun’s economic development authority.

This new gig came with urgency thanks to the bursting of the housing bubble: More than 80 percent of the county’s revenue came from residential real estate. The goal, at the time, was to raise the commercial tax base from about 19 percent of revenue to something like 23 percent, Rizer recalls. Today, just over half of the county’s tax revenue comes from commercial sources. To jumpstart that turnaround, Rizer turned to the carcasses of another recent bubble burst — those of the dot-com era.

title: No ‘DMV for AI’: US Pushes Against AI Regulations at Global Forum
snippet: A US regulatory agency for AI would be a “disaster,” Trump’s AI czar said during a G20 forum on technology.
fullText:
The US government’s message at the G20 Innovation Ministerial is clear: Nothing should slow down AI innovation – not regulation, not power shortages, not even serious safety concerns.

The forum, hosted this week in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, brings together government leaders from the G20 countries, including India, China, Russia and many European nations, to discuss technological advancements and subsequent policy challenges. The theme this year is, unsurprisingly, generative AI. 

Michael Kratsios, director of the Trump administration’s Office of Science and Technology Policy, said in his opening remarks that “slow policy adaptation makes it harder to capture the full benefits of innovation.” 

	

			

“Often, in the US and elsewhere, regulations built for a different technological era prove poor fits for rapidly evolving, generally applicable inventions, creating uncertainty for developers and policymakers alike,” Kratsios said. “That leaves development efforts abandoned, growth unrealized and nations falling behind, as innovation continues elsewhere.”

The US is pushing for a framework it’s calling the Carolina Principles, a “pro-innovation framework” that aims to bolster AI research, form pathways to commercialization and create industry-led standards for emerging technologies. Global leaders will hear from the biggest names in AI throughout their discussions. 

At the end of the week, any policy agreements reached will feed into the broader agreement that the global community signs at the G20 Leaders Summit in Miami this December.

AI regulation is an increasingly important issue as AI models become more capable and autonomous. This week’s summit offers insight into how the global community is approaching the issue – and where it is drawing lines in the sand for Big Tech.

Trump AI adviser: No ‘DMV for AI’

It would be a “disaster” if the US adopted a version of the “FDA for AI,” said David Sacks, the Trump administration’s former AI czar and co-chair of the president’s council on science and technology, on Tuesday. “Any regulatory agency that has to approve AI product releases will become like a DMV for AI, where new models get stuck in a long queue waiting for approval.”

AI is “just too dynamic and fast-moving for that type of approach,” Sacks said in a virtual appearance. “And I don’t think we want to hamstring our innovation that way.”

Sacks argued against the idea of a regulatory agency for AI, one that would be similar to how the Food and Drug Administration authorizes new medicines or how the Federal Aviation Administration oversees airlines.

Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

It’s not the first time the idea of an AI-specific regulatory agency has been floated in the tech policy community, but Sacks’s remarks seem to take a direct swing at the only major AI company not in attendance at the event: Anthropic. Its CEO, Dario Amodei, advocated for such a government review process in a recent essay.

“Frontier AI models, like airplanes, should be required to go through technical testing and auditing, and their release should be blocked or reversed as a threat to public safety if they do not meet high standards of safety,” Amodei wrote. He added that because AI is being used in research, existing agencies like the FDA will have more proposals to evaluate, further taxing the regulators.

Sacks argued that there is already sufficient regulation around AI from existing laws, and existing regulatory agencies could deal with any AI threats. 

This is far from the first time Anthropic and the US government have been at odds. After a deal between the Pentagon and Anthropic blew up, the AI company was declared a supply chain risk, though a judge blocked that order. Later, when Anthropic released its Fable 5 model, the US government ordered the company to prevent any foreign nationals from using it. To comply, Anthropic pulled the model, rereleasing it only after receiving an unofficial green light from the Trump administration.

Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg speak on AI

Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX, which operates xAI, supported a hands-off regulatory approach in a virtual speech at the G20 Innovation Ministerial.

“What most countries tend to do is they tend to provide too much support to the large existing trees in the forest and not enough to the smallest saplings,” Musk said on Tuesday, comparing big corporations and startups to a forest. Musk said this should be flipped, and governments should adopt a philosophy where new inventions are “default legal as opposed to default illegal.”

Notably, Musk is CEO of one of the biggest tech companies in the world and the world’s richest person, aided by SpaceX’s recent IPO, which briefly made him the world’s first trillionaire. His businesses received $38 billion in government funding last year, according to a February report from The Washington Post.

But we’ve already seen how the US government is either unable or unwilling to address the worst, most abusive consequences of AI technology. When millions of AI-generated images of child sex abuse material flooded X months ago, US regulatory agencies did nothing to stop it. 

By contrast, the European Union opened an investigation into X, countries like Malaysia and Indonesia banned the app, and many global leaders spoke out against the Musk-owned AI tool and platform. 

Mark Zuckerberg, also speaking virtually, talked about how publicly available AI models help people create things, like learning to use new software or run small businesses. 

“The ability to start new things is going to be immense, and that’s going to lead to this very dynamic period,” Zuckerberg said on Tuesday. “So I think it leads to wanting to have policies that make it easy to create things [and] easy to evolve and change the systems that we have today.”

The idea is that if AI is publicly available, like through an open-weights AI model, more people can use it. Tech policies that support open source AI fuel that creation. Zuckerberg’s open source approach to AI is unique in the industry, with Meta recently promising to publicly release its newest models. This came after it was rumored that the Trump administration was considering a ban on open-source models; many tech leaders said that would be harmful to global AI innovation and cybersecurity.

“Having the technology diffused … you can set up a system of checks and balances, rather than restricting it to only being available to a small number of people or companies or governments,” Zuckerberg said. (Zuckerberg, notably, would be one of the people with complete access.)

Over the past year, the Trump administration has flipped its previous hands-off approach to regulating AI. It seems to want to be involved, particularly as its tech and government leaders see generative AI technology as simultaneously a threat and a benefit to national security and cybersecurity. 

Policy frameworks that emerge from forums like the G20 Innovation Ministerial could dramatically shape the limits on the power that Big Tech and AI companies have globally.

title: AfterQuery reportedly becomes Y Combinator’s fastest-ever unicorn, now valued at $3.2B
snippet: AI model-training startup AfterQuery has reportedly raised a round that valued it at $3.2 billion, just five months after announcing its $30 million Series A at a $300 million valuation in April.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

3:08 PM PDT · September 1, 2026

Image Credits:Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

AI training-data startup AfterQuery has reportedly raised a round that valued it at $3.2 billion. This just five months after announcing its $30 million Series A at a $300 million valuation in April.

That’s more than a 10x increase in less than half a year and, according to Y Combinator partner Gustaf Alströmer, the fastest that any startup has gone from launch to unicorn status in the accelerator’s history. AfterQuery’s founders, today 22 and 23 years old, attended Y Combinator’s Winter 2025 cohort, just 18 months ago.

In April, the San Francisco startup said it had reached an annualized revenue run rate of $100 million and that it was working with many of the biggest labs. It has named companies such as Nvidia, Legora, and the Korean AI lab Motif Technologies as customers.

AfterQuery is among the new crop of startups following in the footsteps of Mercor and Scale that employ knowledge professionals like doctors, lawyers, and other specialists to do model training. However, rather than ensuring that models answer questions accurately, AfterQuery trains models and agents on how to work like professionals would to complete tasks — what the company describes as “encoding the patterns, decisions, and reasoning of the world’s best practitioners.”

Forbes first reported on the round. AfterQuery could not be immediately reached for comment.

title: Sequoia-incubated Empirik launches with $21M to predict outages before they happen
snippet: The startup wants to do for IT infrastructure what Cursor did for software engineering.
fullText:
Before joining Sequoia Capital in 2020 as chief digital and information officer, Avon Puri spent over a decade running infrastructure at Rubrik and VMware. Three years ago, as large language models began showing their true potential, Puri, alongside another Sequoia IT leader, Sudheer Dhurjati, recognized that AI could help autonomously solve a major challenge for infrastructure engineers — preventing tech outages before they occur.

The two tech veterans realized that instead of reacting to system failures after the fact, they could build a tool to predict them. This insight led them to build Empirik, a product that tracks system changes and infers their potential ripple effects across the entire infrastructure.

Sequoia recognized that Empirik could be a new type of observability tool that helps prevent and resolve incidents. After incubating the startup in 2023, Sequoia recruited former Quantum Metric CPO and Salesforce observability VP Kartik Chandrayana as CEO earlier this year.

Empirik announced Tuesday that it is spinning out as an independent company after raising $21 million in seed funding from Sequoia, Canapi, and Alumni Ventures.

“There has always been a lot of money spent in keeping systems up and running,” Sequoia partner Bogomil Balkansky told TechCrunch, adding that most existing observability tools fail to understand complex system dependencies. Empirik, he claims, is one of the first dedicated tools focused on tracking changes across massive environments. It acts as an autonomous “traffic cop” — permitting low-risk changes, setting guardrails on larger ones, and flagging the most dangerous updates for human review.

By serving as an autonomous infrastructure engineer, Empirik allows busy DevOps and site reliability engineering teams to offload routine troubleshooting and focus on higher-value priorities.

Since launching earlier this year, Empirik has already brought on customers ranging from startups to several Fortune 500 players, including S&P Global, Guardant Health, and a major consumer packaged goods (CPG) company.

Empirik’s goal is to do for infrastructure engineers what Cursor and Claude Code did for software developers: automate certain tasks so they can work significantly faster.

As AI accelerates the pace of software development, tools that help infrastructure engineers keep up with constant system changes are more vital than ever, Chandrayana told TechCrunch.

“What agentic AI did for software, Empirik wants to do for infrastructure engineering,” he added.

As for competition, Balkansky claims Empirik is in a category of its own for now, acting as a complementary layer to AI SRE platforms like Resolve and Sequoia-backed Traversal.

snippet: Google is rolling out a trio of updates that boost AI Mode’s travel capabilities, starting with the ability to get price alerts for flights. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out a trio of updates that boost AI Mode’s travel capabilities, starting with the ability to get price alerts for flights.

Google Flights price tracking is coming directly into AI Mode. This integration starts with the ability to “describe where and when you want to fly.” You’ll see a list of flights and prices from “more than 300 partner airlines and travel sites.”

If you’re ready to book, you can build your full itinerary in AI Mode and buy your tickets through the airline’s website or your preferred booking platform.

Otherwise, you can follow up with “track these flight prices for me.” AI Mode will have you confirm the route, dates, and filters. Price changes will be delivered via email. Flight price tracking in AI Mode is now rolled out in over 180 countries/territories.

AI Mode can now show the cost of flights and hotels in points or miles. Support for Accor, Flying Blue, Hyatt, LATAM Airlines, and Lufthansa Group will be available in the coming weeks.

	

This lets you ask: “I want to travel from Atlanta to Miami using my AA miles. Help me find some options for nonstop flights departing Oct 9 and returning on Oct 12.”

…you’ll see how many miles you need to book matching flights, based on the latest data directly from our partners.

The final travel update for AI Mode is hotel booking. This lets you chat about your preferences to get a list of hotels “complete with guest reviews and key factors to compare.” Once found, “Continue on Google” will appear for supported partners. 

From there, it’s just a few taps to pick your room type, review details like the cancellation policy, and complete the booking securely via Google Pay. When you book hotels through AI Mode, the hotel or booking platform will act as the merchant of record and handle any customer service.

title: Google’s answer to Canva is an AI tool where you prompt instead of design
snippet: With Google Pics, Google is pushing deeper into the creative software market dominated by Canva and Adobe, but with a distinctly AI-first approach.
fullText:
Google is entering the creative design market with a new image-creation and editing tool called Google Pics, which will become a part of its Google Workspace suite for business customers and premium Google AI subscribers.

The company says the product, which is powered by Google’s Nano Banana image-generation model, will roll out over the coming weeks to most Workspace customers and those who pay for Google AI Pro or Ultra.

Similar to popular design tools like Adobe Express and Canva, Google’s new product is meant to be used for the sort of everyday design tasks you might come across at work and sometimes in your personal life. For instance, you could use Google Pics to create a poster, social media posts, and other visuals and illustrations. 

But unlike Canva, where artists, illustrators, and photographers can publish templates, graphics, photos, and other art to a marketplace where they earn royalties, Google Pics is about creating things based on AI, which was trained on artists’ work.

And unlike Adobe Express, a tool creators often use to make that work in the first place, Google Pics is a tool where you prompt to create, not where you design something new from scratch.

The app also includes other editing tools, like those to isolate and transform objects, modify or translate text inside images, and others. Plus, it supports collaborative editing and the ability to create several different generations of the image you’ve requested, so you can pick the best one. 

The software will be built into Google Workspace, initially starting with Docs and Slides, which rolls out today. It will later come to Google Drive, the company says.

title: Google Pics is Workspace’s new ‘pro-level’ AI image creator & editor
snippet: Following the announcement at I/O 2026 in May, Google Pics is launching in general availability today. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement at I/O 2026 in May, Google Pics is launching in general availability today.

Google Pics, which comes after Google Vids, is “built natively into Google Workspace.” You can click on an image in Google Docs or Slides and access the Pics editor as an overlay to start editing. An update in the coming weeks will let you edit images uploaded to Google Drive.

You can also access the tool from pics.new:

Besides generating a new image (with multiple options offered), you can import files from your computer, Google Drive, or Google Photos to start editing.

	

Leveraging Nano Banana, Google Pics offers “precise, object-based image editing.” Tools let you: 

Select and edit individual objects within an image 

Edit, reformat, or even translate individual text elements 

Crop your image for web, social media, print, or digital

Upscale your image to 2K or 4K

Process multiple edits at once, and revert any unwanted changes easily

The object segmentation capability lets you isolate a specific part and leave other parts of the image untouched. After selecting, you just provide text comments with the ability to “execute multiple edits at once.” Similarly, you can edit text that appears in images without changing anything else, which also allows for translation. 

Pics eliminates the frustration of wrangling pixels and feeling like you need to be a graphic designer to deliver a great image.

Based on the same editor as other Workspace apps, you can invite others to collaborate and share images via a link. Enterprise use cases include:

Create and translate social, digital, and web assets for global markets

Bring product concepts to life by placing them into any background or context

Brainstorm print designs, event collateral, or branded merchandise

Develop flyers, business cards, and much more

Google Pics is available for the following tiers starting today:

Google AI Pro and Ultra personal plans

Workspace Business Standard, Business Plus, Enterprise Standard, and Enterprise Plus plans

Google AI Pro for Education

title: Here’s how Apple Watch Ultra 4 will differentiate itself from prior models
snippet: Apple Watch Ultra 4 is coming on September 9, here are the key ways it’s rumored to differentiate itself from prior models. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Ultra 4 is coming on September 9, here are the key ways it’s rumored to differentiate itself from prior models.

‘Significant upgrade’ to health sensors

Digitimes has reported on multiple occasions that Apple Watch Ultra 4 will bring significant upgrades to internal sensors. It went as far as saying “the number of sensor components will double.”

Mark Gurman reported this week that “upgrades to fitness tracking” are coming. And there’s evidence that a new high blood pressure-related feature has been reviewed by the FDA for release soon.

Though many specific details around these sensor additions are still unknown, it sounds like Apple Watch Ultra 4 could lean more than ever into health and fitness tracking.

New S-class chip, the first built in AI era

Last year’s Apple Watch models used the same S10 chip that first debuted in 2024. But the last time the Watch got a truly meaningful speed and performance bump was 2023.

Rumors indicate Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12 will have a brand new, more powerful chip—likely dubbed S11 or S12.

The timing lines up perfectly with Siri AI’s debut in watchOS 27. And no doubt, the first CPU boost in an S-class chip since 2023 will pack improvements that benefit AI features.

There’s a lot of potential for Apple Watch to be the first mass-market AI wearable. I’m excited to see how the new chip might help move that needle.

Wildcard: Design updates

	

There are conflicting reports concerning Apple Watch Ultra 4’s design. While Digitimes claims a redesign is coming, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said last month: “None of this year’s watches is expected to get a major design overhaul.”

We do know that a ceramic case option is expected for Apple Watch Series 12. So it’s possible that Apple will similarly offer something unique for Apple Watch Ultra 4’s design. Reporting is unclear, but perhaps we’ll see design updates that differentiate the latest Ultra model.

title: Poco F9 Pro and F9 Ultra launch with 185Hz panels, 8 Elite Gen 5 chips, and huge batteries
snippet: Xiaomi sub-brand Poco is officially expanding its flagship smartphone line with the launch of the Poco F9 Pro and Poco F9 Ultra. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi sub-brand Poco is officially expanding its flagship smartphone line with the launch of the Poco F9 Pro and Poco F9 Ultra.

Under the hood, the top-tier Poco F9 Ultra packs Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor paired with up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of UFS 4.1 storage. The standard Poco F9 Pro relies on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 V Series (SM8850-1-AB) with up to 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage. Both handsets incorporate a dedicated 12nm VisionBoost D8 graphics chip to handle AI frame insertion and super-resolution processing.

On the front, both devices feature HyperRGB AMOLED panels with a 185Hz refresh rate and peak brightness up to 4,500 nits. The Poco F9 Pro features a 6.59-inch display with a 2510 x 1156 resolution, while the Poco F9 Ultra expands to a 6.9-inch display with a 2608 x 1200 resolution. Both screens feature 480Hz 10-point touch sampling, 4800Hz instant touch sampling, Gorilla Glass 7i protection, and integrated ultrasonic fingerprint sensors.

Camera hardware sees a major overhaul on both models, starting with a shared 200MP primary sensor with optical image stabilization (OIS) and 4K video recording. The secondary camera configurations branch off from there. 

	

The Poco F9 Pro pairs the main camera with a 50MP floating telephoto lens capable of 2.5x optical zoom and an 8MP ultra-wide sensor. The Poco F9 Ultra steps up to a 50MP periscope telephoto lens with 5x optical zoom alongside a 50MP ultra-wide sensor. Both phones include a 32MP front-facing selfie camera.

Audio performance has been tuned in partnership with Bose. The F9 Pro comes equipped with symmetrical dual stereo speakers, whereas the Poco F9 Ultra introduces a 2.1-channel audio configuration that combines dual stereo speakers with an independent 1620 rear subwoofer.

Power endurance is handled by a 6,330mAh battery on the F9 Pro, while the F9 Ultra houses a, frankly, massive 8,050mAh silicon-carbon battery with a 16% silicon content ratio. Both models share the same charging speeds: 100W wired fast charging, 50W wireless charging, 27W wired reverse charging, and 22.5W wireless reverse charging.

Additional standard hardware specifications include IP68 dust and water resistance, NFC support, and Xiaomi HyperOS 3 running out of the box. Color choices for the F9 Pro include Black, White, and Aurora Green, which features a glow-in-the-dark rear cover. The F9 Ultra is available in Black and Dark Cherry with a glass fiber finish and interactive lighting accents on the rear housing.

Pricing for the Poco F9 Pro starts at $699 for the 12GB/256GB base model (early-bird $649) and reaches $769 for the 12GB/512GB tier (early-bird $699). The Poco F9 Ultra starts at $799 for the 12GB/256GB option (early bird $729), $949 for the 16GB/512GB option (early bird $799), and tops out at $1,199 for the 16GB/1TB option (early bird $1,059). Global availability and localized ordering options are available directly on the official Poco Global page and Xiaomi launch portal.

title: iOS 27 beta 8 now available as Apple tests major Siri AI upgrade
snippet: Apple has released the eighth iOS 27 beta for developer testing. iOS 27 beta 8 continues Apple’s summer beta cycle ahead of a public release in September. We’ll update our devices and share what we discover. Update 5:04 p.m. ET: Now available for public beta testers as well. more…
fullText:
Apple has released the eighth iOS 27 beta for developer testing. iOS 27 beta 8 continues Apple’s summer beta cycle ahead of a public release in September. We’ll update our devices and share what we discover.

Update 5:04 p.m. ET: Now available for public beta testers as well. 

Apple releases eighth iOS 27 developer beta for testing

The eighth developer beta is available now through the Settings app on eligible iPhones. If you’re enrolled in the Apple Developer Program, go to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates and choose the iOS 27 Developer Beta.

Today’s developer beta release will likely become iOS 27 public beta 6. The final version for everyone will arrive in the next few weeks.

iOS 27 is all about Siri AI

iOS 27 is one of Apple’s most AI-focused iPhone updates yet. The headline change is Siri AI, Apple’s rebuilt assistant powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and new Apple Foundation Models.

Siri AI brings richer conversations, personal context, broader world knowledge, on-screen awareness, and deeper app actions across the system.

On iPhone, Siri AI also gets a new visual experience tied to the Dynamic Island, plus a dedicated Siri app for revisiting conversations across devices.

Visual Intelligence joins Siri too, including a new Siri mode in the Camera app and improvements that affect Camera Control on iPhone.

Apple Intelligence is also expanding across apps. iOS 27 adds AI-powered improvements for Photos, Safari, Passwords, Mail, Messages, Phone, Shortcuts, Home, and more. As we covered in our breakdown of Apple’s new Foundation Models, some capabilities run on-device, while others use Private Cloud Compute.

More iOS 27 features and changes

Beyond Siri and Apple Intelligence, iOS 27 includes a variety of iPhone-specific changes. Apple has refined the Liquid Glass design introduced last year, including a new Liquid Glass transparency slider for adjusting the look of system UI.

There are also performance improvements for app launches, Photos loading, Camera launch in Low Power Mode, AirDrop transfers, and Wi-Fi-to-cellular transitions.

Other iPhone changes include Photos keywords and star ratings, customizable slideshows, smoother Camera behavior, continuous sending in Messages, Dual Capture in FaceTime, custom EQ for AirPods, new recovery options, easier Apple Pay card switching, and AI-generated wallpaper creation.

We’re installing iOS 27 beta 8 now and will update with any notable changes. In the meantime, you can catch up on everything new in iOS 27 from Apple’s keynote list.

title: ChatGPT Health adds Epic integration for clinicians to import patient data
snippet: OpenAI said that the integration provides read-only access to health records for clinicians.
fullText:
OpenAI said today that it is integrating ChatGPT Health with Epic’s electronic health record (EHR) system, which holds data for over 325 million patients, to let clinicians import patient data and use AI to ask questions. The company said that in certain systems, it will also integrate ChatGPT directly within EHR workflows.

With ChatGPT, clinicians can now access information like appointment notes, laboratory results, medications, and specialist documentation and summarize them easily. They can also look at patient history, identify changes, and prepare for future appointments. OpenAI said that in some deployments, clinicians can directly access ChatGPT for getting pre-visit review and building clinical timelines without leaving a patient chart. The company specified that the integration allows only read-only access to health records, and AI doesn’t write anything back.

OpenAI is also adding a new Healthcare Public Data plug-in, which can fetch information from sources including ClinicalTrials.gov, CMS Coverage, RxNorm, DailyMed, and PubMed. The company said that the new plug-in can help healthcare workers synthesize data for trial eligibility criteria, medication identifiers, coverage policy versions, and provider records.

The company said that apart from enabling these new features, it is allowing organizations with a Business Associate Agreement to use ChatGPT Work, Codex, apps, and connectors in their workspace for compliant workflows.

Last month, OpenAI rolled out ChatGPT for health to all U.S. consumers. The company said at that time that people are asking 300 million health-related queries to ChatGPT every week. Despite many deep integrations with medical systems, the company has maintained that AI is not suitable for diagnosis or treatment.

OpenAI said that it collected over 4,300 responses from physicians across 27 clinical use cases, including pre-visit review, clinical timelines, medication review, and handoff summaries, and found that 99.1% of responses were safe. However, even a few unsafe answers can lead to harmful results for humans.

A few days before this rollout, a Florida-based pastor sued the company, alleging that ChatGPT gave him a near-fatal recommendation. The company was also sued in May by family members of a user who blamed ChatGPT for giving wrongful advice related to dosage.

fullText:
Google has reportedly been reaching out to a number of Hollywood’s biggest studios, hoping to strike licensing agreements that would allow it to train its AI models on copyrighted material in exchange for massive piles of cash. In theory, these deals would be a win-win: a huge financial boon to the studios that would also give Google a significant advantage in its race to outpace other AI companies. But while there’s little downside for Google, these deals pose a distinct set of risks to each of the studios that might be thinking about going all-in on AI. Getting into bed with Google this way might benefit Hollywood in the short term, but it could just as easily backfire and leave the public feeling burned by the entertainment industry.

Though Google has not yet been able to get Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, or Universal to agree to anything officially, the company’s executives have been reaching out to multiple studio representatives with pitches focused on its AI technology, according to unnamed sources speaking to The Los Angeles Times. Google wants permission to train its AI models on the studios’ vast libraries of copyrighted content, and it’s willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to get ahold of them. Per The LA Times, Google could pay a studio like Disney / Pixar around $40 million just for the rights to generate outputs featuring a single copyrighted character. That payout could swell well into the billions the more characters Google’s deals encompass, and studios might be able to secure a portion of however much advertising revenue Google makes from AI-generated content featuring that IP on platforms like YouTube.

As expensive as these partnerships would be for Google, they would also be an invaluable tool as the company continues to crystalize its position as one of the most prominent players in the AI game. Gemini being able to spit out Disney-approved images of Darth Vader and Snow White might not seem all that significant on its face, but that’s exactly the sort of thing that could get more ordinary, non tech-obsessed people seeing generative AI in a more positive (if innocuous) light. After years of hearing AI companies boast about their plans to disrupt society and eliminate jobs, public sentiment — especially among young people — about the technology has shifted into the negative. Even with tools like ChatGPT being as popular as they are, the larger AI industry has been so mired in controversy and plagued by concerns about its real world harms that it would now be hard-pressed to put out products that would immediately curry widespread goodwill. Striking deals with film and TV studios would give Google a convenient way to shift the larger narrative about its AI ambitions.

The content developed through these partnerships would presumably look better than the slop currently being churned out by models trained on ill-gotten source data, and having Google’s name and logos slapped all over official AI-generated Disney content would do wonders to legitimize this technology in people’s minds. But even if it didn’t, the partnership would still signal to the public that the entertainment industry sees generative AI as a tool worth embracing. It’s hard to quantify how valuable that framing would be to Google, whose DeepMind arm struck a $75 million investment deal with A24 earlier this summer. But it’s very easy to imagine how taking Google’s AI cash could put studios on a path that ultimately alienates their workers and audiences.

Regardless of whether a studio were to incorporate AI tools into their production workflows or simply feature user-generated AI content on their platforms (which was Disney and OpenAI’s plan before their partnership collapsed), striking a licensing agreement with Google would be a watershed moment.

Lionsgate, a notable studio but not a major player, struck a licensing deal with Runway in 2024. So far, nothing concrete has come out of that partnership, but the companies say they’re working on a plan to release AI-generated shorts. Once any one of the big legacy studios hop on to the AI bandwagon and manage to actually make something they can show the world, more production houses have a reason to follow suit. AI’s potential to speed production timelines up while keeping costs down is one of the main things that has kept studios interested in utilizing the technology. Shareholders would absolutely love it if production houses could put out more movies while spending less money, but doing that by using AI tools would almost certainly put a significant portion of the entertainment workforce out of jobs.

What may be keeping Disney and other studios from rushing to take Google up on its offers is the way that people have reacted to seeing AI used in the production of films like Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Fans were dismayed to find AI-generated images in Brand New Day’s official artbook, and the negative reaction might have been even more intense had people known about the technology’s use before the film hit theaters. It’s impossible to know for sure whether awareness about AI’s presence in Brand New Day’s production would have kept it from making $2 billion at the box office. But it stands to reason that none of the studios is eager to be the first to learn what happens when they release a project that’s presented as being the product of Google’s AI tools.

Though Google has everything to gain from Hollywood embracing AI, the studios have to be mindful of how endorsing this technology could leave them out on a limb. And as much as Google might be presenting its products as the solution to all of the entertainment industry’s issues, the AI industry needs Hollywood more than Hollywood needs more slop.

title: GoPro to be acquired for $285M, will remain a public company
snippet: GoPro is merging with a company that builds AI infrastructure, and will continue supporting existing consumer products.
fullText:
After years of financial struggles, action camera pioneer GoPro is being acquired for $285 million.

A company called Starman Optical has agreed to merge with GoPro. The deal involves Starman Optical paying GoPro shareholders $1.14 per share and leaving those shareholders with about 10% of the newly combined company. The deal, expected to close by the end of this year, will wipe away GoPro’s outstanding debt of $92 million.

The merger, announced Tuesday morning, comes a few months after GoPro revealed it was considering pivoting from building cameras to becoming a defense tech company. A day or so ago, YouTuber Markiplier revealed he had amassed an 8.5% stake in GoPro.

That appears to still be in the cards, as the company said the merger will “maximize the value of GoPro’s IP and growth potential in consumer, commercial and defense markets by recapitalizing the company, strengthening its balance sheet, investing in growth and onshoring the manufacturing of products for strategic markets.”

GoPro will also “fully support” its existing consumer products while “investing in growth and a broader, diversified product roadmap.”

It’s not exactly clear what all that means, and Starman Optical doesn’t have a significant track record to judge its performance.

The company bills itself as an “optical-photonics company focused on the development and domestic manufacturing of optical transceivers and related photonics technologies through its Starman New Photonics business.” Both Starman Optical and Starman New Photonics are part of Starman Holding, which owns consumer tech brands like Incase, Incipio, and Griffin.

Starman Optical was only incorporated in Delaware on August 31, while Starman New Photonics appears to have been created in 2025 and is building a manufacturing facility in New Jersey.

“Advanced optics and imaging are essential to AI, national security, and the broader economy, yet much of the critical hardware supporting these technologies continues to be manufactured overseas,” Charles Tebele, the CEO of Starman Holdings, said in a statement. “The combination of GoPro’s world-class optical expertise and intellectual property with Starman’s advanced transceiver capabilities and U.S. manufacturing platform creates a unique opportunity. Together, we intend to bring production of these critical components back to the United States.”

GoPro went public in 2014, when its action cameras were selling millions of units per year. In the decade since, the company tried branching into new categories like drones and 360-degree cameras, but it didn’t find much luck with either. GoPro then refocused on high-performing versions of its action cameras, and kept them targeted at pros, prosumers, and athletes, but it had to conduct multiple rounds of layoffs as it narrowed the business.

In June, GoPro warned shareholders that it may go out of business without new funding. The following month, founder and CEO Nick Woodman said he was putting $20 million into the business to keep things going.

“We expect this merger to enable GoPro to grow across consumer, commercial and defense markets as a leading American imaging and optical solutions company, addressing important areas of national security related to cameras, optics and AI infrastructure. We’re excited to combine with the Starman team to capitalize on this opportunity and play an important role in America’s future,” Woodman said in a statement.

title: OpenAI faces 30 more lawsuits tied to Tumbler Ridge shooting
snippet: Edelson PC is filing 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI over the Tumbler Ridge shooting, escalating claims to aiding and abetting and naming Chris Lehane, though evidence remains unconfirmed.
fullText:
Edelson PC, the law firm that filed seven lawsuits against OpenAI in April on behalf of victims and families connected to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, is filing 30 additional complaints this week. The new plaintiffs include teachers, a principal, and students who were in the building during the attack but not physically shot. 

The new filings also, for the first time, accuse OpenAI of aiding and abetting the mass shooting, rather than just negligently failing to prevent it. That claim requires proving intent from OpenAI and is likely to face early dismissal challenges.

The complaints come as OpenAI continues to deal with the fallout of another high-profile safety incident after one of the company’s AI models escaped its sandbox during cybersecurity evaluations and hacked into the servers of Hugging Face’, a company that hosts open-source AI models and datasets. OpenAI has also faced several lawsuits alleging that ChatGPT’s design contributed to users’ suicides, violent acts, and severe mental health crises.

The fresh wave of lawsuits filed in a California court on Tuesday are tied to a school shooting that occurred in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada on February 10. That day, teenager Jesse Van Rootselaar killed her mother and half-brother at home, then went to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed six more people and injured dozens of others before dying by suicide. 

The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI staff had been alarmed by VanRootselaar’s use of ChatGPT, including conversations around gun violence and advice for how to plan an attack. OpenAI employees reportedly urged leaders to alert Canadian law enforcement about Van Rootselaar’s potential for real-world violence, but leaders decided not to contact the authorities. Instead the company deactivated Van Rootselaar’s account, but she was able to make another one shortly after. 

OpenAI has justified its actions, claiming Van Rootselaar’s activity didn’t meet the company’s internal bar for an “imminent and credible risk” of serious physical harm to others required to engage with law enforcement. 

“That judgment is not infallible, but it is always rooted in looking out for this balance for people,” Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer who oversees the team of human reviewers and the company’s legal department, said in a statement shared with TechCrunch.

The new set of complaints specifically name OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer Chris Lehane as the person who told staff to stand down and not contact the authorities, though the complaints offer no direct evidence that he was personally involved, and OpenAI has denied his involvement.

Lehane is a well-known political operator and PR spin master with particular expertise in damage control, having worked in that capacity on behalf of the Clinton administration, at Airbnb, and now at OpenAI. The plaintiffs allege that his background contributes to a culture at OpenAI that prioritizes public relations and damage control over safety. 

“The Intelligence and Investigations Team—the only team inside OpenAI responsible for identifying ChatGPT users who pose a threat of real-world violence—was placed under [Lehane’s] control,” reads  one of the complaints, shared with TechCrunch. “As a result, the decision whether to alert law enforcement to a user planning a mass attack was not made by the trained threat-assessment professionals who urged OpenAI to contact the [Canadian police]. It was made, on information and belief, by Lehane himself, or by someone in his chain of command, and ratified by Sam Altman.”

“On information and belief” is a legal term meaning the plaintiffs believe a claim to be true based on secondhand information, even though they can’t yet prove it directly. TechCrunch was unable to confirm whether Lehane indeed has the authority to override recommendations from the intelligence and investigations team, or whether he was involved in this specific case at all. Notably, Lehane is not listed as a defendant in the complaints, though, as in the previous seven complaints, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is.

“We are not laying out all of our evidence at this point,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer on the cases, told TechCrunch, noting that Lehane and Altman will be “critical witnesses” alongside the safety team. “We can tell you that we are basing this in part on the org chart, but also our broader investigation, which includes what we have learned about how Lehane operates within the company.”

“It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision, or that our investigators report to him in any way,” Kwon said. “It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.” 

The fresh complaints also seek to rebut OpenAI’s previous defense that it did not alert Canadian authorities to Van Rootselaar’s conversations with ChatGPT due to “imminence” and “privacy” justifications. The complaints point to an incident in November 2025, during which OpenAI locked down its San Francisco offices following an alleged threat from an activist. 

“Although OpenAI acknowledged there was ‘no indication of active threat activity’—and thus no indication of an ‘imminent’ attack—the company… immediately locked down its offices, warned employees, distributed the suspect’s name and photograph, and notified the San Francisco Police Department,” a complaint reads. 

“When its own people were at risk, no ‘privacy’ interest stopped OpenAI from notifying the police or circulating the man’s name and photograph to thousands of employees. Nor did it wait for the attack to become imminent because it recognized that waiting would jeopardize employee safety.”

Local AI development gets faster

Parallels Desktop 27 also adds support for Scalable Matrix Extension (SME2) instructions in Linux and Windows VMs on M4 and newer Macs. Wrap up

There’s a lot to like in Parallels Desktop 27 for everyone, depending on whether you are an engineer, developer, or gamer. So much of our ecosystem is either cross-platform or web-based, but when you need to run a Windows app on macOS, it’s never been better or felt more native. I know some customers don’t like the subscription model, but if you rely on running VMs on macOS, it’s worth the annual upgrade as it’s much more of a rolling development to match Apple’s latest features.

title: AI will be the defining test of Apple’s environmental commitments, says Greenpeace
snippet: Greenpeace says the adoption of AI poses the biggest threat to Apple’s environmental track record, and argues that how the company responds will be the “defining test” of whether it really means what it says. Apple’s environmental achievements to date have been unrivalled, but the massive data center demands created by Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features could change all of that … more…
fullText:
Greenpeace says the adoption of AI poses the biggest threat to Apple’s environmental track record, and argues that how the company responds will be the “defining test” of whether it really means what it says.

Apple’s environmental achievements to date have been unrivalled, but the massive data center demands created by Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features could change all of that … 

Greenpeace has praised Apple’s environmental initiatives for more than a decade now. That included a 2015 report on the company’s use of renewable energy to power data centers.

Apple continues to lead the charge in powering its corner of the internet with renewable energy even as it continues to rapidly expand. All three of its data center expansions announced in the past year will be powered with renewable energy. Apple is also having a positive impact on pushing major colocation providers to help it maintain progress toward its 100% renewable energy goal.

Just last year, Greenpeace East Asia gave the company a B+ grade for introducing more renewable energy in its supply chains.

However, as Apple finally launches Siri AI next month, that could all change. While the company aims to carry out as many tasks as possible on-device, it relies on large-scale data centres to perform more complex actions, and these consume a great deal of electricity and water. The Verge cites concerns expressed by Greenpeace spokesperson Avex Li.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Apple responded by pointing The Verge to its most recent environmental progress report, as well as past statements on the topic.

title: Galaxy S26 Ultra is the world’s most popular Android phone, and that’s a first
snippet: Android phones are never the top-selling smartphones globally, but the ones that get closest are almost always budget models. In Q2 2026, though, Samsung achieved a major win with the Galaxy S26 Ultra topping the charts as the best-selling Android phone globally. more…
fullText:
Android phones are never the top-selling smartphones globally, but the ones that get closest are almost always budget models. In Q2 2026, though, Samsung achieved a major win with the Galaxy 

S26 Ultra topping the charts as the best-selling Android phone globally.

Counterpoint Research details the top 10 best-selling smartphones globally in Q2 2026 with, shocker, three iPhones at the top. The base iPhone 17 topped the charts, followed by a duo of iPhone 17 Pro models. It’s basically identical to the same time in 2025, but with a key difference – they’re followed up by the Galaxy S26 Ultra instead of a budget device.

Where the Galaxy S25 Ultra barely broke into the top 10 last year, Samsung’s latest flagship beat out the budget-focused Galaxy A07 and A17 for that #4 spot. 

The Galaxy S26 series launched in late February, but the Ultra didn’t make it into Q1’s best-seller list, showing that a huge portion of Samsung’s sales came after the initial launch. Counterpoint explains:

	

The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra was the best-selling Android smartphone, marking the first time an ultra-premium Android device has led Android sales in a June quarter. Meanwhile, the later launch of the Galaxy S26 series compared with the Galaxy S25 series shifted more sales into Q2, the Galaxy S26 Ultra outperformed its predecessor and accounted for more than half of the series’ sales. Industry-first privacy display along with enhanced AI capabilities differentiate the smartphone from its peers. Samsung has further increased its focus on flagship smartphones, boosting promotions and strategically allocating resources to mitigate the revenue decline amid rising costs.

title: Google is making AI Overviews even bigger on some search queries
snippet: As AI continues to be a bigger and bigger part of Google Search, the company is making AI Overviews bigger on some searches. more…
fullText:
As AI continues to be a bigger and bigger part of Google Search, the company is making AI Overviews bigger on some searches.

Already placed above traditional search results, Google’s AI Overviews provide an AI-generated answer to your query, pulling that information from links around the web and placing some of those links within the answer. 

Now, those are getting bigger.

In some search queries, Google will automatically fully expand AI Overviews, effectively turning the whole page into an AI response rather than just taking up the very top of the page. The change was first spotted by Chris Long, and Google has confirmed the update to Search Engine Roundtable, saying:

	

For some queries, AI Overviews may dynamically expand for topics where our systems determine it’s most useful for people. Our research has shown that with this dynamic experience, users find Search more helpful and engage deeper in follow-up exploration.

One example of where this happens consistently is with definitions, where AI Overviews take up the entire screen.

title: FBI investigates as hackers sell digital scans of 153M drivers licenses
snippet: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more. The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … more…
fullText:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more.

The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … 

Krebs on Security was able to confirm the authenticity of the claim made by the cybercriminals as they were able to provide a scan of his own driving license, with other victims likewise confirming their scans were correct.

A new identity theft service [dubbed Nexus] launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada […] The people behind Nexus claim the license images are coming from an active breach at “a major identity verification company” whose customers include multiple Fortune 500 companies.

KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

The report says that the ID verification company appears to be one based in Louisiana. The criminals claim that they still have access to the source of these scans, a claim supported by their adding almost 400,000 new ones within the past 24 hours.

There are indications suggesting that at least some of the data was stolen from a verification service used by rental car company Hertz. The report points to a New Orleans-based company as a potential source, and that company’s client list includes Hertz, Target, Fedex, Motorola Solutions, Jack Henry, and Caesars Entertainment. There are many more details in the full report.

9to5Mac’s Take

The irony of criminals being able to hack an identity verification service in order to provide documents that can be used for identity theft would be amusing if it weren’t so serious. This type of breach is depressingly common.

It was recently estimated that online scams cost Americans almost $150 billion last year as the number of cyber scams continue to increase dramatically.

title: Unusual timing of Mac mini and Mac Studio updates all about AI, claims report
snippet: Apple surprised many when it quietly announced updated Mac mini and Mac Studio models shortly before its September event. We would normally have expected these announcements to be part of that event. One strong theory is that the company may be making a lot of big announcements in its ‘Surprise and shine‘ keynote, and therefore wanted to get these updates out of the way beforehand. But a new report presents another theory … more…
fullText:
Apple surprised many when it quietly announced updated Mac mini and Mac Studio models shortly before its September event. We would normally have expected these announcements to be part of that event.

One strong theory is that the company may be making a lot of big announcements in its ‘Surprise and shine‘ keynote, and therefore wanted to get these updates out of the way beforehand. But a new report presents another theory … 

Announcing the new Mac mini and Mac Studio models just a fortnight ahead of the September 9th event seemed surprising. Why not wait the extra couple of weeks and do it properly, rather than just via press releases?

The Information says that the decision was made because the company was taken by surprise by the level of demand for the models for AI applications, and with some configurations unavailable for months, Apple brought the announcements forward for this reason.

9to5Mac’s Take

There’s certainly no doubt that the power of Apple Silicon has made both the Mac mini and Mac Studio popular options for those wanting to run AI models locally. For example, we’ve seen researchers use Thunderbolt 5 to turn four Mac Studios into an extremely powerful AI cluster.

I can also believe that Apple did not initially predict the scale of demand this was going to generate.

What seems less likely, however, is the idea that two weeks makes any worthwhile difference to the situation. To me, it’s just too small a gap for this to be a credible explanation. Personally, I think the existing theory we outlined is the more likely one.

Apple will want to make a very big fuss about the launch of its first foldable iPhone and also ensure that the iPhone 18 Pro isn’t seen as an also-ran. If Apple does indeed unveil the HomePad smart home hub as we expect, that too will be a major announcement.

We then need to add in a new Apple TV and HomePod mini 2 – both with Siri AI capabilities – two new Apple Watch models, and potentially new AirPods too. That’s a lot of announcements for a single keynote, so I could absolutely understand wanting to launch the new Mac desktops beforehand.

What’s your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Android 17 boosts network security by hiding domain names, lets carriers disable 2G
snippet: Google is out with a blog post today recapping new network security measures in Android 17. more…
fullText:
Google is out with a blog post today recapping new network security measures in Android 17.

Even with HTTPS connections, the domain names of websites (including apps) are “still visible to network operators and eavesdroppers.” 

This unencrypted data can be used to build user profiles or, in the hands of malicious actors, leveraged for targeted phishing and scam campaigns.

Android 17 aims to resolve this with Encrypted Client Hello (ECH). Working with private DNS, this new privacy standard will “obscure the domain names you visit.” This works by hiding the “domain name using a secret encryption key that only the destination website can unscramble.”

By encrypting the destination website name from the very start, ECH helps ensure that, for supported websites and apps, network providers and network snoopers can no longer easily see which websites or apps you are accessing.

With OS support now available, app developers have to upgrade to OkHttp 5.5.0 and enable ECH.

	

Domain name data leaks in two places, (1) the initial DNS lookup and (2) the unencrypted ClientHello in the Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake. Recent progress with the rollout of encrypted DNS and the launch of support for Encrypted ClientHello on Android 17 are helping to make online activity more private

On the network front, Android 17 allows mobile carriers to turn off 2G connectivity by default for their users. (Android 12 first introduced this user setting.) This is intended to counter SMS blaster attacks that “force nearby smartphones to drop their LTE or 5G connections and downgrade to less secure, legacy 2G networks.” Phishing texts are then sent to devices.

Meanwhile, Android 17 enforces Local Network Protection wherein apps must now request permission “before they can scan or connect to other devices on your local network.”

For everyday tasks like casting a video to your TV, developers should adopt a secure system tool, which allows you to select your TV without the app ever needing permission to see the other devices in your home.

Finally, Certificate Transparency requires “all certificates to be logged in a public registry, making such an attack much less likely to go unnoticed.”

When you connect to a secure app or website, your device verifies a certificate to confirm the site is authentic. However, if a certificate issuer is compromised, hackers could potentially create fake certificates to intercept your traffic and cause harm.

title: Microsoft is enabling a Windows 11 security feature that can hurt gaming performance
snippet: Microsoft is getting ready to roll out its memory integrity security feature of Windows 11 to more devices next month. The kernel-level protection feature is designed to stop malicious code or drivers running on a Windows 11 machine, but Microsoft previously warned it can also impact PC gaming performance. "Windows quality updates will begin enabling memory integrity protection on eligible devices," says Peter Waxman, group program manager at Microsoft. "If not already enabled, these updates will also enable Virtualization-based Security (VBS), helping make additional security capabilities available and reflecting our commitment to making W … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Tom Warren

 

is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Microsoft is getting ready to roll out its memory integrity security feature of Windows 11 to more devices next month. The kernel-level protection feature is designed to stop malicious code or drivers running on a Windows 11 machine, but Microsoft previously warned it can also impact PC gaming performance.

“Windows quality updates will begin enabling memory integrity protection on eligible devices,” says Peter Waxman, group program manager at Microsoft. “If not already enabled, these updates will also enable Virtualization-based Security (VBS), helping make additional security capabilities available and reflecting our commitment to making Windows secure by design and secure by default.”

While memory integrity only allows trusted kernel-mode code and drivers to run on a Windows 11 system, it also impacts PC game performance on certain hardware. There’s less of an impact if you have a more modern CPU, but you might notice more of a frame-rate drop in select games on older processors. Microsoft won’t automatically enable memory integrity again next month if you’ve already previously disabled the feature.

If you want to check whether memory integrity is enabled on your Windows 11 PC, you can type “Core Isolation” into Windows search and then open the result and toggle memory integrity on or off in the Windows security app. If you decide to disable this security feature in favor of more PC gaming performance, Microsoft’s recommendation is to re-enable memory integrity after you’ve finished playing a game.
