title: Amazon Alexa can now alert you when something new might tempt you to shop
snippet: Amazon is adding a new Alexa-powered feature called “Update Me When” that can send personalized alerts about product launches, tours, books, shows, and other events that could trigger a purchase.
fullText:
Amazon continues to experiment with how AI can be used to improve the shopping experience, resulting in Tuesday’s launch of a new feature within its Alexa for Shopping AI assistant called “Update Me When.” This latest addition can send consumers personalized notifications when something new or relevant happens that could lead to a purchase.

For instance, Amazon suggests people could use the feature to track when a favorite brand launches a new product line, when a new season of a favorite TV show drops, when an artist they like announces a concert tour, when an author they read releases a new book, when a tech company releases a new product, and more.

The launch is one of several AI-powered shopping features that Amazon highlighted on Tuesday, many of which point to a broader shift in the company’s AI strategy. Historically, Alexa has mainly answered product questions when shoppers ask directly. Now it can help anticipate when something might prompt a user to make a purchase — before the shopper even thinks to ask.

While initially, consumers have to configure these alerts directly, it’s not hard to imagine a future where Amazon automatically generates alerts or may suggest alerts for shoppers to subscribe to as they browse favorite products.

Among the other Alexa for Shopping features, the most useful of these is the existing price-tracking feature that lets you ask the assistant to alert you when a product reaches a particular price or a certain discount percentage. The feature can even automatically buy the item for you if it meets these conditions, if you prefer.

The retailer has also been using Alexa to source personalized deals and create shopping guides, build carts with items from past purchases, track a product’s pricing history, and see AI overviews when searching for products or on the product detail pages, transcribe handwritten lists to add items to a cart, compare items, and more.

title: Dell Doubles Down on Cheap Student Laptops With Lower-End Dell 14S Configs
snippet: The big question remains: How much will they cost?
fullText:
Dell seemingly isn’t content with taking on Apple’s MacBook Neo with just the XPS 13 for student dollars and attention. On Wednesday the company brought in budget laptop reinforcements with new lower-end, more colorful versions of its mainstream Dell 14S laptop. Dell is playing coy and won’t reveal pricing until we get closer to seeing these new laptops later this fall, which is understandable given the volatility around the ongoing component shortages. 

While we await pricing details, here’s what we do know about these new machines. They’ll come in four fun Neo-esque colors, offer Intel Wildcat Lake processors and start with just 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. 

New Dell 14S models: Colorful and affordable

The Dell 14S isn’t new. Dell released the 14S series along with its larger 16S sibling back in May. These mainstream laptops are based on Intel Panther Lake processors and were priced north of $1,000. Currently, the cheapest Panther Lake Dell 14S model costs $1,350 (and that’s after a $50 discount).

The new Dell 14S models feature Wildcat Lake processors, which are less powerful, more efficient versions of Panther Lake. You’ll have a choice of either a Core 5 320 or Core 7 350, each of which is a six-core processor made up of two performance cores and four efficient cores. The popular Panther Lake chip, the Core Ultra 7 355, that Dell offers on the inaugural 14S is an eight-core chip with four performance and four efficiency cores. Wildcat Lake processors run at 15 watts with a turbo power limit of 35 watts, while Panther Lake operates at 25 watts with a max turbo power of 55 watts. 

So while you are giving up two performance cores in dropping down to Wildcat Lake, you are getting greater efficiency, which should result in longer battery life and quieter operation. Dell says you can expect all-day battery life from the relatively modest three-cell, 61-watt-hour battery.

The Dell 14S offers four color options, including a bold green.

Along with a choice between Core 5 and Core 7 Wildcat Lake processors, the Dell 14S offers a pair of 14-inch display options. Both are IPS panels, but one has a 2K resolution (1,920 by 1200 pixels), 60Hz refresh rate and 300-nit brightness rating, while the other has a finer 2.8K resolution (2,880 by 1,800 pixels), smoother 120Hz refresh rate and brighter 450-nit rating.

Like the XPS 13, the Dell 14S comes with 8GB or 16GB of RAM. Unless you plan to use your laptop for the lightest, most basic of tasks, you are probably better off spending more for 16GB of RAM. I tested both 8GB and 16GB versions of the XPS 13 and concluded that the 16GB model is worth Dell’s steep $200 upcharge for most people. Unlike the XPS 13, the Dell 14S starts off with an undersized 256GB SSD. That’ll fill up fast. Dell offers 512GB and 1TB storage upgrades.

The Dell 14S has a larger display than the 13.4-inch XPS 13 and weighs a bit more because of it. It weighs 2.5 pounds, and the trim XPS 13 is just 2.2 pounds. The 13-inch MacBook Neo is the heaviest of the three at 2.7 pounds. All three laptops offer all-metal designs, which is not a given among the budget class where all-plastic or partially plastic constructions aren’t uncommon.

The Dell 14S has a better port selection than the XPS 13. It has the same pair of 10Gbps USB-C ports as the XPS 13 but also adds an HDMI port and headphone jack.

The Dell 14S in dusty rose looks strikingly similar to the blush color Apple offers for its MacBook Neo.

I really liked the XPS 13, but one of my complaints was targeting it toward students and then not offering any of the fun colors that Apple does with the Neo. With the Dell 14S, you get four color options that rival the cheerful hues Apple offers for the Neo. There’s dusty rose (a soft pink), washed denim (a light blue), velvet green (a bold green and my favorite of the bunch, based on Dell’s photos) and linen (a beige-y gold).

How low can Dell 14S pricing go?

It’s difficult to form too firm an opinion of the Dell 14S before we get pricing for it, but it will face steep competition from Apple’s MacBook Neo and Dell’s own XPS 13 when it’s released later this fall. 

With their premium designs and high-resolution displays, both the Neo and XPS 13 are excellent budget options at their discounted student prices starting at $600. The upgraded Neo with more storage and Touch ID at $700 and the upgraded XPS 13 with more memory at $800 are also great buys with their student discounts. 

The Dell 14S will need to limbo below those low bars to add a competitive third option for the school set.

title: Mammotion Luba 3 changed my mind about robot lawnmowers
snippet: Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models. more…
fullText:
Robot lawnmowers have long intrigued me, but I never really wanted one. After a few weeks with the Mammotion Luba 3, though, I’m sold, because this fixed my biggest issue with other models.

I’m all for smart home advancements, but a robot lawnmower was one I was never really a fan of. I like mowing my lawn, crazy as that sounds, and leaving that to a robot felt like more set up and maintain than it was going to be worth. Inevitably, though, curiosity won over. When Mammotion sent over the Luba 3 AWD mower, my attitude flipped.

The main reason for that boils down to how this mower operates. Unlike many others, which require the use of a boundary perimeter or RTK base station, the Mammotion Luba 3 operates with what’s called a “NetRTK,” which is effectively just a highly accurate satellite positioning system combined with LiDAR.

The results here really blew me away. 

	

After mapping the robot to the areas of my yard I wanted it to work on, it stayed nearly perfectly within those lines, to the point where I actually had to go back and redo the lines. Initially, I’d set up several feet of buffer zone between the mower and the fairly-busy road in front of my lawn for fear that, if the positioning shifted, the mower might risk getting run over. The first two runs showed how misplaced that fear was. It hit its lines almost perfectly, which left plenty of room for me to adjust those lines much closer to the road. There’s still a small buffer, but I now know I can trust that Luba 3 isn’t going to go rogue into the road. It’s not without hiccups. Another part of the yard with a ditch left the mower stuck a couple of times when the positioning was off by a few inches, and a tough-to-access area of the property also proved tricky. But in most cases, it goes off without a hitch.

It’s all managed through the app, where you use a virtual joystick to set up a map and the pathways the mower can use to get to various zones, including crossing over driveways or perhaps portions of your neighbor’s lawn. The same app can be used to set schedules, view progress, and even watch a first-person-view of the mower’s main camera as it runs through your yard.

Taking a step back, the initial setup is an absolute breeze. Assembly and setup took around 30 minutes, with the included tools making it easy to attach the front bumper and side covers. 

Luba 3 has a docking station in the box that just needs a power outlet in the vicinity, with a generous length of cable included. You want a fairly level location for this, but I’ve found that even my slightly uneven and unstable mulch base works well enough. I’ve only had one occasion where it didn’t fully seat for charging in several weeks of use. You do get a physical RTK base station in the box but, really, you don’t need it unless you’re in some very specific circumstances. 

Like most robot mowers, grass is cut using some fairly small blades underneath, and this also makes the whole thing feel safer. Not only is there a giant “STOP” button at the top, but the blades themselves won’t be able to do nearly as much damage as a real mower would.

The physical hardware is huge, easily 2-3x the size of a robot vacuum, and it turns heads. My dogs still go crazy every time they see this in the yard, and I always see neighbors and drivers passing by turn to look when Luba 3 is out in the front. But it’s not an eyesore either. The white finish shows all dirt and dust that’s kicked up – most of the pictures in this post are after about two weeks without a wipedown – but it’s a sensible color choice as it rejects heat. It is heavy at 41lbs, but that’s totally managable for the rare occasions where you need to move it manually.

How’s the actual mowing performance? 

Good, but not perfect.

Luba 3 thankfully cuts at up to 3.9-inches in height, which matters to me. Overly short grass is how you kill a lawn in a hot summer, so it was nice to see Mammotion offers the right amount of height to keep everything fairly healthy. Whether sending it off into a thick lawn or one that’s mostly been scorched by the heat and drought of the North Carolina summer I’ve been living in, Luba 3 gets the job done well. The cut is fairly even with only the occasional straggler blade left behind, particularly when cutting at maximum height or when running it less frequently. This benefits great from running on a regular basis rather than the “as needed” schedule you’d use with a traditional mower.

It also handles slopes like a champ, with it able to cover my steep front lawn and some other raised portions of the yard without skipping a beat. Mammotion says it can handle a slope of up to 38.6-degrees with its all-wheel-drive setup. There are a couple of spots in my lawn where I can tell there’s some dead grass from Luba’s tracks, but I’ll mostly blame that on the local conditions. In some particularly uneven parts of my lawn, I do need to go back with my push mower or weed-eater, but Luba 3 really takes the bulk of the work off of my plate – complete with stripes in the finished yard.

I do think that’s an important note to make. Mammotion’s Luba 3, and really any robot lawnmower, isn’t going to fully end your yard work. There are certain sections you’ll need to do yourself, especially with regard to weeds and edging along the sides. There are options that aim to solve this, but you’ll still inevitably need to do cleanup here and there. 

But most weeks, this cuts my mowing time from an hour or two to just a few minutes – a couple of passes along the road, checking for spots it might have missed, and then weed-eating around the driveway and fence.

As for battery life, the 0.75-acre model I’ve been testing can run for about two hours before it takes a break to recharge, but that’s largely due to the hills it has to deal with. Mammotion says that, under ideal conditions, it can run for up to 215 minutes (about 3.5 hours).

Another point in favor of its navigation, too, is that it can easily handle jumping around to different portions of the yard. Zones are easy to set up and can make it easy to mow different areas at different times, or juggle things like fences. Part of my yard is gated, so having a specific zone I can run just when the gate is open is a really handy option.

All-in-all, Mammotion really changed my mind about robot lawnmowers. Luba 3 works like a charm and addresses every complaint I thought I’d have about setup, navigation, and cutting performance. 

Really, the only tough part left is price.

Mammotion Luba 3 AWD starts at $2,399 in the US, which is not cheap. But this is also on the bleeding edge and, in a world where time is money, might be worthwhile for anyone who just can’t seem to keep up with their lawn. It saves so much time.

title: OpenAI’s Astra model is on the way — and very good at breaking into computer systems
snippet: OpenAI previewed the precautions it is taking as it prepares to release Astra, its newest, cyber-critical LLM.
fullText:
OpenAI shared new details on its forthcoming Astra model, which the company said is the first large language model to meet its “critical cybersecurity threshold,” in preparation for its imminent release.

“We plan to make Astra available soon,” OpenAI’s blog post reads, “but access to its most advanced cybersecurity capabilities will be more limited.”

The frontier lab determined that Astra is capable of finding unknown security flaws in computer systems, and exploiting them without a person’s guidance. That’s similar to the concerns Anthropic raised about its Mythos model earlier this year, and OpenAI is taking comparable precautions as it prepares to roll out the Astra.

Without any third-party confirmation, it is difficult to evaluate OpenAI’s claims about safety or preparedness. The company said it would preview the model with a group of testers but did not say who they were or how they would be chosen. It’s not clear if OpenAI is working with the U.S. government to evaluate the model ahead of release.

OpenAI noted that Astra scored a perfect score on ExploitBench, an evaluation of an LLM’s ability to hack into known system vulnerabilities. In a modified version of the test developed by OpenAI engineers, the model  discovered and exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities, the company said.

To ensure that its models are neither exploited by bad actors nor capable of bad behavior itself, OpenAI said it had already begun improving the model’s harness to detect abuses and prevent jailbreaks. 

For Astra, however, the company invested in unspecified new techniques designed to make the model safer. OpenAI has also started identifying “accounts assessed as higher risk” and restricting the model’s responses to their prompts, though it also doesn’t say how. Finally, though the company describes Astra as its “most aligned model to date,” it will deploy the model with additional chain-of-thought monitoring to spot and stop bad behavior.

Preparations for the release of Astra come as the industry reacts to OpenAI agents breaking out of a training environment and accessing private data on Hugging Face, a popular model and benchmark distribution platform.

For Astra, OpenAI said it designed a test to tempt the new model to replicate the actions of the rogue agents in the Hugging Face incident, which collaborated to access the open internet despite safeguards applied by OpenAI researchers. They said Astra did not attempt to break out of its testing environment in these experiments.

Yona Shavit, a former OpenAI employee who now works on AI resilience at the OpenAI Foundation, wondered on social media whether Astra’s unwillingness to break the rules may have resulted from knowing what was expected of it or trying to fool researchers.

And for all these new details, it’s still difficult to know exactly what Astra is capable of or if OpenAI is taking the right measures to ensure safety. The company said it expects to release more evaluations of the model and further safety information when it is launched widely to the public.

At that point, however, the cat will be out of the bag.

title: Anthropic’s new Fable release is cheaper, less restrictive
snippet: Fable 5.1 includes changes meant to reduce token cost and false-positive restrictions from the model's safeguards.
fullText:
On Tuesday, Anthropic released Fable and Mythos 5.1, twinned versions of the company’s most advanced AI model. In addition to performance upgrades, the new Fable release includes changes meant to reduce token cost and false-positive restrictions from the model’s safeguards.

As with the previous Mythos model, Mythos 5.1 will only be available to registered Anthropic partners engaged in either cybersecurity or life sciences research. Fable 5.1, the unrestricted version, is available starting today on cloud platforms or through the Anthropic API.

One of the most significant changes is Anthropic’s previously reported embrace of zero data retention, allowing clients to run Anthropic models on their own infrastructure without data outflows. Previously unavailable for Fable due to security concerns, a high-privacy service (called Enterprise Frontier Safeguards) will now roll out to users in the fall. Notably, the system will still monitor for misuse by agents or human users, but clients will control how the monitoring takes place.

As part of the announcement, Anthropic assured customers that their data had not been inappropriately accessed. “Anthropic has never trained on enterprise data without explicit permission, and never will,” the announcement reads.

As is common for an Anthropic release, the new models set records in a range of benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench 4.0 (for CLI-based coding) and Humanity’s Last Exam (for general reasoning). Anthropic also released three novel scientific findings generated by the models before their release, including a custom GPU optimization and a high-resolution map of Venus assembled from existing photos.

As with previous releases, the models come with a detailed system card, which explains their capabilities in most straightforward terms. The system card rates Mythos as “low-risk” for concerns related to automated AI development — where the AI improves itself — which some see as a trigger for a loss of human control. It says “its ability to accelerate internal AI R&D progress is in line with current trends.”

In terms of general misbehavior, Mythos is slightly more prone to it than Opus, possibly as a result of its enhanced capabilities.

“Mythos 5.1 is a slight regression on overall misaligned behavior compared to Opus 5, and an improvement over Mythos 5 and Claude Sonnet 5,” the system card reads. “It cooperates with human misuse and accepts unverifiable claims of authorization somewhat more readily than Opus 5, but it is less likely to ignore explicit constraints, hallucinate inputs, or falsely claim to have completed tasks than previous models.”

title: John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO: Here’s the latest
snippet: Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make. more…
fullText:
Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make.

Luca Maestri

Bloomberg reports that Luca Maestri is stepping down as Apple’s “Corporate Services” leader. Maestri served as Apple CFO until January 2025, when he stepped down to take on a smaller role. As head of Corporate Services, Maestri oversaw information systems and technology, information security, and real estate and development.

According to today’s report, Maestri left that job “in recent weeks.” He is, however, still on Apple’s payroll. His only remaining responsibility is “hosting a popular class at Apple University, an in-house program for teaching Apple’s ways to rising executives and employees.”

Bloomberg says that Maestri’s Corporate Services tasks have been shifted to CFO Kevan Parekh.

Adrian Perica

Mark Gurman points out that Apple’s new Leadership page excludes Adrian Perica, its head of mergers and acquisitions.

Apple’s new leadership page also excludes Adrian Perica, the company’s head of mergers and acquisitions. It remains unclear where he will shift within Apple. Bloomberg reported on Sunday that he would likely be dropped by Ternus as a direct report and could split his responsibilities across Apple’s services and finance teams.

It’s possible this signals a change to Apple’s strategy for mergers and acquisitions. Some analysts expect Ternus to be more aggressive in making bigger acquisitions.

A change to how Apple manages outgoing executives

Gurman also says that “people in and around Apple” expect Ternus to change how the company handles outgoing executives. While Cook made a habit of retaining executives in smaller roles, like Maestri, Gurman says “Ternus may be less likely to continue using this approach.”

More tidbits

Ternus officially joined X today, and his first tweet was an all-lowercase “hello” with no punctuation. The post was quoted by marketing exec Greg Joswiak, who wrote: “Hello, indeed. More to say September 9.”

Gurman says Apple is hosting an event at Apple Park today “to introduce John Ternus as its new CEO to employees and to again celebrate Tim Cook’s tenure.”

Laura Legros, a former Apple VP who Ternus recruited out of retirement last month, will reportedly serve in a “Chief of Staff” style role. Cook did not have a person like this around him, according to Gurman.

title: Are We There Yet? Startup Wants to Launch an 80,000-Year Mission to Alpha Centauri
snippet: AI data centers in space apparently weren’t enough, so the company decided to give interstellar travel a try.
fullText:
A group of executives and entrepreneurs led by Starcloud co-founders Philip Johnston, Adi Oltean and Ezra Feilden teamed up to develop humanity’s first interstellar spacecraft. If everything goes according to plan, it will launch in 2029, headed for Alpha Centauri, the closest star system to our solar system. But it won’t reach its destination for about 80,000 years. 

Known as Fermi Explorer, this non-profit mission aims to build a 10cm cube weighing about 1 kilogram (about 2.2 pounds). Once the cube is built, they plan to attach it to a propulsion system, take it to space and launch it toward Alpha Centauri. It’s the technological equivalent of taking a hefty rock into space, throwing it at Alpha Centauri and waiting for it to get there. 

“The mission is intended to make the idea of interstellar travel real, and to encourage more people to confront one of humanity’s biggest unanswered questions when we look beyond our planet,” the group said in a post on X. The post is accompanied by a video showing the Fermi Explorer being overtaken by hundreds of faster spacecraft also bound for Alpha Centauri.

The wait for this mission to go interstellar is unreal. The exact wait to mission completion is 79,800 years, according to the Fermi Explorer mission calculator, which means once this thing gets underway, it won’t be the problem of anyone currently living, or anyone else, for a few thousand generations. 

Just getting out of the solar system will take longer than any road trip any human has ever taken. The spacecraft is expected to circle the sun for 12 years in an oval orbit. The boosters will fire when the spacecraft gets closer to the sun, a process called the Oberth maneuver, thereby gaining speed through multiple orbits as it approaches escape velocity. Once done, it’ll launch itself and keep going, and going, and going. The Fermi Explorer’s technical feasibility assessment says it should leave the solar system by the early 2040s. 

It’s quite a different mission from what Starcloud’s co-founders usually work on: putting data centers in space to power AI. The company plans to launch its first such full commercial data center, called the Starcloud-2, in 2027, but it did send an Nvidia H100 GPU into space via Starcloud-1 in 2025.

More symbolic than scientific

We hope they packed enough snacks, because that’s one long road trip.Fermi Explorer

Interstellar travel takes so long that humanity has focused far more on speeding up the journey than actually making it. One of the big projects addressing this was Breakthrough Starshot, a multi-billion-dollar initiative that would’ve used laser-based propulsion to propel a ship to another star in a matter of decades rather than millennia. That project collapsed in 2025 with no launches. 

The only other interstellar missions ever conducted, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, entered interstellar space in 2012 and 2018, respectively, over four decades after their launches. 

According to the non-profit group, the purpose of the Fermi Explorer is to just toss something into the cosmos and see what happens. It sounds silly, but it’s the truth. The group’s thinking is based on the Fermi Paradox, which seeks to explain why there are so many stars and planets yet no signs of extraterrestrial life. 

One potential reason is the Fermi Great Filter, which suggests a barrier so hard to cross that intelligent life rarely survives long enough to be detected.

There are dozens of potential filters, ranging from the various steps of abiogenesis — the natural process by which life arises from non-living matter — to technological filters such as the inability to get into space, or, once there, the lack of motivation to search beyond a species’ host star. 

“By launching the Fermi Explorer mission, we can for the first time tick two possible Fermi Great Filters off the list,” the group wrote on its website. “That it is impossible for an intelligent species to leave their nearest stars (and) that all intelligent species decide not to leave their home star for some reason.”

The goal is to fund and build this entire project for about $15 million, using existing technology and piggybacking on a commercial rocket, such as SpaceX’s, to reach orbit. This project exists only to prove that humans can and are willing to do it, even if it’s something no one alive today is ever going to witness.

title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
snippet: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API. more…
fullText:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour. 

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

title: Sonos unveils ‘Sonos 27’ software with four new features
snippet: Today alongside launching two new products, Sonos has unveiled ‘Sonos 27’ branding for its software platform and detailed four new features coming soon for Sonos users. more…
fullText:
Today alongside launching two new products, Sonos has unveiled ‘Sonos 27’ branding for its software platform and detailed four new features coming soon for Sonos users.

Here are four new ‘Sonos 27’ features launching this fall

Sonos has launched Sonos Ace Ultra headphones today alongside a Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar. And in addition to the new hardware introductions, the company has rebranded its software.

‘Sonos 27’ is the official name of the Sonos software platform that already exists, but is getting a proper name starting today. More than just a rebrand though, Sonos announced four new software features coming this fall to Sonos users:

Portable surrounds

Personal listening

Sonos 27voice

Sonos MCP

Portable surrounds

Turn two compatible portable speakers into wireless rear surrounds for movie night — then move them right back to wherever they usually live when the credits roll. No wires, no permanent setup, no rearranging furniture.

Personal listening, without missing a beat

Headphone linking which is available in Early Access, allows you to seamlessly move audio between Sonos Ace Ultra and a compatible Sonos speaker or group streaming over the same WiFi connection with just the press of a button. You will also be able to pick and control your music on your headphones directly in the Sonos app while on your home network. For more information, read our support article here.

The new Sonos voice experience

Sonos 27voice is a new way to ask for music, built specifically for that purpose in the home, and the shortest path from wanting a song to hearing it. Instead of remembering exact commands, you can ask the way you’d talk to someone in the room with you. Say things like “Play that song I had on in the kitchen last night,” or “Put on something downstairs that the kids will like.” The system works out the rest.

Control Sonos with the AI you already use

Sonos has always been an open platform. Sonos MCP expands it. Sonos MCP connects your system to frontier large language models (LLMs), so you can control Sonos from familiar chatbot interfaces and mix advanced dialog and reasoning with out-loud listening on your speakers.

You can find full details on these new Sonos 27 features, including specific availability and early access, on Sonos’ website.

title: Pixel 11 Pro bug causing static sounds in recordings while using Video Boost, fix coming [U]
snippet: Google continues to improve on video quality with each new Pixel release, but a bug on the Pixel 11 Pro series causes static audio issues when using the Video Boost feature. more…
fullText:
Google continues to improve on video quality with each new Pixel release, but a bug on the Pixel 11 Pro series causes static audio issues when using the Video Boost feature.

Update 9/1: In a statement, Google says that a fix is officially coming for this problem and will roll out via a Camera app update “in the coming weeks.”

We have identified the cause and developed a software fix that will rollout to users in the coming weeks via the Camera app. Additionally, further performance optimizations will be included in an upcoming monthly Android update.

Video Boost first launched on the Pixel 8 Pro back in 2023, delivering major improvements to video quality after adding in some powerful cloud processing. The feature works by uploading your footage to Google’s servers where advanced models can improve the quality quite drastically. It’s still a Pro-only feature, though.

On Pixel 11 devices, though, there’s a problem with static audio when using Video Boost.

	

Users noticed the problem last week and the reports just keep coming in. A video shared on Reddit shows the problem clearly, with static bursts every few seconds during the recording. It’s very obvious and almost sounds like a Bluetooth device that’s just at the edge of its range. Several have chimed in on the thread saying they’ve run into the exact same issue.  

A potential temporary fix for this seems to be clearing the cache on the Google Camera app and/or turning off Audio Zoom, but it sounds like Google is aware of the problem.

title: John Ternus just revealed his priorities in first introduction as Apple CEO
snippet: John Ternus is officially Apple’s CEO starting today, and his new bio page on Apple’s website reveals some of Ternus’s key priorities, as noted by Myke Hurley. more…
fullText:
John Ternus is officially Apple’s CEO starting today, and his new bio page on Apple’s website reveals some of Ternus’s key priorities, as noted by Myke Hurley.

John Ternus’s new Apple bio signals his priorities on day one as CEO

Today Apple updated its leadership page with John Ternus’s new title as CEO.

Alongside the leadership refresh, Ternus’s official bio has been updated and expanded too.

As noted by Myke Hurley at The Enthusiast, the new bio highlights three key narratives around Ternus’s time at Apple and the work that he cares deeply about. And two of those narratives are based on an all-new bio addition.

While the bio partly carries over details that were there before, there’s one brand new paragraph quoted below. From Apple’s website:

John has led much of the company’s focus in areas like reliability and durability, introducing new techniques that have made Apple products remarkably resilient. He has also driven much of Apple’s innovation in materials and hardware design that have reduced the carbon footprint of its products, including the creation of a new recycled aluminum compound that has been introduced across multiple product lines, the use of 3D-printed titanium in Apple Watch Ultra, and advancements in reparability that have increased the life spans of several Apple products.

This is the only entirely new paragraph. The rest of the bio either remains the same as before, or has been reworded but with the core message unchanged.

The new paragraph takes up nearly half the length of the whole bio, which is relatively brief overall.

As a result, this one paragraph is a strong indicator of priorities that matter a lot to Ternus, and that he wants to specifically highlight as he starts his CEO role.

To sum up the paragraph, Ternus cares about hardware “reliability and durability,” and “innovation in materials and hardware design,” with the goal of a reduced carbon footprint and increased product lifespans.

We’re seen a big emphasis from Tim Cook on reducing Apple’s carbon footprint. Ternus is clearly signaling that will continue under his leadership. But this paragraph also emphasizes that Ternus is an innovator in hardware design, and aims to create products that last for many years.

title: YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required
snippet: Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube. more…
fullText:
Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube.

As described in an announcement post on the YouTube support forums, Google is rolling out some big changes to how YouTube on your smartphone interacts with your television. The company is describing your device as a “companion” now, even ditching the classic Cast icon for something a little more generic. It’s a change that, based on Reddit threads, seemingly entered testing earlier in 2026, and is now ready for a full rollout. 

It’s not just a new way to describe pairing your devices, though. With this refresh, casting videos from your phone to a television now sounds like it has a whole lot less friction, thanks in part to a shift on completely relying on account-based management. These changes include:

No longer requiring both devices to be on a shared Wi-Fi network to cast. Instead, users will need to be signed in on the same account on both devices.

The ability to like videos, leave comments, and subscribe to channels while the video plays in the background.

The option to consume YouTube Shorts content on your phone while a different, full-length video plays on your television.

A built-in “Play on different device” option found within the menu button on every video listed in your homepage feed.

There are, of course, some caveats to these upgrades, and it primarily revolves around the shift to forcing account-based pairing between devices. While this should work wonders for private viewing sessions — i.e., casting a video from your own phone to your own television to watch either independently or with someone else in the room — it’s unclear if this completely removes the ability to cast over Wi-Fi, something that’s genuinely useful in larger gatherings with multiple participants. That’s a pretty common use case for watching YouTube on a television, so I’m hoping generic Cast support continues to exist in this format. Otherwise, this feels like a particularly anti-social change from Google.

	

Generally, though, these are all steps in the right direction, taking a lot of the existing Cast elements and simply streamlining them for a more modern second-screen experience. That “Play on different device” option, for example, appears to be pretty similar to the current casting menu, but won’t require you to begin playing a video on your phone prior to beaming it to your TV. Personally, browsing Shorts while watching a full-length video on your television sounds pretty overwhelming to me, but it’s certainly Google meeting modern viewers where they’re already at.

Today’s announcement did not include a specific rollout window, but it does sound like it’ll be coming to a mobile device near you very, very soon.

title: Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Fable 5.1 model, details here
snippet: In June, Anthropic first released Fable 5, its Mythos-class AI model for Claude. Three months later, Anthropic is enhancing Claude with its new Fable 5.1 model upgrade. more…
fullText:
In June, Anthropic first released Fable 5, its Mythos-class AI model for Claude. Three months later, Anthropic is enhancing Claude with its new Fable 5.1 model upgrade.

Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 arrive today

In Anthropic’s world, Fable is Claude’s most capable model. Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus are the small, medium, and large models below Fable. 

“Claude Fable 5.1 sets a new standard on coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks,” Anthropic says. The company says the new model has a higher level of performance compared to Fable 5.

Anthropic also says Fable 5.1 “achieves similar or better results than Fable 5 at a much lower cost” when set to low or medium effort.

More from Anthropic below:

Fable 5.1 avoids shortcuts that result in poorer-quality work, and it’s smart enough to fix the root causes of software issues. For example, in testing by the investment firm Millennium, Fable 5.1 found the cause of a rare crash on their internal systems that none of their engineers (or any other model) had been able to explain after several years of trying.

In addition to Fable 5.1, Anthropic is also releasing Mythos 5.1 for users with Mythos access.

“Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 are the same model, but with different levels of safeguards,” Anthropic explains. “Fable 5.1 is generally available, while Mythos 5.1 is available only through our trusted access programs; its safeguards are specifically designed to support work in cybersecurity and the life sciences.”

Here’s pricing data for Fable 5.1:

Fable 5.1 will cost an estimated 25% less than Fable 5 for typical workloads, wherever usage is billed by token. This is because we’re reducing our pricing on cache reads (where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored). For highly agentic work, the savings will often be much larger—up to approximately 45%.

In terms of pricing, Anthropic says it has “reduced the price of Fable 5.1’s cache reads (where the model reuses context it has already processed) wherever usage is billed by token, such as on our API.” The company says this “leads to a substantial reduction in the overall cost of running the model.” Pricing is otherwise unchanged from Fable 5.

You can learn much more in the announcement post here.

title: Runway’s New AI Model Creates Digital Worlds Without Code
snippet: The company calls Solaris an interface world model.
fullText:
The AI company Runway has unveiled a new type of AI model it’s calling an interface world model, allowing you to create interactive websites and more by directly interfacing with elements on screen. 

Announced on Monday, the new model, named Solaris, doesn’t require hard programming knowledge to create something new, potentially opening up a new world of design possibilities for those without typical coding skills. This isn’t vibe coding, though — this is live rendering in a way we haven’t seen before. 

Runway makes this novel model work by combining reasoning and rendering. Solaris itself generates the interface frame by frame, while a language model “determines how that interface evolves.” The combination of the two enables real-time environments that adapt to how you interact with them.

Solaris generates digital environments in real time, frame by frame, creating applications or other interfaces. When you click on or drag an element, the model will treat these interactions as conditioning signals to generate additional frames. It really needs to be seen to be believed, and if it works as well as some of the demo videos do, we may be at a point where effortless design is within reach for everyone. 

	

			

Since the model is entirely visual, there are a lot of interesting things you can do with it. Runway gives the example of using an image of yourself as a reference point in a clothing store, where you would simply click on a new shirt on the clothing rack and drag it onto you to see how it looks. This isn’t the first time we’ve seen AI help you try on clothes, but it’s very different from what we’ve seen from Google. 

You can also provide text-based prompt instructions, like asking to change the color of an object or move an element in a photo somewhere else. 

	

			

Solaris essentially feels like a livestreaming video that constantly changes in response to user interaction.

AI world models are expected to be the next big thing, and Solaris is one of the fruits of this next frontier. World models extend themselves beyond the realms of a typical large language model as they’re built to translate and transform our physical world. 

The announcement did not specify when Solaris would be available to customers, and Runway did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Google Wallet for Android adds 11th digital state ID, first addition in 10 months
snippet: After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android. more…
fullText:
After a 10-month pause, Google Wallet is now rolling out support for Ohio state IDs on Android.

Open the Google Wallet app, tap the ‘plus’ button next to “View more” at the bottom, IDs & personal info, and then Driver’s license or state ID. This reveals Ohio as the 12th Google Wallet option. It joins Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, and Puerto Rico.

The card design shows the Northern Cardinal, which is Ohio’s state bird.

The set-up process requires taking photos of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of your face for verification that gets sent to the OH BMV. This review can take a few minutes with a notification confirming once it’s available. You’ll also get an email confirmation from the state agency.

	

First, tap on the reader or scan your QR code: Your personal info won’t be shared yet. On your phone, review what info you want to share.

Next, review what info will be shared: Make sure you’re comfortable sharing the info they request

You don’t need to hand your phone to anyone: Your ID will be securely shared using Bluetooth, so make sure it’s on

Lastly, verify it’s you to share your info: For extra security, verify that this ID is yours using your face, fingerprint, password, or PIN

“Details” next to “Show code” lets you enable an “Activity history,” while “Driver’s License information” lists license number, date of expiry, address, and more.

IDs can be read via NFC or by having the QR code scanned. It is accepted at some airports by the TSA. Officially, you still have to carry your ID card as the one on your phone “does not replace the requirement for individuals to carry a physical card.” 

Your device must be running Android 8+ and have a screen lock, with Bluetooth and Nearby devices enabled. A state ID can be deleted from Google Wallet any time or remotely via myaccount.google.com. As a private pass, it does not get synced to the cloud and is only available on one device.

Tap Personal Info.

Scroll to “Digital ID.”

Tap Manage Digital ID.

Next to the ID or license that you want to remove, tap Delete.

Confirm that you want to delete your ID from your device and Google Account.

title: Apple’s new M6 adds feature previously exclusive to high-end chips
snippet: Apple’s next-generation M6 chip is here, debuting first in the new Mac mini. And among its powerful upgrades, M6 gets a new feature previously exclusive to higher-end chips like M5 Pro and Max. more…
fullText:
Apple’s next-generation M6 chip is here, debuting first in the new Mac mini. And among its powerful upgrades, M6 gets a new feature previously exclusive to higher-end chips like M5 Pro and Max.

Apple’s M6 has both super cores and performance cores, a first for a base chip

Apple silicon continues advancing in big ways, and this week brought the latest evidence of that: M6 and the M5 Ultra.

Both chips offer innovations in their own ways. For example, M5 Ultra offers Apple’s first quad-die architecture, and M6 is the first 2 nanometer chip.

M6 also has a Pro-level upgrade in the type of CPU cores it has. It offers 12 cores total:

2 super cores

4 performance cores

6 efficiency cores

Historically, Apple’s chips have had only two cores: performance and efficiency. But that changed with the M5 Pro and M5 Max earlier this year.

Apple rebranded its previous ‘performance’ cores as ‘super cores.’ Then added a third, brand new type of core that assumed the ‘performance’ name.

The naming is a bit confusing, but here’s the breakdown from 9to5Mac’s Chance Miller: 

The “super cores” are Apple’s most powerful CPU cores. These were previously called “performance cores,” but Apple renamed them in conjunction with the introduction of the new “performance cores.” 

The new performance cores are now the middle-tier in the M5 chip architecture, offering a balance of power efficiency and multi-threaded performance. The performance core architecture is what’s new with M5 Pro and M5 Max.

M5 Pro and Max were, until this week, the only way to get super cores and performance cores in one chip. Now the M5 Ultra and the base M6 chip offer Apple’s two most powerful CPU cores too.

Previous base chips, like the M5, only ever offered two types of cores. But with M6, users will get all three: super, performance, and efficiency.

It’s just one of the reasons why the base M6 chip is an especially exciting year-over-year upgrade.

fullText:

Press once to capture a conversation, and Gem connects it to what you discussed weeks ago — surfacing the earlier thread with a source link. From $179, shipping August 2026.

In 2023, early adopters were just getting to know ChatGPT and AI chatbot tech. Three years later, OpenAI’s Codex agent, now part of the ChatGPT desktop app, has brought about a similar season of learning. Here’s how I’m using ChatGPT, Codex, and more on my Mac.

The summer I turned Codex

Like a billion other people, ChatGPT has become a regular part of my tech stack. But I’m a writer, not a programmer, so Codex as an agentic coding app didn’t immediately appeal to me.

That started to change in April when Codex for Mac added Computer Use.

First, a brief history lesson. 

Back in December 2014, Ari Weinstein and friends launched a new iOS 8 app for mobile automation. Here’s my 9to5Mac coverage of Workflow’s launch, a friendlier version of OS X’s Automator made for iPhone and iPad.

In March 2017, Apple bought Workflow. Workflow gained system integration and became Apple Shortcuts with iOS 12 in 2018.

Weinstein and other Workflow veterans later left Apple to create Software Applications Incorporated. The startup previewed Sky, a modern AI assistant on the Mac, before being acquired by OpenAI.

Sky never publicly launched. Instead, Codex for Mac delivered the technology in April in the form of the Computer Use plugin. 

So excited to share that we're bringing Computer Use to Codex. Computer Use lets Codex see, click, and type into your Mac apps, with its own cursor.

It's a magical feeling to have agents using your apps in the background, and still get to use your computer at the same time. pic.twitter.com/wdgxiHAKyX

— Ari Weinstein (@AriX) April 16, 2026

Trusting an AI with using your Mac, especially in the background, requires a level of trust. I don’t know what my adoption of Codex and Computer Use would be like without the history behind it.

I just know that, for me, there was a great level of inherited trust and continuity that gave me confidence in the system.

Here’s where I admit that Workflow and Shortcuts never super clicked for me. I’ve used both systems with tools that others built, but I haven’t been a builder myself.

Codex has completely changed that, but not overnight.

ChatGPT to Codex to ChatGPT … a journey

I initially found Codex to be too intimidating and outside my comfort zone compared to ChatGPT. Now ChatGPT without Codex feels like a toy. 

I’ve mentioned before that it was actually a toy-like feature inside Codex called Pets that served as the training wheels for me. (The real Codex pets are the personal projects you hatch along the way.)

I started using Codex daily in May. The first project I started with Codex is a Mac app called Flow — because it helps my story writing flow. It’s mostly a way to monitor app releases and updates. 

In my early 9to5Mac days, I used iTunes on the Mac for this purpose. It required local (and otherwise unusable) iPhone app files. More recently, I’ve used iPhone Mirroring to check the App Store on my iPhone for app updates as part of my work routine.

Describing this “workflow” to Codex started the process of building Flow. Being able to describe every little feature and change that I wanted, as if I was messaging a colleague, made it feel natural.

Because it’s my first project and built just for me, the icon is my first initial, handwritten by me (Apple Pencil, iPad Pro, Procreate), made with Apple’s Icon Composer Mac app.

Closing the loop

Because you can iterate forever, I’ve found it’s important to “close the loop” and consider a project mostly complete.

With Flow, I’ve definitely moved to the stage where I can measure the number of my 9to5Mac posts that originate from using the tool. This is an important distinction from measuring the amount of time spent invested into building the tool itself.

But because building with Codex has been such a joy, there are naturally other projects that have followed. You can just make your own Mac apps, specific to your very particular needs.

In my case, I’ve made more modern versions of apps I’ve used for years, tailored to my specific needs, right down to very specific narrow column widths.

This is very specific, but it’s very cool to me. I have a column view for social media, and a column view for RSS, on either side of my Mac display. Both are 275 pixels wide (and made for macOS 27 Golden Gate specifically). This is much narrower than the solutions I previously used, which weren’t even optimized for macOS 26.

Using X2 and Flume, I’m able to open up a significant amount of screen real estate in the middle without overlapping windows.

Social media and RSS are also mostly passive viewing apps for me. By default, toolbar button accent colors turn gray for non-active windows. But because these apps are made for me, I’m able to express that I prefer the touch of color to stay active, just desaturate a step, adding a splash of joy to my Mac.

But wait, there’s more 

At this point, if you’re still reading, this post is probably starting to feel like the guy who just discovered going to the gym and can’t stop telling everyone about how great it makes them feel. 

For that reason, I’ll just flag a few more hobby projects that Codex has unlocked for me.

First, Better Remote. It’s on the Mac App Store. If you’re already using your Mac, it makes tvOS feel like just another Mac app. Here’s a look at the update currently in the queue.

Outside of work (and spending more time outside), iterating on Better Remote has been my main side project this summer. The project started in June.

Second, Better Battery. I adore the look of macOS 27 Golden Gate, but I can’t read the battery indicator with the percentage displayed as well.

Prior to Codex, I’d probably write a blog post as a feature request to flag the issue. Instead, I’ve been able to make my own solution — during the beta period — which others can use for free.

I’ve also been testing ChatGPT Sites with a custom domain to make sharing all of this easier. I initially thought OpenAI’s Sites feature wasn’t really for me.

Publishing Better Remote on the Mac App Store required a web presence, though, which gave me a reason to test the ChatGPT/Codex feature.

Now I’m pretty excited to see where ChatGPT Sites can go from here. OpenAI recently added shared site management tools, and there’s a big opportunity for a more defined interface — like a modern Apple iWeb.

It’s still very early days for these tools, but I find it all very promising and exciting. I haven’t had this much fun using my Mac to make things since GarageBand two decades ago.

Every day, important conversations happen in meetings, on calls, over coffee, and on the go. By the time you sit down at your desk, half the details are gone. And AI tools are only as smart as the context you feed them.

Your iPhone stops recording the moment a call comes in. Your Apple Watch can’t capture what’s happening across the table. Neither connects what was said today to a decision made three weeks ago.

Memoket Gem was built for exactly that gap. An 11g AI wearable that captures conversations with one press and connects them across time. title: John Ternus hypes ‘huge launch next week’ in first memo as Apple CEO
snippet: Apple is hosting its iPhone release event next week, which is rumored to feature the first-ever foldable iPhone.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:45 PM PDT · September 1, 2026

Image Credits:Adam Gray/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

John Ternus has officially taken the reins as Apple CEO, succeeding Tim Cook, who held the role for 15 years.

The company’s former senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, Ternus enters the CEO role at a critical time for Apple. On September 9, the company will host its annual iPhone event, which is rumored to include the launch of Apple’s first foldable iPhone. Apple is also expected to roll out its new-and-improved Siri AI more broadly, which marks an important opportunity for the company to position Siri as an equal to chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude.

“We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” Ternus wrote in a memo to staff on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg. “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together.”

Apple is rumored to be working on several new products, like camera-equipped AirPods, smart glasses, and a touchscreen laptop.

“I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” Tim Cook wrote to staff on his last day as CEO. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”

title: Plaud’s new AI recorder is a pair of earbuds
snippet: Plaud got its jumpstart in popularity with a view on agentic AI that centered around recording summaries for students and professionals. Now, it wants to become a full-time assistant with the Plaud One earbuds. more…
fullText:
Plaud got its jumpstart in popularity with a view on agentic AI that centered around recording summaries for students and professionals. Now, it wants to become a full-time assistant with the Plaud One earbuds.

You might be familiar with the Plaud Note Pro, and that might be just because it looks like a modern retro voice recorder. It essentially is – recorded audio gets turned into highly detailed AI summaries through the Plaud app. Over the last year or so, Plaud has implemented more features to position the app as not just a summary tool, but an assistant of sorts.

The Plaud One is the next step, starting at $249. Unlike the Note Pro, the Plaud One Explorer Edition looks and acts like a pair of earbuds. The case has a lot of the same new-age retro design cues as the Note voice recorders, and it doubles as its own sort of recorder when the earbuds aren’t in use.

It isn’t an always-listening device, but it seems to skirt the line before it becomes invasive. Plaud says users can record everything the Note can, but the earbuds can also capture online meetings. It sounds like the Plaud One earbuds can capture the audio it plays, which could circumvent the difficulty of recording a call with a third-party device.

	

The earbuds themselves have all of the expected features, like ANC and transparency mode. Plaud notes they are equipped with 12mm dynamic drivers and support LDAC audio, surprisingly. With the charging case, the battery life is stated at 36 hours. On a single charge, the earbuds can record or play audio for up to 6 hours (without ANC). The case, however, can record for up to 25 hours continuously on a charge with 21 days of standby power on the 830mAh battery.

The big thing here seems to be Plaud Agent, which runs on Plaud Intelligence. In all respects, it’s an AI agent that handles tasks using the context surrounding your recorded meetings and conversations. Plaud says the Plaud One will integrate with apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, Notion, and Slack to perform tasks. Just like another agentic AI platform, the user has the option to manage skills so it does the job right.

The Plaud One earbuds seem like a logical evolution of the Note Pro and the app itself. How it handles summaries has always been extremely helpful in my personal usage, but it can be pricey.

It sounds like Plaud One will use usage credits the same way the Note recorder does. It’s unclear whether Plaud Agent usage counts towards those credits, or if, like the previous recorders, generating summaries on recorded material is what drains your limits.

The Plaud One Explorer Edition earbuds are available for pre-order starting today. Shipments will begin in Q4 2026.

title: Here’s the likely reason the iPhone Ultra isn’t getting an Apple Pencil
snippet: A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it. Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor … more…
fullText:
A report yesterday suggested that Apple considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra before deciding against it.

Bloomberg suggests that there are three reasons behind this decision, one of them being a desire not to conflict with the position adopted by Steve Jobs when launching the original iPhone. However, this was almost certainly not the deciding factor …

The idea of a shorter Apple Pencil that could be used with the iPhone Ultra is certainly an appealing idea on the face of it. The device is essentially an iPhone that turns into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same capabilities obviously makes a lot of sense. 

Samsung gave its Galaxy Note phablets an S-Pen stylus when the device was launched back in 2011. The thinking was that this was a device that would in part substitute for a paper notebook, and it survived for a decade with a definite fanbase before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman lists three reasons Apple decided against the idea in the end:

It would have made the device awkward to hold, with a Pencil on the side rather than the top

It would have conflicted with Steve’s view of a stylus being a poor substitute for a finger

It would have made unsightly marks on the display

I’m not convinced the first of these would have been a major consideration, as mounting it to the top of the device would have been an option. Although this would have required a very short design, it would still have worked well enough, I think.

I’m also not persuaded by the second. Steve’s objection was not to the fact that you could use a stylus with a smartphone, but rather that existing models required this. Designing the iPhone so that it was practical to use with a finger was the breakthrough.

In any case, Steve also famously rejected touchscreens on Macs because he felt the ergonomics were terrible, but we’re still expecting the upcoming MacBook Pro model to incorporate one, so clearly Apple isn’t afraid to contradict the positions once taken by its co-founder.

I think the third factor was the one that actually killed the idea. A folding display necessarily has a far thinner and softer surface than those of existing devices. Apple reportedly waited a long time to launch the first folding iPhone precisely because it was concerned about both the appearance and longevity of the display, and allowing an Apple Pencil to be repeatedly scraped across it would have put both at risk.

If Apple can ever solve this problem, would you want to see an Apple Pencil Mini for use with a future iPhone Ultra? Please let us know in the comments.

title: Ford explains why it chose Apple Maps over Google for its new EVs
snippet: Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom.

In a new interview, Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced vehicle projects, elaborated on the decision to use Apple Maps instead of Google Maps and what this means for CarPlay Ultra.

In an interview with GreenCars, Clarke said Ford spoke with Apple, Google, and others about mapping for the Fathom. Ultimately, the company turned to Apple:

“We had to optimize for performance capabilities cost, quality, you name it. We spent time determining which was the best solution.

A couple of things about Apple Maps.

One is that it has gotten so much better over the last few years. It’s a really great solution. The team that we worked with at Apple was very flexible to ensure that we get the absolute best customer experience.”

Clarke said Ford wanted a close working relationship with the Apple Maps team. There are a lot of factors that go into mapping for an EV, including things like range, charger availability, weather, and more. Taking all of those things into account, Ford determined Apple offers “the best solution.” 

“We wanted to make sure that we had really tight integration with that team when we’re talking about the things that have to happen on a vehicle: range estimation and determining how much range you have and how you want to precondition the batteries and how you charge.

You need a great maps provider that has the capability to get elevation, weather, and the maps data to have accurate updated information about chargers.

I think we thought that Apple was the best solution for this vehicle in order to get the customer the best solution.

It’s amazing to be first as well. Apple Maps looks beautiful, and having a large display to be able to put it on we think will be a really big wow factor for our customers when they get to see it.”

Clarke also confirmed that this is Ford integrating Apple Maps into its native, in-car software platform. The automaker is not adopting CarPlay Ultra in the Fathom. Instead, it will offer native Apple Maps, plus standard CarPlay and Android Auto.

With CarPlay support, Ford drivers can choose between Apple Maps, Google Maps, Waze, and other mapping solutions. They can also easily access many excellent third-party CarPlay apps.

You can watch the full interview on the GreenCars YouTube channel.

fullText:
Antonio G. Di Benedetto

 

is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Acer is announcing a new laptop poised to rival the MacBook Air’s thinness and lightness — and in the process, it cops another laptop’s name. The Acer Swift Blade 14 (not to be confused with the Razer Blade 14) is a productivity machine weighing just 1.76 pounds / 799g and measuring as little as 0.51 inches / 12.95mm thin. That’s around 1.7mm thicker than Apple’s svelte 13-inch MacBook Air, but Acer’s Blade is nearly a pound lighter. Its featherweight stature is partly due to Acer using carbon fiber in the laptop’s top lid and bottom plate.

Inside the Swift Blade will be a range of Intel Wildcat Lake processors, from the lowly five-core Core 3 304 that I tested in the Chuwi UniBook to the six-core Intel Core 7 350. And regardless of which exact chip is inside, the Acer will come with 12GB of RAM. So it’s not likely that the Acer will go toe-to-toe with the MacBook Air’s M5 chip in terms of raw performance, but it could make a compelling case for someone who prefers their laptop to be about as light as they come.

1/3Pretty thin for marshmallows. Image: Acer

The Swift Blade will come with a basic 1920 x 1200 / 60Hz IPS LCD screen with just 300 nits of brightness, but there will be a couple of OLED options as well (up to 2880 x 1800 / 90Hz and 400 nits). The OLED versions make the chassis ever-so-slightly thicker. And the laptop will have three USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 ports (one of which will be data-only) and a 3.5mm audio jack. Acer isn’t sharing pricing for any configurations of the Swift Blade 14 until closer to its December launch.

It’s the same story for the other Swift laptop Acer is announcing today: the Swift Air 16. This is a larger version of the Swift Air 14 announced at Computex. Despite being named Air, the Swift Air 14 was aimed squarely at the MacBook Neo — especially with its price of $699. While we don’t know yet what the Swift Air 16 will cost, we know it’ll offer similar Intel Wildcat Lake chips, Thunderbolt 4 ports, options for OLED screens, up to 16GB of RAM, and up to 512GB of NVMe storage. It’s not as light as the Swift Blade 14, but at 0.53 inches / 13.5mm thick and 3.31 pounds / 1.5kg, the Swift Air 16 sounds pretty light and thin for a 16-inch. It’s due to arrive in North America in Q1 2027 and other regions this December.

title: Samsung Galaxy flagships are a hit in the midst of RAMageddon – why?
snippet: As the impact of RAMageddon continues, a couple of this week’s key stories have had me thinking – is the somewhat-boring nature of Samsung’s year-over-year Galaxy flagship refreshes the exact thing making these devices a hit? fullText:
As the impact of RAMageddon continues, a couple of this week’s key stories have had me thinking – is the somewhat-boring nature of Samsung’s year-over-year Galaxy flagship refreshes the exact thing making these devices a hit?

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Outside of the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s wider new form factor, 2026 has been a pretty boring year for Samsung Galaxy devices. The Galaxy S26 series is nothing more than a chipset refresh and the Ultra’s Privacy Display, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Flip 8 were both refinements, the latter feeling like it’s on its last legs. Then the Galaxy S26 FE launched this week, which might as well be a poster child (right next to the Pixel 11 series) for the impacts of RAMageddon with its barely-updated package that costs more than last year.

Yet, it’s working.

	

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is, as of the latest update, the world’s most popular Android phone. A $1,300 flagship is outselling Samsung’s uber-cheap budget phones that the company’s success is built on. That’s wild, and it’s also the first time that’s ever happened. It comes alongside foldables as a whole being the one segment of the smartphone market that isn’t shrinking back right now – it’s actually growing steadily. New forecasts from the IDC this week claim that the “cheap smartphone era is over” and that price hikes are essentially never going away, and it’s just looking so bleak.

So how is Samsung actually pulling it off?

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a hit, and that’s probably in large part because not only is it new, but it directly addresses feedback from users. Thin and light, media-centric designs have been among the biggest requests from foldables right up there alongside ditching the crease – which the Fold 8 also more or less does. The Galaxy S26 Ultra manages this in far less exciting fashion. There was nothing especially new or groundbreaking about the latest Samsung flagship – Privacy Display rules, but it’s not exactly a game-changer – but it proved incredibly popular. I suspect that comes down largely to the simple fact that, if you’re looking for a new smartphone, the Galaxy S26 Ultra is an incredibly safe bet. For the millions on older Galaxy flagships, it’s a no-brainer, especially with trade-in deals thrown up on top.

The strategy is working. No one has to like it, but it is working. On that note, the other thing on my mind was an opinion post asking if Samsung is actually the problem, or if slab smartphone design as a whole has “peaked.” On the one hand, yes, smartphone design has pretty much peaked. On the other, yes, Samsung is the problem. As we’ve discussed repeatedly at this point, Samsung’s existing Galaxy design is an actual problem for users and for the future of smartphone accessories. The market is moving in a direction that Samsung’s phones are incompatible with, and Samsung’s answer to that is apparently to make changes on its highest-end designs and leave the base models stubbornly in the same place. Yes, Samsung is the problem.

But as RAMageddon continues and Samsung’s devices remain a steady rock in the turbulent market, I can’t blame anyone for going for a Galaxy flagship. Boring or not, it checks all of the boxes, and that’s really all that matters for the time being.

fullText:
Antonio G. Di Benedetto

 

is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Dell’s new Dell 14S laptop sounds a lot like a MacBook Neo: it comes in four colors, is aimed at students, and it starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Announced at IFA 2026, the 14S is meant to sit below the recently launched XPS 13 and offer another affordable laptop option as most other models continue to climb in price. The 14S will come in linen (beige), dusty rose (pink), washed denim (blue), and velvet green (yep, that’s green). That’s much more colorful than the XPS 13, and like its fancier brethren, the 14S can be configured with 16GB of RAM and a 512GB or 1TB SSD.

The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or as light as the XPS 13, but in addition to the same two USB-C 3.2 Gen 2 ports with DisplayPort and Power Delivery, it also has HDMI 1.4 and a 3.5mm audio jack. (Why the XPS 13 lacks a headphone jack, I’ll never understand). But the 14S has much more basic, non-touch display options: a 300-nit 1920 x 1200 / 60Hz LCD or a 450-nit 2880 x 1800 / 120Hz one.

1/5Those are some decent colors all around. Image: Dell

There are some other niceties for students on the 14S, including a 1080p webcam with Windows Hello face unlock support, and battery life that Dell claims can last for up to 23 hours of Netflix streaming. For chip offerings, it’ll be either the Intel Core 5 320 or Core 7 350 — the 14S won’t scale up to Intel Panther Lake options like the XPS 13 is soon expected to.

We don’t know how much any of this will cost just yet, as pricing is TBD for now, but in a virtual briefing Dell reps said the 14S will be close to the XPS 13’s $700 starting price yet slightly more accessible. We’ll know actual prices closer to its release later this fall. I’m currently testing and reviewing the XPS 13, and I’ve been very impressed with the hardware (except for the missing headphone jack). I’m all for seeing more good, affordable laptops out there — hopefully the 14S makes the right compromises to get the price down.

title: Samsung is randomly deactivating some accounts for ‘security reasons’
snippet: A bizarre issue has left many Samsung Galaxy owners locked out of their Samsung accounts which were “deactivated for security reasons.” more…
fullText:
A bizarre issue has left many Samsung Galaxy owners locked out of their Samsung accounts which were “deactivated for security reasons.”

Over the past 24 hours or so, a number of Samsung Galaxy users have taken to the web with reports of being locked out of their Samsung accounts. A message appears saying that the account is “deactivated.”

Can’t sign in. Account deactivated for security reasons.

Dozens of users have reported the issue across Reddit threads and Samsung’s Community forums. Samsung hasn’t directly provided an explanation for the issue. This can have a pretty big impact on using a Galaxy device, especially if a user is invested in Samsung’s software ecosystem including apps like SmartThings, Wallet, and Find. 

Some users appear to have had success getting back into their account with the help of support, but it’s very hit or miss. 

	

While there’s no clear problem at play here, it does appear that alias email addresses may play a role – adding “+” or “.” to an address. One support representative apparently mentioned this and a number of those affected mentioned that they do indeed use an alias of their email address for their Samsung account. But not everyone affected uses an alias, so this is likely not the sole cause.

Samsung has yet to confirm the issue or comment on a fix beyond generic troubleshooting. We’ve reached out to Samsung for more information and will update this article when we hear back.

If you’re running into this problem, let us know in the comments below.

Thanks Evan!

title: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Could Come in Black, but Skip Silver This Year
snippet: The next iPhone Pro lineup might not repeat any colors from last year, with silver reportedly not in production.
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to be unveiled at the company’s Sept. 9 launch event, and a new rumor appears to be firming up the three-color lineup for these phones.

According to leaker Fixed Focus Digital on Weibo (h/t MacRumors), the iPhone 18 Pro is now in full production and is set to come in sky blue, pure black and burgundy models. Prior iPhone 18 rumors have pointed to these colors, although the names have varied (dark cherry instead of burgundy, for instance).

For anyone hoping for a silver or gray shade, this report suggests Apple may skip that color this year, instead bringing back black after abandoning it on the iPhone 17 Pro series. Last year, black was available on other iPhone models, such as the iPhone Air, the base iPhone 17 and the iPhone 17E.

	

			

With just about a week to go until Apple’s official event, it’s likely that reports on the iPhone 17 Pro’s looks will continue to leak. 

Even more prescient than the color of the iPhone 18 Pro will be its cost. The tech giant has hiked prices across other Apple products amid the ongoing memory shortage that’s making consumer electronics more expensive. 

The new Mac Mini with an M6 processor, for instance, starts at $899, which is quite a bit higher than the $599 Mac Mini with an M4 processor it replaced. It’s entirely possible that the iPhone 18 Pro line could have a higher starting price than the $1,099 iPhone 17 Pro, should Apple follow this trend. We’ll find out more on Sept. 9.
