title: Firefox Now Lets You Block Some Ads on iOS Devices
snippet: Ad Blocker is a new feature for a browser that prides itself on privacy and customization.
fullText:
Fewer ads, better browsing? Firefox has added a new feature called Ad Blocker for Firefox on iOS, which the company says will block many third-party ads and ad-related trackers when you use the browser on iPhones, iPads and other iOS devices.

Ad Blocker is turned off by default, but you can enable it in Settings > Browsing > Ad Blocker. If you get ads that should have been blocked or other oddities while using the new feature, go to this Mozilla Connect page to report them.

A representative for Mozilla told CNET that Ad Blocker will work on iPhones running iOS 15 or later and on iPads running iPadOS 15 or later. The feature is being rolled out progressively, so some people may not see it right away.

Firefox, owned by Mozilla, is a web browser launched in 2004. Though it’s less popular than other browsers like Google Chrome, Apple Safari and Microsoft Edge, Firefox fans cite privacy protections and customizations as some of the main reasons they like the browser.

Other niche browsers also block ads, including Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, Avast and DuckDuckGo. If you use Chrome or Edge, you can install extensions such as uBlock Origin or AdGuard from their respective stores.

“Advertising helps fund much of the open web, supporting the publishers, creators and websites people rely on,” Mozilla said in its announcement. “We also know that ads can sometimes crowd the screen or interrupt what you’re trying to do.”

What it does, what it can’t

When you’re checking out a web page, it can be fairly annoying when pop-up ads and overlays cover up content you’re trying to see. Mozilla says Ad Blocker can stop many of those before they load, reducing clutter on that particular page. 

Mozilla says the Ad Blocker tech uses Apple’s WebKit Content Blocker technology and EasyList, a filter list used by browsers and ad-blocking extensions, to determine which ads to block.

Even with the new tool, you’ll still see ads here and there. For example, if you search “best air conditioners” on Google, merchant ads for AC units are likely to appear somewhere on that Google page. Ad Blocker also won’t block sponsored shortcuts and other sponsored content shown by Firefox when you open a new tab.

Mozilla said another privacy protection already built into Firefox includes Enhanced Tracking Protection, which blocks many trackers and limits tracking across the internet. Ad trackers are methods, such as cookies and tracking pixels, that help companies determine your online preferences and then target you with products they think you might want to buy.

title: Google Meet hardware dropping ChromeOS for Android
snippet: As we wait for consumer Googlebooks to launch, Google shared today that it is “transitioning [its] Google Meet hardware portfolio from ChromeOS to Android.” more…
fullText:
As we wait for consumer Googlebooks to launch, Google shared today that it is “transitioning [its] Google Meet hardware portfolio from ChromeOS to Android.”

Existing Google Meet hardware consists of touchscreen controllers, cameras, microphones, speakers, and what’s essentially a Chromebox to run scheduling software and the actual video conferencing suite.

Google is replacing ChromeOS with Android going forward. That said, “existing investments in ChromeOS devices are protected,” with full software support: “We will continue delivering security patches, stability updates, and ChromeOS releases for all Google Meet hardware running ChromeOS.” There are no changes to support timelines, with hardware continuing to work until 2030 for recent models. 

Hardware partners like Logitech, CTL, and Asus will “gradually end manufacturing and sales for ChromeOS-based hardware according to the following timelines.”

	

Logitech / CTL Google Meet Compute System: February 2027

ASUS Google Meet Compute System: April 2027

For customers looking to purchase ChromeOS devices to complement their existing fleet, particularly for large event spaces, we encourage you to purchase devices as soon as possible.

Google says Android for Google Meet hardware “provides several benefits”:

Device variety: Android-based room hardware offers a broader range of form factors, including compact all-in-one devices, video bars, and integrated room solutions. Whether equipping a focus room, collaborative huddle space, or boardroom, you have options to find the right fit.

Enterprise stability: Android-based devices deliver the performance, responsiveness, and stability you rely on with ChromeOS.

Hardware flexibility: Certified AOSP devices can run multiple video conferencing solutions, protecting your investment by allowing rooms to be repurposed without replacing equipment.

Long lifecycles: Devices certified for Google Meet are engineered for long-term reliability and predictable software support.

The company teases “several exciting Android devices intended for large-format spaces planned for 2027.”

title: Will Apple’s ‘revamped’ Health app with AI health coach debut next month?
snippet: Earlier this year, rumors were rampant about a revamped Health app coming to iOS 26.4. Then the project was delayed, and iOS 27 came and went, and the revamp still didn’t arrive. With the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 debuting next month, it’s worth asking: will we see the features debut alongside new hardware? more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, rumors were rampant about a revamped Health app coming to iOS 26.4. Then the project was delayed, and iOS 27 came and went, and the revamp still didn’t arrive.

With the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 debuting next month, it’s worth asking: will we see the features debut alongside new hardware?

Precedence

First and foremost, it’s worth going over why it’s probable that the features will debut in September. You might think “Shouldn’t all the software be unveiled in June?” – but there’s actually some precedence here.

Low Power Mode in watchOS 9, Sleep Apnea detection in watchOS 11, and Hypertension notifications in watchOS 26 were all features that weren’t unveiled until September despite not requiring the latest hardware.

So, for those reasons – it’s incredibly likely that Apple would wait until September to unveil its latest Health app upgrades, even if they don’t necessarily require the brand new Apple Watch.

There’s still time

Prior to WWDC27, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman warned that the new Health app upgrades, dubbed Project Mulberry, might not make an appearance at the WWDC keynote. Obviously, that now ended up being the case:

The Apple Health app is getting a range of new AI features that were originally planned for a comprehensive health coach service internally dubbed “Mulberry” that was scaled back. The upgrade, which includes improved blood sugar-related tracking and the ability to use a device camera to monitor a person’s workout, is not expected to arrive in the initial release of iOS 27. Apple may also announce these at a later date than WWDC.

Does this necessarily mean that Project Mulberry will for sure debut at the September keynote? No. That said, given the past feature unveils in September and the fact that we already knew it could be released later than WWDC, a September unveil feels somewhat likely, even if it ultimately ends up debuting in iOS 27.1 in October.

Feature recap

The rumors have been a bit wishy-washy regarding this feature set, since there are tons of variables at play. One of the things you may have heard was that there’d be a standalone Health+ service with videos from doctors. However, that plan was reportedly scaled back in favor of integrating the features into the usual Health app experience.

There are two very clear things though: there’ll be an AI health coach that gives you tips on your health based on health app data, and it’ll also have the ability to use your camera to give you real-time advice on workouts and other health-related tasks. Another key part of this upgrade is a new Health app design that makes it easier to make sense of all of the data.

Beyond that, we’ll have to wait and see. I, for one, am looking forward to having a much better way of making sense of my Apple Health data.

title: Razer Prio is an Android and iPhone game controller that folds down to roughly the size of a credit card
snippet: Razer has just launched its new Prio game controller, a USB-C controller for your smartphone that folds down to the footprint of a credit card. more…
fullText:
Razer has just launched its new Prio game controller, a USB-C controller for your smartphone that folds down to the footprint of a credit card.

Available now, the Razer Prio’s claim to fame is that it’s very compact. 

Like countless other mobile game controllers, it attaches to either side of your phone and plugs in via USB-C, but when you’re not actively using it, the controller folds down into a size that’s roughly the same footprint as a credit card – around 10-15mm wider and taller. It’s obviously a lot thicker, but it’s still a much smaller footprint in your pocket or bag. It weighs 101g. 

Despite the size, it still features tactile low-profile thumbsticks and dual bumpers and triggers, as well as a D-Pad and ABXY buttons. The thumbsticks avoid drift issues by using contactless sensors. 

	

Razer Prio is available today for $99.99 from the company’s online store, the same price as Kishi V3. Prio is also already available and shipping via Amazon.

title: OpenAI calls trade secret dispute ‘a mess of Apple’s own making’
snippet: Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more. The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” … more…
fullText:
Apple yesterday presented what it said was “shocking evidence” based on analysis of a MacBook owned by Chang Liu, a former employee who moved to OpenAI. The company is alleging that two of its former employees stole trade secrets relating to hardware design and more.

The AI company hit back with its own legal filing, saying that the whole situation is “a mess of Apple’s own making” …

The ongoing lawsuit is to determine whether Liu and Tang Tan stole confidential information acquired from their employment at Apple in order to help OpenAI develop an AI hardware device. In particular, it alleges that both engineers downloaded confidential engineering files after leaving the iPhone maker.

Apple was granted access to a MacBook belonging to Liu in order to carry out a forensic analysis to determine whether it held evidence of unlawful access to the company’s intellectual property. The firm yesterday submitted a court filing claiming it had found four “shocking” pieces of evidence backing its allegations.

In its own filing made the same day, Reuters reports that OpenAI doesn’t hold back.

Employees “can leave a company like Apple that has struggled to ⁠adopt ​AI and move to an exciting startup that builds innovative products,” ​OpenAI wrote. “Apple may not like those choices. But it cannot claim those choices are unlawful, and it cannot use its own sloppy ​procedures to blame others for its own mess.”

	

Specifically, it says the problems were caused by three issues:

Apple encourages employees to use personal iCloud accounts to access Apple documents

Departing employees aren’t given enough time to return company devices, transfer files back to the company, and hand over responsibilities

Former employees are contacted by their erstwhile team members for assistance after they have left, requiring them to access company information

9to5Mac’s Take

On the face of it, the evidence Apple provided yesterday does appear damning. OpenAI doesn’t seem to be denying that confidential Apple information was used by the company, but rather claiming that the iPhone maker failed to properly protect it.

However, while I’m not a lawyer, my understanding is that this could become a crucial argument – since companies can only claim information comprises a trade secret if they have taken appropriate steps to protect it. If OpenAI can show that Apple did not do so, then the AI company could prevail even if use of the information is proven.

title: Reliance’s JioHotstar takes its streaming empire global — without sports
snippet: JioHotstar will only have entertainment content when it launches in the UK, Canada, and Singapore.
fullText:
JioHotstar, the streaming platform controlled by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries, is taking its brand outside India for the first time and will replace Hotstar in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore as it begins a wider global push.

The streaming service will launch with more than 160,000 hours of entertainment content but without the live sports that have helped drive its massive audience in India, including the Indian Premier League (IPL), Women’s Premier League (WPL), and Indian national cricket matches. JioStar said it is not offering sports at launch because of existing content deals but did not rule out adding them in the future.

The absence of sports at its global debut marks a significant difference from JioHotstar’s offering in India, where the company says it has more than 500 million monthly active users and sports is a major audience draw. The service streams some of India’s biggest cricket events alongside the English Premier League; tennis tournaments, including Wimbledon and the U.S. Open; and domestic leagues for sports such as kabaddi and hockey.

JioStar confirmed to TechCrunch that starting September 2, Hotstar will “cease to exist” in the U.K., Canada, and Singapore, with JioHotstar replacing it. Hotstar users in the three markets will no longer be able to access the service through the Hotstar app, though their existing login credentials will work on JioHotstar, the company said. The JioHotstar app will be available in all three markets through the App Store and Google Play Store on mobile devices, as well as on connected TVs.

For years, Hotstar has operated internationally, including in the U.K. and Canada. It also previously had a stand-alone service in the U.S. before shutting it down in 2021. However, JioHotstar is not launching in the U.S. as part of this initial international rollout. The company plans to expand into additional overseas markets over time.

JioHotstar will launch with a trove of Indian films, TV originals, and reality shows like “Bigg Boss,” along with live TV channels under the Star banner such as Star Plus, Colors, Star Vijay, Asianet, Star Jalsha, and Star Pravah. The company said its content is available in 12 languages, including English, Hindi, Gujarati, Malayalam, Kannada, and Marathi, with dubs and translations also available.

In 2024, Reliance merged its media assets with Disney to form an $8.5 billion joint venture. As part of the deal, streaming services Hotstar and JioCinema merged to create JioHotstar for Indian consumers. At the time, the two services accounted for 85% of the streaming audience in India.

Data from India’s Ministry of External Affairs suggests that across the three countries where JioHotstar is launching, the service could have a target audience of more than 4 million people. Some of its content could also appeal to the broader South Asian diaspora.

“South Asian audiences have a deep connection with Indian entertainment across languages, generations, and households. At the same time, audiences globally are increasingly seeking stories and cultures beyond their own. We see an opportunity to build for this broader, underserved global audience — not simply export an Indian streaming service to new markets,” JioStar’s Head of International Business, Amit Malhotra, said.

JioStar has priced JioHotstar at £19.99 (about $27) quarterly and £69.99 (around $95) annually in the U.K. In Canada, subscriptions cost CA$19.99 (about $14) quarterly and CA$49.99 (around $36) annually, while in Singapore they cost SG$29.98 (about $24) and SG$69.98 (around $55), respectively. The prices are similar to what Hotstar charges, but JioHotstar will offer only entertainment content at launch. Customers who want sports may have to pay extra for another service.

By comparison, JioHotstar subscriptions in India start at ₹79 (about $0.80) a month for viewing on a single mobile device and go up to ₹2,199 (around $23) a year for its top-tier plan.

fullText:

One UI 9, based on Android 17, is live out of the box on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series and the Flip 8, but it’s yet to roll out to the broader Galaxy ecosystem. Galaxy S26 users have been able to test the update in beta for the past few months, but it’s only now that the beta is expanding.

Galaxy S25/+/Ultra/FE

title: iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad
snippet: Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order. Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad. iOS 27 is currently in beta, and the behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, eight developer betas so far show this change will ship this month — even if I’d change it. more…
fullText:
Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is currently in beta, and the behavior has changed slightly between the first two releases. However, eight developer betas so far show this change will ship this month — even if I’d change it.

Siri AI takes over the swipe gesture for a lot of the iPhone and iPad top edge

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Notifications now live in the top left corner

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

	

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri. 

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

iOS 27 is currently available as a developer and public beta. The official release is expected this month.

title: Apple announces App Store price changes in four countries
snippet: Apple’s Developer blog today announced tax and price updates for apps, In-App Purchases, and subscriptions in several regions. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple’s Developer blog today announced tax and price updates for apps, In-App Purchases, and subscriptions in several regions. Here are the details.

Tax changes hit three countries starting today

In a new post on the Apple Developer blog, the company announced two rounds of tax and price updates that will be applied to apps and In-App Purchases across several App Store storefronts.

The first, starting today, changes developer proceeds to account for new or updated taxes in three countries:

Morocco: Value‑added tax (VAT) introduction of 20%

Republic of the Congo: VAT introduction of 18%

Tanzania: Digital sales tax (DST) rate increase from 2% to 3%

The second, beginning September 14, will adjust App Store prices in four countries. From the post:

Pricing for apps and In-App Purchases will be updated for Israel, Indonesia, Morocco, and the Republic of the Congo if you haven’t selected one of these storefronts as the base storefront for your app or In‑App Purchase. These updates also consider the VAT introductions listed in the tax updates section above.

If you’ve selected Israel, Indonesia, Morocco, or the Republic of the Congo as the base storefront for your app or In-App Purchase, prices on that storefront won’t change. On other storefronts, prices will be updated to maintain equalization with your chosen base price.

While Apple didn’t detail the specific price changes in its announcement, the company says that the new prices are already available in the Pricing and Availability section of App Store Connect.

Apple adds that “prices won’t change in any region if your In-App Purchase is an auto-renewable subscription,” nor on storefronts where developers manually manage prices instead of using the company’s automated equalized pricing.

The company says these adjustments are part of its routine process for accounting for changes in tax regulations and foreign exchange rates.

title: Oura’s Menopause Impact Scale Expands Out of the App and Into Women’s Health Care
snippet: The creator of the Oura Ring is partnering with women’s health companies in the name of menopause.
fullText:
Despite 1.3 million women entering menopause each year, this stage in a woman’s life remains stigmatized and understudied. But a rise in femtech centered on menopause could help change that.

In June, Apple announced that its Health app now supports cycle tracking for both menopause — when a woman’s menstrual period permanently stops, and she can no longer get pregnant — and perimenopause, the transition to menopause. One month earlier, Oura released its Menopause Impact Scale, a self-reported questionnaire in its app that establishes how menopause symptoms impact a woman’s quality of life.

On Wednesday, Oura, maker of the Oura Ring, announced in a press release that its MIS is expanding beyond the app and into women’s health care and tech. The first 10 partners include menopause-focused clinical care companies Alloy Health, Gennev, Wisp and Pomelo; women’s health care companies Maven, Tia and Xella; and hormone and biomarker tracking companies Oova, Mira and Hertility.

“By integrating the MIS into how our partners work with patients, we’re giving women a measurement that travels with them and gives every provider they see the same starting point,” said Dorothy Kilroy, Oura’s chief commercial officer, in the press release.

How the MIS works

Developed by Oura’s own science and clinical teams, the company explains on its website that the MIS differs from current menopause assessment tools, which were created decades ago and measure only symptom frequency and severity. Instead, the MIS has Oura app users reflect on 22 symptoms associated with perimenopause and postmenopause across seven domains: sleep maintenance, cognitive functions, body image, hot flashes, sexual function and vaginal symptoms, musculoskeletal pain and urinary tract symptoms.

Both the total and domain scores can be exported as a PDF, so users can share this information with a doctor.Oura

For each symptom, a user is asked about how much it has affected their quality of life over the past two weeks. They can select: none, a little, moderately, quite a bit or extremely. 

A mean score is calculated for each of the seven domains, ranging from 0 to 4, and the sum of these scores yields a total impact score from 0 to 28: 0 to 7 means minimal impact, 7 to 14 means mild impact, 14 to 20 means moderate impact and 21 to 28 means high impact.

Once the first assessment is complete, a reminder is sent 30 days later for reassessment and to monitor symptom trends over time. 

According to the press release, over 600,000 Oura members have taken the MIS, and 35% of the members who have completed it once complete it at least one additional time. 

Note that just like the Oura Ring and the Oura app’s other features, this questionnaire is not for diagnosis or treatment of medical conditions. A doctor is still required for that.

When will the MIS partner integrations occur?

Starting Wednesday, Oura members can integrate their MIS results with Alloy Health, Oova, Xella, Pomelo and Wisp.

Although there’s no specific release date, Maven, Mira, Hertility, Gennev and Tia integrations will be available later this year.

How much does Oura cost?

To access the MIS, you need both an Oura Ring and an Oura subscription. The Oura Ring 5 starts at $399, and the membership is $6 per month, totaling $72 per year. 

The transition to menopause typically lasts between seven and 14 years, adding up to an additional $504 to $1,008 if someone wants to use the MIS repeatedly and, most importantly, as intended to keep track of their symptom trends. 

Oura and privacy

In its privacy policy, Oura states that it doesn’t sell or rent members’ personal information. Members control third-party integrations and can disconnect them at any time. 

Following an Electronic Frontier Foundation report in July about how most smart fitness devices lack essential data protection, Oura committed to issuing transparency reports in the future.

However, you should always exercise caution before sharing your information — especially health data — with any company. 

What this means for women’s health

As femtech expands and more companies create technology that brings women’s health to the forefront, the stigma surrounding topics such as menopause could decrease, expanding into doctors’ offices as medical professionals start to take women’s symptoms seriously.

At the same time, this also means more companies will attempt to capitalize on the trend or, as a 2022 New York Times article called it, the “menopause gold rush.” We’ve already seen devices costing hundreds of dollars that are marketed toward women experiencing menopause in the name of hot flash relief. 

With the rise of menopause-focused femtech, there are both benefits and drawbacks. Hopefully, the former will outweigh the latter, making it easier for women to have conversations about what they’re experiencing in their bodies — especially where it may matter most: in doctors’ offices.

Over the past 12 years, Anna has also written for the LA Times, Elle, Bust Magazine, Dazed, Apartment Therapy, Well+Good and more. title: X says attackers are targeting user accounts after the launch of X Money
snippet: X is investigating a wave of unsolicited password reset emails that it believes may be tied to the rollout of its new payments service.
fullText:
Attackers are attempting to target X users following the launch of X Money. After numerous X users reported receiving unsolicited password reset emails, a representative said the social media company was actively investigating the issue but had not yet found evidence that the hacks were successful.

On Tuesday, X product engineer Mridul Singhai posted to the social network that the company was looking into users’ complaints about the mass password reset attempts.

“Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts,” he wrote. “We are actively investigating the issue and, so far, have found no evidence of any breaches. We apologize for the multiple emails and appreciate your patience as we work to resolve this.” 

X Money is X’s newly launched payments service, which includes a bank card and other benefits. For X, the service could make it easier for creators to collect payments on the platform, further facilitating X’s digital economy.

Of course, money changing hands has a tendency to attract bad actors, which is what X says may be happening here. 

Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts. We are actively investigating the issue and, so far, have found no evidence of any breaches.

However, X general counsel James Burnham wrote a threatening post, saying, “The legal and security teams @X will stop at nothing to identify, locate, and hold criminally accountable any person anywhere on or off earth who attempts to victimize our platform’s users.”

As the attacks continue, users are warning each other about the problem and reminding others to enable two-factor authentication, if it’s not already enabled, to protect their accounts. X’s chatbot Grok has also replied to some posts with the steps on how to do so, while also confirming that the attackers are “mass-triggering” the form for password resets using public usernames.

title: Instagram cracking down on accounts that feature AI-generated influencers
snippet: As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach. more…
fullText:
As AI slop continues to dominate the web, Instagram is cracking down on accounts that leverage AI-generated influencers by threatening to restrict their reach.

In a blog post, Instagram details that its “AI creator” label for accounts is now going to say “AI-generated profile,” better reflecting that the account is not just using AI, but that viewers are interacting with an influencer that is entirely AI-generated. 

Accounts that were using the “AI creator” label will have a chance to review the status and have it removed if it no longer fits their content. 

The bigger change, though, is that Instagram will actively crack down on accounts that don’t use the label at all if they are using “AI-generated influencers.” This includes not showing content in recommendations such as the “For You” page. 

	

Instagram explains:

For unlabeled profiles that feature an AI-generated person, creators can and should apply the label by editing their profile and toggling on AI-generated profile. The label will then begin to appear on their profile and alongside their content if their specific media doesn’t already have a label indicating that it was created or edited with AI. Creators who proactively add the AI-generated profile label will not see a change to their profile’s reach.

Adding the label or appealing the decision can reverse the impact, but this is a considerable change on Instagram’s part, especially as AI-generated content has become incredibly prevelant on both Instagram and Facebook, both Meta-operated platforms.

title: Apple TV and Peacock Bundle Prices Have Changed, Too
snippet: Last week’s price bump also hit these Apple TV streaming bundles.
fullText:
Sorry to interrupt your Ted Lasso streak, but you’ll need to check your subscriptions to see if you have one of the Apple TV-Peacock bundles, because the streamer’s price hike affected those, too. 

On Aug. 28, Apple announced it changed the pricing for its TV streaming service in the US, increasing rates on its monthly and annual plans, as well as on Apple One. Those changes have also affected the Apple TV bundles that package the platform with Peacock, which are available to purchase through both services. If you have Peacock Premium (with ads) and Apple TV, the bundle price is now $18 a month, while the Peacock Premium Plus (without ads) with Apple TV bundle has increased to $23 per month.

The bump reflects a $3 hike, as these packages were initially priced at $15 and $20 per month when they launched in October 2025. The bright side? If you have one of Xfinity’s StreamSaver bundles that includes Apple TV, there’s no price increase. Of the eight StreamSaver packages, five include Apple TV, with monthly costs ranging from $18 to $35.

							Senior Editor

title: Everyone’s talking to their phones again
snippet: Good morning and happy Thursday. Today I’m donating to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in her honor, reading about OpenAI’s incredibly powerful new AI inference chip, pretending to read Bill Gates’ 6,000-word essay about AI’s diverging futures, and actually watching this 2-hour deep dive of the upcoming Thief: The Dark Project Remastered instead. As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe. more…
fullText:
Good morning and happy Thursday. Today I’m donating to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in her honor, reading about OpenAI’s incredibly powerful new AI inference chip, pretending to read Bill Gates’ 6,000-word essay about AI’s diverging futures, and actually watching this 2-hour deep dive of the upcoming Thief: The Dark Project Remastered instead.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column.

⭐️ Starred

Is talking the new typing? Despite a persistent trend towards resurrecting physical keyboards on smartphones, improvements to voice-to-text AI models have set up a parallel future where we hardly touch our devices at all anymore.

	

Purpose-built dictation and transcription apps have also taken off. I’ve cycled between Wispr Flow, Yaps, and Typeless on mobile, and Aqua Voice and Monologue on my Mac, and while they all have their advantages and quirks, they ultimately do the same thing. And like so many SaaS products, they run on a freemium pricing model that provides a small amount of free usage and an $8 to $12/mo fee for premium features.

Last month, OpenAI unveiled GPT-Live, a model that allows close to real-time full-duplex communication and sits on top of a multimodal LLM it can delegate tasks to. It was the latest in a long line of products focused on overhauling the reliability of voice inputs on any device with a microphone, from laptops to desktops to phones.

Now, Google has (re)entered the fray with Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, a model that promises to be faster and more accurate than GPT-Live and, if you’re a Pixel 11 owner, is already integrated into the excellent Rambler tool that’s Sherlocking many of the above products.

It can do all the things GPT-Live can, just faster. And unlike OpenAI’s, Google’s digital canvas is enormous. It wants you to talk to your Google Docs and Sheets, Gemini Live and Spark on Mac and mobile, and potentially more disruptively, through its Gemini API, by which developers can integrate voice input into their own apps.

Voice input isn’t new or novel — I’ve been sending WhatsApp voice memos to friends and family for years — but this new paradigm combines accurate transcription, where a model intelligently removes verbal tics and reformats text into tables or charts, with dynamic action. Think dictating an email that includes instructions to insert a specific photo from your camera roll and embed a map with directions. The combination of speed and dynamism is certainly enticing, but I’m not yet a complete convert.

There’s something tactile and contemplative about typing and communing directly with a thought that can’t be recreated with voice. And a world where everyone on the subway is dictating their commands to an agent sounds awful. But there’s a growing contingent of people, particularly those with fine motor impairments, who will find massive benefit from intelligent voice models, and that’s a world I’m OK with.

✉️ Inbox

Galaxy S27 Ultra’s major redesign detailed in new renders, price hike rumored. Of course the next Galaxy flagship will be more expensive, but it’ll also wobble less on a table, so it’s a fair trade-off.

Galaxy S27 leaks reveal a design that Samsung just won’t kill

Galaxy S26 Ultra is the world’s most popular Android phone, and that’s a first. The iPhone 17 is the world’s most popular phone, but Samsung’s most expensive phone that isn’t a foldable is, for the first time, the top-selling Android phone.

Nothing’s Android 17 update debuts this week with redesigns, new apps, 3D emoji [Gallery]. Nothing’s tasteful take on Android meets a bunch of really nice Android 17 features. Looking forward to this one.

Nothing starts Android 17 beta rollout, Phone (3) immediately met with error messages

Motorola details Android 17 update that you might get eventually

Galaxy Watch 8 starts getting Wear OS 7 in beta

Qualcomm’s next Snapdragon flagship chip has 5 GHz Oryon CPU. Qualcomm hasn’t revealed the manufacturing process of its latest chip, but Apple’s newly announced M6 is being built on TSMC’s 2nm fab, so it’s almost certain the Elite Gen 6 will be a fast follower.

Xiaomi’s version of the wider Galaxy Z Fold 8 shows up in hands-on leak ahead of launch. Now that Samsung’s gone and done it, and with Apple soon to debut its own, we’re seeing wide foldables from the big Chinese OEMs. 

Google Play mandating reduced memory usage & seamless device migration in 2027. As I talked about in a previous Inbox edition, thanks to the RAM crisis, Android is entering its efficiency era.

The ‘cheap smartphone era is over’ and price hikes are ‘permanent,’ bleak forecast reveals. Think prices will drop when demand for components levels out in 2028 or so? Don’t be silly.

Google Keep for Android rolls out ‘Find in note’ search. I’m still waiting for Google’s big Gemini-based Keep redesign, but I also like that the note-taking app feels like a vestige of an older, simpler time.

Our team also played with a few gadgets this week. First, Ben toyed with this weird Pebblebee tracker that fits inside a bike handle or golf club and works across iOS and Android. Then Andrew got testy about Google’s mid-quality default Fitbit Air straps. Damien compared the Pixel 11 to its predecessor, and then Ben told it like it is re: the Pixel 11 Pro Fold:

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold isn’t the best, but it’s also not bad either. Sort of like how every smartphone has a good camera now and it all comes down to your priorities and taste, the same applies to foldables. You’re checking every important box with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, but are you hitting the parts you care about most? If so, Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899.

🍎 Upcoming

It’s been a busy week on the Apple front. First, the company unveiled new M6 and M5 Max/Ultra chips, and then the Mac Mini and Mac Studio updates powered by them. The quick takeaway is that the M6 is very efficient and the M5 Max/Ultra is almost certainly too powerful for most people, but all the new hardware comes with considerable price bumps at every tier. The most expensive M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 256GB of RAM and 16TB of storage costs a cool $18,300, but Apple promises that a 512GB version is coming in October. Any guesses on what that one will cost?

Apple then unleashed a long-anticipated change to its Maps app: ads. It’s a controversial change and one that hasn’t gone down well with users, particularly because its App Store and News+ ads are already of such low quality.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, Apple announced a new “Surprise and shine” hardware event slated to take place on Wednesday, September 9. Of course, we’re expecting a new foldable iPhone “Ultra” alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, but what’s interesting is what’s rumored to be absent: any mention of the lower-end iPhone 18. 

Apparently Apple is keeping its fall event spendy while waiting until next spring to launch updates to its cheaper iPhones, which may include the iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and iPhone Air 2.

🎾 FWD:

The end of summer brings mixed emotions, but it’s also wonderful for a very specific reason: the US Open. I’m a huge tennis fan, and you’ll find me lounging in front of the TV at all hours of the day or night watching the Australian Open, Wimbledon, or Roland Garros, but the US Open is the best of all of them.

That’s why I was so excited to see the attention this incredible mixed doubles point between the husband-and-wife duo of Gaël Monfils and Elina Svitolina and the pairing of Henry Patten and Kateřina Siniaková has been getting. I’ve already watched it a dozen times and I’ll likely see it a dozen more.

Staying on the topic of tennis, I’ve been really enjoying this four-hour Netflix documentary about Spain’s favorite gentle giant, Rafael Nadal. And if that weren’t enough, Roger Federer has been making the rounds at this year’s pre-Open press conferences in his run-up to playing some exhibition matches, and discussed one of my favorite controversies in the sport: the death of the one-handed backhand. As someone who grew up emulating Sampras, I find its demise bittersweet, but at least we’ll always have this supercut.

🗑️ Trash

You’re likely to have seen news of Meta’s $18 billion settlement around kids’ usage of Instagram and Facebook. Paid out over the next decade or so, the agreement between Meta and most of the US states’ Attorneys General comes with binding promises of limiting how much time teenagers can spend on the platform and what types of content they’re allowed to see.

It’s good news all around for advocates of youth mental health, but some $5 billion of the total is being set aside to encourage YouTube and TikTok to implement similar restrictions. It’s a savvy outcome that Meta is using as a publicity tool, releasing a statement that will run as a print ad in the New York Times, Washington Post, and Los Angeles Times.

It will be interesting to see whether Google and ByteDance will rise to the occasion (or bait, depending on how it’s framed), but either way, the scrutiny on social media’s effects on young people isn’t going away anytime soon.

You can also support us by becoming a 9to5Google Pro member, starting at just $5/month. You get bonus podcast episodes, access to our members-only Discord server, and lots more.

Thanks for reading, and have a great weekend.

title: iPhone 18 Pro: Three reasons you might want to upgrade from iPhone 17 Pro
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week, and while most iPhone 17 Pro owners won’t upgrade so soon, for those considering a new iPhone there are three main features likely to motivate them. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week, and while most iPhone 17 Pro owners won’t upgrade so soon, for those considering a new iPhone there are three main features likely to motivate them.

#1: Maxed out battery life

Better battery life is often at the top of iPhone users’ feature wishlists. Who doesn’t want an iPhone that lasts longer between charges?

Last year’s iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max brought big improvements in this area, but rumors indicate Apple will push battery life even further this year.

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected to benefit from efficiency gains in multiple areas: an LTPO+ display, 2nm process for the A20 Pro chip, and possibly an Apple-designed C2 cellular modem.

Beyond these improvements, recent leaks point to larger physical batteries in this year’s Pro models, especially iPhone 18 Pro Max.

#2: Big camera improvements

Mark Gurman says that iPhone 18 Pro will bring “the biggest leap in camera hardware” in years.

Rumors indicate the Main and Telephoto cameras will be Apple’s primary focus, with a new variable aperture feature coming to the former and a larger aperture for the latter.

Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital also recently said that iPhone 18 Pro’s camera plateau will be 2mm thicker than last year due to an “enlarged main camera module.” This is another hint at big changes coming.

It would be nice to have more specific details at this point, but all signs point to Apple preparing some especially noteworthy camera upgrades.

#3: Revised design

For most people considering a year-over-year iPhone upgrade, design matters. If the new iPhone looks basically identical to your current model, the idea of upgrading is automatically less compelling.

While Apple isn’t expected to overhaul iPhone 17 Pro’s look and feel, it does reportedly have three design updates coming for iPhone 18 Pro:

New color options

Smaller Dynamic Island

Unified rear glass and aluminum

Current rumors point to Dark Cherry, Light Blue, and Silver color options—possibly Black/Space Gray too.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Dynamic Island is expected to shrink about 35% compared to the previous design, for a modern look and more useable screen space.

Finally, last year’s polarizing two-tone rear color scheme should give way to a more uniform look on iPhone 18 Pro.

title: Dropbox breach seemingly caused by egregious authentication failure [U]
snippet: Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account. Update: the company has said that about 5,000 accounts were compromised, with files downloaded from around 1,500 of them. The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company … more…
fullText:
Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account. Update: the company has said that about 5,000 accounts were compromised, with files downloaded from around 1,500 of them.

The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company … 

Developer Yoni Levy posted a copy of the email he received on X.

We are writing to let you know that we’ve observed unauthorized access to your Dropbox account between August 4 and August 21, 2026. While our logs show no evidence that your files were viewed or downloaded, we want to share with you what happened, what we are doing about it, and what additional steps you can take.

Other Dropbox users reported receiving the same email in which the company said it resulted from a problem with a single sign-on (SSO) option using Lenovo IDs.

Dropbox partners with Lenovo as an identity provider so that users can log in to their Dropbox accounts using verified Lenovo IDs. While you may not have an existing Lenovo ID, our investigation determined that an issue with Lenovo’s email verification process allowed an unauthorized party to register a Lenovo ID using your email address and then use that Lenovo ID to log into the Dropbox account associated with that email address.

However, while Dropbox claims the flaw was in Lenovo’s email verification process, the bigger issue appears to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to use their existing login to verify the new SSO, as The CyberSec Guru reports.

Recon/selection: The attacker compiles target email addresses (breach corpora, LinkedIn, customer lists — email addresses are effectively public data).

Rogue IdP enrollment: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID as victim@example.com. No inbox access is needed because Lenovo’s verification step is missing or bypassable. The display name is set to something disposable — one victim who reclaimed the rogue account found the name “John Madden,” the late NFL broadcaster, a strong tell of bulk, low-effort registration.

Federated sign-in: The attacker clicks “Continue with Lenovo” on Dropbox. Lenovo’s authorization server issues a token whose email claim matches the victim’s Dropbox account.

Implicit account linking: Dropbox resolves the email claim to the existing account and mints a session. No password prompt, no step-up, no “link this new identity?” consent. From Dropbox’s perspective, a trusted IdP had already vouched for the address.

9to5Mac’s Take

While there was certainly a failure to verify email addresses at the Lenovo end, it would not have done any harm if Dropbox had authenticated the linked ID before it could be used to sign in. Failing to do so is an egregious fault.

The company has now fixed the flaw and expired all sessions previously ‘authenticated’ through a Lenovo ID.

If you don’t already have two-factor authentication enabled for Dropbox, it is highly recommended to change this immediately.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra finally dies in bend test, unlike past models [Video]
snippet: Despite their increasingly-thin designs, Samsung’s foldables have held up well to torture tests that include more bending than you’d ever see in real life. But it seems the Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra might finally be too thin, as it’s the first mainstream Samsung foldable that’s died in a bend test. more…
fullText:
Despite their increasingly-thin designs, Samsung’s foldables have held up well to torture tests that include more bending than you’d ever see in real life. But it seems the Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra might finally be too thin, as it’s the first mainstream Samsung foldable that’s died in a bend test.

The Galaxy Z Fold 7 showed that, yes, Samsung could actually make a thin foldable. And for good measure, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra pushes that a step further with another slight reduction in thickness. 

In the usual torture test from YouTube channel JerryRigEverything, the Fold 8 Ultra holds up just about as well as anyone would expect. Durable outer display, easily scratching inside, and some deeply unsettling crunching noises when dust gets into the hinge. But it’s the bend test that’s out of the ordinary here.

Save for the very-limited Galaxy Z TriFold, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the first of Samsung’s foldables to break during a bend test. It’s no spectacular failure, though. The hinge and frame both stay intact; the inner display just… dies.

	

It’s interesting that the Ultra fails here despite the wider Fold 8 living through the same bend test.

title: iPhone 18 Pro is coming: Here’s what’s new with each model
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week on September 9, with new Pro and Pro Max models debuting. Here’s what rumors say is new with each model. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro will be unveiled next week on September 9, with new Pro and Pro Max models debuting. Here’s what rumors say is new with each model.

iPhone 18 Pro: Upgrades in performance, cameras, design, and battery life

Apple’s flagship iPhone 18 Pro will have the same 6.3-inch size as last year’s model, and focus on key improvements that many users care about most: performance, cameras, design, and battery life.

Performance: A20 Pro is Apple’s new chip that will make the iPhone more powerful than ever, and hit at just the right time for Siri AI in iOS 27. It’s part of the same family of chips as the just-unveiled M6, which points to big upgrades coming.

Cameras: The iPhone’s camera system is set for a big year too. The Main camera is reportedly getting a whole new module that will make the plateau thicker than ever, and a variable aperture feature either on Pro Max or both models. Telephoto performance will improve thanks to a wider aperture for better low-light photos. And there’s reportedly a redesigned Camera Control coming.

Design: iPhone 18 Pro will look a lot like its predecessor, with some key enhancements. The Dynamic Island cutout is shrinking by about 35%, the rear of the device will have a more unified color blend between glass and aluminum, and new flagship colors are coming—including a dark cherry/burgundy.

Battery: Due to the efficiency gains of A20 Pro, and also a new C2 Apple modem, battery life on iPhone 18 Pro should be better than ever. There will also be a slightly larger battery.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: Everything above, plus more

iPhone 18 Pro Max will feature everything listed above, except in a larger 6.9-inch form factor. And it is rumored to have at least one exclusive advantage, possibly two:

Larger battery gains than iPhone 18 Pro

Exclusive camera feature, possibly variable aperture

Apple’s Pro Max models always pack more battery life than the smaller Pro. But rumors indicate iPhone 18 Pro Max could extend its lead in that department.

Regulatory leaks point to iPhone 18 Pro Max having about a 10% larger battery than iPhone 17 Pro Max. Combined with efficiency gains in Apple silicon, Pro Max will more than ever be the go-to model for maximum battery life.

Additionally, a new variable aperture camera feature could be exclusive to iPhone 18 Pro Max. We’ve seen conflicting reports on whether the feature will be available in both models or not. But in his latest newsletter, Mark Gurman specifically mentioned the Pro Max model as getting it.

Will you upgrade to iPhone 18 Pro, or do you plan to skip it? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

If you lose track of things you’d like to reference later, Laytr might be a nice solution for you. All of us save things all over the place, whether that be browser bookmarks, built-in bookmarking features within apps, taking a screenshot to hopefully find later, or just leaving a tab open and hoping we find it again later. Laytr aims to be a nice all-in-one solution for keeping track of your digital bookmarks.

Highlights

Laytr offers an incredibly organized UI for keeping tabs on everything. It works with the native iOS share sheet, so when you find something, just hit share and click on Laytr. After that, you can set what to categorize it as, as well as when you want to be reminded again.

Within the app, there are three core tabs. The first one is the Now tab, where it highlights things you need to see imminently. There’s Timeline, which lets you scroll ahead and see things based on the date you set the reminder for, and Library, where you can see everything you’ve ever saved, both in categories or grouped together. Beyond that, you can also search.

One differentiating feature is that there’s no sync, even with iCloud, and no accounts. Everything lives on your device in its own separate bubble, and your data will never live on someone else’s server.

Download the app

Laytr is available for free on the App Store for iPhone models running iOS 17 and later. You can use the app for free, but for unlimited access you’ll need a $1.99/month or $14.99/year subscription. There’s also a discount on lifetime, which normally fetches $39.99 but can be had for just $24.99 for early adopters.

Features like searching and exporting will never be limited by the paywall, so even if you decide to unsubscribe later, the app will remain usable.

title: Apple tells Mac App Store developers they can now drop Intel support
snippet: Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs. more…
fullText:
Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs.

In the email, Apple says:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

To remove Intel support, update your app build settings to “arm64” only. Then rebuild and submit your app to the Mac App Store.

Previously, developers were required to offer Intel compatibility. With today’s change, developers can drop support for Intel-based Macs. Intel users, however, can continue using the last version of the app compatible with their machine.

The changes come as macOS 27 Golden Gate drops support for Intel-powered Macs altogether. Apple also announced last year that Rosetta 2, the software that translates Intel apps for Apple Silicon, will be discontinued after macOS 27 (with some exceptions for for certain games).

title: Elon Musk’s heterodox robotaxi philosophy gets put to the test
snippet: Believe it or not, the Tesla Cybercab is coming. Nearly two years after Elon Musk first unveiled the gold-tinted, gull-wing door sporting, steering wheel-free two-seaters as the future of Tesla's autonomy efforts, the company is finally putting them into operation as part of its robotaxi service in Austin, Texas. Public rides are here, and as Musk fans will assert, the era of Tesla's robotaxi dominance will begin. Or will it? Musk has bet his company - and his trillion-dollar pay package - on a stripped down, barebones autonomous driving system that eschews multiple sensors used by all of his rivals in favor of a camera-only approach. Th … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Nearly two years after Elon Musk first unveiled the gold-tinted, gull-wing door sporting, steering wheel-free two-seaters as the future of Tesla’s autonomy efforts, the company is finally putting them into operation as part of its robotaxi service in Austin, Texas. Public rides are here, and as Musk fans will assert, the era of Tesla’s robotaxi dominance will begin.

Or will it? Musk has bet his company — and his trillion-dollar pay package — on a stripped down, barebones autonomous driving system that eschews multiple sensors used by all of his rivals in favor of a camera-only approach. The Cybercab, as a purpose-built autonomous vehicle without traditional controls, embodies this bet. Musk believes he can forge his own path to robotaxi success — and the Cybercab is his gilded vehicle of choice. We’ll soon know if he’s in for a crash.

The Cybercab will be using a modified version of Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (FSD). For the company’s millions of vehicle owners, FSD remains a Level 2 driver assist feature that requires human supervision. In the Cybercab, it will be monitored by remote operators who theoretically can step in if there’s a problem.

FSD and Autopilot have been linked to dozens of fatalities and thousands of crashes. Using only cameras and an AI-powered neural net, the Cybercab will need to navigate a complex, unpredictable environment. Without conventional controls, there will be no human fallback in case the autonomous system fails. And after years of blaming crashes on their drivers, Tesla will now bear full legal responsibility if something goes awry.

For years, Musk has coasted on brash promises for an autonomous future. With tomorrow’s Cybercab launch, those promises are going to face harsh scrutiny that’s not easily overshadowed by rows of gleaming robot cars hitting the road.

For over seven years, Musk has thumbed his nose at the conventional wisdom around self-driving cars — specifically that more sensors equals more safety. At Tesla’s inaugural “Autonomy Day” event for investors in 2019, he laid out his vision for a sleek, simplified autonomous driving system that avoided the protruding sensors of the Waymo cars of the time. The top target for his ire: lidar.

The light beam sensor that practically everyone views as an essential ingredient for self-driving cars is “a fool’s errand,” Musk said at the event in 2019. And “anyone relying on lidar is doomed. Doomed. Expensive sensors that are unnecessary. It’s like having a whole bunch of expensive appendices... you’ll see.” The crux of his argument is that humans use their own eyes to make driving decisions, so why not autonomous vehicles?

Tesla once relied on radar, in addition to cameras, as part of its perception system, only for Musk to do away with the sensor in 2022. The company’s own engineers tried to persuade Musk to keep radar. They worried that without radar, Tesla’s self-driving system would be susceptible to basic perception errors if cameras were obscured by rain or sunlight — which could lead to crashes. They were rebuffed.

The reason everyone else uses lidar underscores the limitations of Musk’s camera-only approach. Cameras only provide flat, two-dimensional images, requiring Tesla to use computer vision and neural networks to approximate depth and distance. A camera-only system leaves itself vulnerable to sunlight glare, while a multi-sensor system has additional data in case its perception is blinded. And cameras struggle in adverse weather, like snow or fog, while lidar and radar can often pierce through these conditions.

Few of Musk’s predictions have come true, including his condemnation of lidar. Waymo, which uses lidar in addition to cameras and radar, is operating a fleet of 4,000 fully driverless vehicles in up to 14 cities across the US. This is the largest, more fully realized deployment of self-driving cars in the US — and possibly the world. Lidar hasn’t slowed Waymo’s progress; in fact, its engineers strongly believe the sensor helps accelerate it.

In a recent talk at Y Combinator’s Startup School, Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov agreed that cameras have gotten good enough to closely approximate human driving. But if the goal is to exceed humans and build a system that truly excels at safety, then cameras alone aren’t good enough. If you’re targeting full autonomy and superhuman performance, Dolgov said, “you find that weak sensing just leads to a safety curve that flattens out way too early.”

But Musk claims that a camera-only system is more affordable to mass produce, and thus will enable Tesla to deploy Cybercabs more quickly than Waymo. There’s no arguing that the Cybercab is cheaper to produce than Waymo’s sensor-laden robotaxis, but the lack of lidar isn’t the only reason. Tesla’s also saving money by leaving out traditional controls like steering wheels, pedals, and mirrors. The company argues this helps create more passenger space, but the hope is that it will also make the vehicle more profitable to manufacture.

“You find that weak sensing just leads to a safety curve that flattens out way too early.”

— Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov

At Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in 2024, Musk promised that people could buy the Cybercab for a price “less than $30,000.” Someone could theoretically buy a small fleet of Cybercabs to operate as a bespoke robotaxi service, he said.

But to sell the Cybercab to regular people, Tesla will need an exemption from federal safety rules that require vehicles to have steering wheels and pedals. If it tries to self-certify, it may run into the same trouble that tripped up Zoox for several years. (The Amazon-owned company eventually got its exemption, with heavy conditions.) Tesla will also need a permit from the California DMV to operate fully driverless vehicles on public roads. And in order to do that, it will need to demonstrate that its vehicles can operate safely — which so far, the company has not done.

What happens when a Cybercab is disabled or breaks down? Other AV operators like Waymo have procedures in place for remote operators to try to move the vehicle out of the way. And if all else fails, they dispatch crews of technicians who come out and manually drive the vehicle away. For a vehicle without steering wheel or pedals, teleoperation becomes the primary failsafe. That explains why Tesla has taken to installing Starlink connections in all its Cybercab — a convenient, if not double-dealing, solution for Musk.

The Cybercab may find itself stuck in Austin while Tesla works out these technological and regulatory hurdles. The Texas capital is where Tesla’s robotaxi service features the most unsupervised vehicles. It’s where Tesla feels most confident in its driverless capabilities.

There is no federal policy dictating driverless car deployments in the US. Legislation that could open the gates to more Cybercab-type vehicles has been stalled in Congress for years, with no sign of budging. That leaves Tesla to fight for permission state by state, or sometimes city by city. That’s expensive, not to mention time consuming.

Tesla’s current Robotaxi business has been extraordinarily difficult to nail down. The fleet’s size and supervised-vs-unsupervised status has vacillated wildly for months. Sometimes there are dozens of robotaxis available, depending on the city, but more often less than a handful are actually doing paid passenger trips. In Tesla’s most mature market of Austin, where it has been running robotaxis since June 2025, the company has approximately 110 Model Y vehicles in operation, according to Robotaxi Tracker.

With the addition of the Cybercab, we should expect those numbers to grow dramatically. But as we’ve seen in the past, just because the vehicles are on the road doesn’t mean Tesla is necessarily using them for passenger trips.

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

If you ask Tesla, its safety record is unimpeachable. The company’s dashboard of 2 billion miles claims that Tesla vehicles that use the supervised version of Full Self-Driving are involved in 40 to 90 percent fewer crashes than manually driven vehicles.

But its actions also speak louder than words. Despite marketing materials that suggest the system is more autonomous than it actually is, FSD remains just a Level 2 feature that requires constant human driver supervision. The driver, not Tesla, is legally responsible when something goes wrong.

Meanwhile, fatal crashes involving FSD continue to rack up. Under a 2021 standing general order by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla is required to report crashes where its Level 2 driver assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was hurt, killed, or the vehicle was towed.

According to Electrek, Tesla accounts for roughly 85 percent of the entire industry’s reports — nearly 4,000 crashes — thanks to its status as the automaker with the most ADAS equipped vehicles. And independent trackers like Tesla Deaths record roughly 65 fatalities involving Tesla Autopilot or FSD systems between 2013 and 2025. (There could be more; Tesla redacts most of the details in its reports to NHTSA.)

Tesla likes to trumpet the good stats, while hiding the bad ones. Its vehicles enjoy some of the highest safety ratings in the country, but its autonomous driving statistics remain a black box. Unlike Waymo, Tesla hasn’t submitted its safety data to any independent group for validation. Its own AI trainers have told Reuters they don’t trust its safety stats. And the company is currently under investigation by NHTSA for how it reports these crashes.

Autonomous driving is all about trust, and Tesla currently doesn’t enjoy a lot of it. A recent survey found that most people think the company is misleading its customers by using terms like “Autopilot” and “Full Self-Driving.” They also don’t think the company is doing enough to ensure its drivers follow the rules — and a quick survey of social media backs up this belief. And they don’t want it to deploy fully driverless taxis.

The Cybercab is sure to scramble some of these perceptions. With its future at stake, Tesla is barrelling ahead with fully driverless vehicles. A well-managed launch will no doubt be enough key-jangling to impress investors. But the public may be harder to convince.

title: Waymo goes on offense ahead of Tesla’s Cybercab launch
snippet: Waymo argued that fully autonomous vehicles aren't possible without using a mix of sensors and warned that pure end-to-end AI systems aren't safe enough.
fullText:
Waymo argued last week that fully autonomous vehicles are not possible without using a mix of sensors, and that “pure end-to-end” AI systems are not safe enough — shots at Tesla, despite the Alphabet-owned company not naming names.

The company took these swings in a blog post and an interview with Axios just one week ahead of a September 3 event where Tesla is expected to formally introduce its two-seater Cybercab into its own small-but-growing robotaxi fleet. Waymo also announced three new markets on Tuesday morning, further extending its robotaxi network, which is serving customers in more than a dozen U.S. cities.

Despite being technical and a bit wonky, Waymo’s claims kicked off a social media fight that lasted all weekend.

“Arguments they bring forward are poor,” Pierre Ferragu, an analyst and managing partner at New Street Research who covers Tesla, wrote on X. “My read: Waymo built a driving gas plant that AI at scale makes irrelevant, and now falls into incumbent rhetoric. Innovator dilemma 101.”

“How it feels to say your data and record of success leads you to believe driverless mileage, AI interpretability, and multiple sensor types are critical for safe, fully autonomous driving at scale,” wrote Ethan Teicher, a Waymo spokesperson, while sharing a John Wick promo image that depicts more than a dozen guns pointed at the head of Keanu Reeves’ character.

The metaphorical knives — or guns, apparently — are out because if Tesla can prove the Cybercab is capable of performing at scale, it would set up a major fight between the two companies and their disparate approaches to developing autonomous vehicles. At stake is a market that could be worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

For years, this fight was more academic or philosophical than anything. But last week Waymo flexed its real-world experience.

“Cameras are incredible, but they aren’t enough,” Srikanth Thirumalai, a VP who oversees Waymo’s driving software, wrote in the company’s blog post. “For years, there’s been a debate over whether cameras alone could solve full autonomy. Now, after more than 200 million real-world miles, the data is clear: safe, fully autonomous operations at scale require more. By combining inputs from cameras, lidar, and radar, the Waymo Driver creates a rich, redundant world view that no single sensor can replicate.”

Thirumalai also wrote that a pure end-to-end neural architecture that “takes in raw pixels and directly outputs steering commands” — which is Tesla’s approach to autonomy — will “run the risk of black box failures.”

“Even the best AI models with trillions of parameters still hallucinate,” he told Axios. “There is no click reboot or reload or refresh [in] physical AI. You have to deal with the consequences of it.”

Waymo has long taken the approach of integrating a mix of cameras, radar, and lidar sensors into vehicles built by other manufacturers. While it’s a more conservative technological approach, it has allowed the company to scale to a fleet of around 4,000 robotaxis across 14 U.S. cities, which provides 500,000 paid trips per week.

At Tesla, Elon Musk has long derided the use of lidar, calling it a “crutch.” The company has instead put all its efforts into trying to make fully autonomous cars using just cameras and AI. And Tesla has spent the last few years developing the Cybercab, a purpose-built two-seater gold sedan designed to be autonomous from the get-go.

The Cybercab has no steering wheel or pedals and a relatively small battery, and Tesla plans to pump out thousands of them — a recent filing shows the company aiming to build more than 125,000 annually.

Of course, Tesla still needs to show that its self-driving software is capable of full autonomy. The company is years behind schedule; Musk once promised there would be 1 million robotaxis on the road in 2020 — though the company has spent the last year trialing its own Tesla Robotaxi network in a handful of cities in Texas and Florida using modified Model Y SUVs.

Those trials have stayed small, with Tesla claiming it’s prioritizing safety over scale. It’s only within the last few weeks that Tesla has pulled safety monitors out of a majority of those cars. 

But that is likely about to change. Tesla has started registering Cybercabs with the Texas DMV ahead of the September 3 event. It’s unclear how quickly the company plans to scale the fleet after introducing the shiny two-seater, though social media users have spotted dozens of them sitting in parking lots around the country.

If Tesla can show that its AI-first approach to self driving can work at scale, it would be a major accomplishment for the company and validation for its software engineers.

The company will still have to demonstrate that it can solve all the other problems that come with operating a robotaxi network, though — problems that Waymo continues to discover as it operates thousands of self-driving cars. Those include navigating harsh weather, steering clear of emergency situations, and operating safely around school zones.

But beyond the technological differences, there’s another fight brewing: cost. Waymo’s technological approach is naturally more expensive. It uses more sensors, and installs them on vehicles that other companies manufacture. That means Waymo has to buy those vehicles and, in the case of the Zeekr-made Ojai, pay import taxes on them before they’re even outfitted with self-driving technology.

Tesla makes its own cars and is betting its AI will be capable enough to never need anything other than a few cameras to navigate the world. It’s a major gamble — one Waymo clearly thinks won’t pay off. But if it does, it gives Tesla the chance to outcompete Waymo, or possibly even Uber, on price.

title: HomeKit Weekly: Linkind’s Smart Light Stick brings flame effects with Matter support
snippet: “Flame effects” is not something I’d used before in a smart bulb, so this was a super interesting concept to me. Linkind’s Smart Light Stick aims to bring the idea of a “live flame” to a smart bulb, and it works with Apple Home out of the box thanks to Matter. more…
fullText:
“Flame effects” is not something I’d used before in a smart bulb, so this was a super interesting concept to me. Linkind’s Smart Light Stick aims to bring the idea of a “live flame” to a smart bulb, and it works with Apple Home out of the box thanks to Matter.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

The Light Stick is an E26 bulb, so it screws into a standard light socket, just like any other bulb in your lamp or ceiling fan. The pitch for the Linkind Smart Light Stick here isn’t just “another color bulb.” It’s a bulb built specifically around dynamic lighting effects, with flame simulation as the main feature.

The flame effects

Instead of a single flicker pattern, Linkind lets you independently adjust flame size, brightness, flicker speed, and motion type.  You can dial it down to something closer to soft candlelight, or push it toward a more intense, fiery look, depending on the room and the mood you’re aiming for.

Beyond flame effects, the bulb ships with more than 120 presets, including sunset glows, lava-inspired motion, and Christmas scenes. I kinda always take preset counts with a grain of salt, since these numbers are often padded with minor variations to inflate them, but the range described here at least covers many of your most varied use cases rather than just 120 shades of slightly different color effects.

Where Apple Home fits in

The bulb works with Amazon Alexa, Apple Home, and Google Home via Matter. That gets you the core functionality, on and off, brightness, and color in the Home app, alongside the rest of your Apple Home gear.

It’s worth being clear about what Matter does and doesn’t cover here, though. The deeper customization options, like the flame control, will live in Linkind’s own AiDot app rather than being fully exposed through Apple Home’s interface. That’s not the fault of Linkind, but rather the limitations of this category of Matter accessory at the moment. You get basic on/off control and automation integration through Apple Home, and you use the manufacturer’s app to actually design a scene.

Wrap up on the Linkind Smart Light Stick

If you just want a bulb that turns on and off via Apple Home, this is overkill; you can spend less elsewhere. If you want a genuinely cool light for a lamp or accent fixture, something that can go from a calm living room light to a full flame effect for a party, the Light Stick is one of the more feature-rich options I’ve seen, and the Matter support means it won’t be siloed away from the rest of your smart home.

You can grab it from Amazon.

fullText:
Just weeks after announcing price increases for Apple Music, Apple today announced that Apple TV is also getting more expensive. The company confirmed to 9to5Mac that the price of Apple TV is increasing from $12.99 to $14.99 per month. 

The Individual tier of Apple One is also getting more expensive. 

Apple TV, Apple One get more expensive

Here are the full details on the price increases: 

Apple TV (monthly): $14.99 (up from $12.99) 

Apple TV (annual): $119 (up from $99) 

Apple One Individual: $21.95 (up from $19.95)
