title: Google Play mandating reduced memory usage & seamless device migration in 2027
snippet: In response to the “significant hardware supply constraints that are altering device memory availability,” Google aims to reduce the memory usage of Android apps. more…
fullText:
In response to the “significant hardware supply constraints that are altering device memory availability,” Google aims to reduce the memory usage of Android apps.

On Android 17, this involves per-app memory limits that are first available on Pixel devices but will soon be adopted by an “increasing number of manufacturers.” Applications that exceed these limits “will be slowed down and may be terminated.”

Meanwhile, Google Play is establishing performance thresholds across three areas:

Dynamic memory usage (anonymous RSS + swap): This tracks the memory used for your app’s private data storage, including both active and compressed memory. It excludes files stored on the device, such as code or assets. We will assess this usage across different app states (like when your app is in use or running in the background) and device performance categories.

Bitmap memory usage: This evaluates the memory consumed by bitmaps. While bitmaps occupy memory when your app is in the foreground, they should not be held in memory for extended periods of time in non-visible app states such as background and cached.

Optimized DEX code:  A well-optimized Android App Bundle uses less memory, starts faster, reduces ANRs, and improves rendering and runtime performance. To ensure an optimized footprint, apps published on Google Play apps published on Google Play must be optimized with a minimum of 25% coverage across optimization, shrinking, and obfuscation using a tool such as R8 or any other shrinking tool.     

Memory enforcement starts in February 2027, with Google offering several Play Console tools and metrics. Apps and games that don’t meet these thresholds “will see reduced app visibility and publishing capabilities on Google Play,” with more details coming later this year. 

	

Today’s other announcement is a “requirement for app developers to make log-ins faster and safer during device transfers.” This will be done through a Zero-Tap Sign-In standard that requires apps to “automatically restore a user’s sign-in state when they move from one Android device to another with the Android Restore Credentials API.”

This API ensures that when a user opens your app on their new Android device for the very first time, they are instantly recognized and securely signed in without additional taps. 

This will be required by Google Play starting in April 2027. Games are currently exempt, with more plans coming next year.

fullText:
iRobot has announced a new flagship robot vacuum, which it will showcase at IFA in Berlin this week, the company’s first big tech trade show in years. The Roomba maker will be exhibiting under its new owner, Picea Robotics, the contract manufacturer that purchased the once-troubled American robotics company out of bankruptcy in January.

The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is the company’s newest top-of-the-line robot vacuum and mop, and it debuts alongside the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo. Both models are available now at irobot.com.

The key vacuuming improvement is a new sealing system iRobot is calling SealForce that takes vacuuming “to a level beyond what’s previously been possible,” iRobot chief engineer Adam Pope said.

This works by lowering a sort of skirt around the cleaning head when it detects carpet, enabling a better seal that directs airflow deeper into the carpet. Paired with a new vane-type blower motor that Pope says moves 20 L/s (liters of air per second), SealForce helps the Roomba 875 deliver three times deeper carpet cleaning than without the feature.

1/4The Roomba Max 875 Combo comes in black or white Image: iRobot

The 875 offers 35,000 Pa suction power, the highest iRobot has ever published—for years, the company refused to publish detailed suction-power specs. It uses a single rubber brush rather than the company’s signature dual rollers (my favorite for pet hair on carpet). Pope says this is to accommodate that better seal against the carpet. It uses lidar and camera-based vision to navigate and detect obstacles and has a slimmer footprint than the Roomba 775. It can also climb thresholds up to 3.5 cm high.

The 875 has a roller mop that can extend to the side to clean edges and a new hair-cutting anti-tangle brush. 

The 875 Combo is also a mopping robot, with a self-cleaning roller mopping system that adds more downward pressure than the 775, plus a new heated mist feature called ThermaMist, which sprays ahead of the mop to pretreat stains. The mop includes a retractable mop cover that extends during vacuuming to keep carpets dry and can extend to get along edges. The robot comes with an auto-empty / wash dock that automatically washes the mop with hot water and dries it with hot air.

This SealForce tech is new to iRobot, but not to robot vacuums; Narwal and Dreame have variations on this on their latest flagships, the Narwal Flow 2 and Dreame X60 Max Ultra. But it is novel in the space, and combined with ThermaMist, a new hair-cutting anti-tangle main brush, and an anti-tangle side brush, the 875 shows that iRobot is inching closer to catching up with its competition than with its last relaunch.

1/2The 678 squirts cleaning solution on dried on messes then returns to mop them up.

The company is releasing a midrange version of the 875, the Roomba Plus 678 Combo. This also has a roller mop and the new SealForce tech, but it drops to 30,000Pa suction power and 18 L/s of airflow, and there’s no ThermaMist or mop cover.

Instead, the 678 has its own treatment system called SprayForce, which sprays cleaning fluid on stains to presoak them, then comes back later. It lifts its mop 10mm when it detects carpet. Both new models work with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Siri Shortcuts, and are currently going through Matter certification, according to Pope.

A robot vacuum with better vacuuming is less flashy but more practical than those that sprout legs and arms. We’re seeing several manufacturers adopt this type of sealing technology — one upright vacuum makers have been trying to perfect for decades. It will be interesting to see if Roomba’s version solves that very real problem when it comes to cleaning carpet.

title: Nothing starts Android 17 beta rollout, Phone (3) immediately met with error messages
snippet: Nothing OS 5.0 beta based on Android 17 has begun rolling out, but you might see an error because the demand for the new beta is “more than expected.” more…
fullText:
Nothing OS 5.0 beta based on Android 17 has begun rolling out, but you might see an error because the demand for the new beta is “more than expected.”

Nothing OS 5.0 won’t fully launch in a public release until October. The company’s version of Android 17 packs in a few important changes to the UI, like homescreen transparency updates and new lockscreen clock faces. The phones will also support Google’s new 3D emoji and get new apps.

You can read our coverage of the full release announcement for more information.

The Android 17 build packed into Nothing OS 5.0 has officially gone into its open beta rollout, meaning users can download the software and try it out before all of the bugs are ironed out. The Nothing Phone (3) will be the first device to get access. Nothing’s Phone (4a) Pro will be up next in early September, with more to follow through December.

	

Nothing’s timeline puts the official release at “mid” October for the Phone (3). Other devices will need to wait until November, at least.

But the current beta build, while technically available, has already caused some issues. According to Nothing co-founder Akis Evangelidis, who posted an update on Twitter/X, the company is seeing an “overwhelming response” to the new beta release. He says some users are seeing error messages related to the new beta.

It sounds like users are getting these errors when trying to download the update, not with the installation itself. Bugs are common with beta software, but this seems more like a bandwidth issue on Nothing’s part than any Phone (3) downloading the Android 17 update.

We’re seeing an overwhelming response to the Nothing OS 5.0 Open Beta with far more people downloading than expected. This is causing some users to see error messages. The team is working to stabilise things -please try again shortly.

— Akis Evangelidis (@AkisEvangelidis) August 26, 2026

The company says a fix is being applied, so it might be a short-lived blip during the initial Android 17/Nothing OS 5.0 beta phase.

Have you tried installing the Nothing’s Android 17 beta? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
Apple TV has picked up a new comedy series, Small Prophets, for its streaming service in an atypical fashion for the streamer. Rather than commission the project upfront, Apple has bought out the worldwide rights for the series a few months after the show debuted in the UK to record ratings.

Small Prophets was the biggest new scripted series launch for the BBC this year, and Apple will be hoping to replicate its success around the world. It streams on Apple TV starting October 7.

Thanks to this deal, the series will now stream worldwide on Apple TV. Most markets, including the US, will get to watch it on October 7, and it will come to Apple TV in the UK next year. (It is currently exclusive to BBC iPlayer in Britain.)

With a sensibility very much in the vein of other light and airy Apple comedies, like the currently airing Ted Lasso, Small Prophets will fit in well as part of Apple’s catalog. 

The show follows Michael Sleep, whose girlfriend Clea vanished seven years prior. He discovers an old alchemy recipe to create homunculi, which can seemingly predict the future and help him learn about exactly what happened to Clea. 

This acquisition play represents the first time Apple has bought out an English-language title in this manner. It has done similar deals in the past for international content, like the French-Japanese drama Drops of God. It shows Apple’s continuing flexibility and willingness to strike deals, as it builds out an ever-growing content library for the service.

Apple TV now features over 300 original TV shows and movies. See everything on Apple TV here.

title: This video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration with iPhone Cinematic mode
snippet: I recently observed that Apple appeared to have abandoned Cinematic mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration at this fact. That’s not because the feature is bad, but rather that it comes so close to being good enough for real-life use that it’s hard to see why Apple hasn’t taken advantage of the massive increases in power between the iPhone 13 on which it launched and the latest iPhones. Let me show you what I mean … more…
fullText:
I recently observed that Apple appeared to have abandoned Cinematic mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration at this fact.

That’s not because the feature is bad, but rather that it comes so close to being good enough for real-life use that it’s hard to see why Apple hasn’t taken advantage of the massive increases in power between the iPhone 13 on which it launched and the latest iPhones. Let me show you what I mean … 

I said previously that I understood why Apple hasn’t made updating it a priority, but also argued that it should do so to encourage future videographers and filmmakers – especially teenagers who may not have access to any other camera kit.

A friend of mine uses a smartphone to interview complete strangers passing by on the street, and somehow succeeds in having them open up in ways you could never imagine. I decided to turn the tables and put him on the stool and to likewise film using a smartphone, in this case my iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to see how well Cinematic mode could cope with a relatively simple challenge: a person in the foreground with around 25 feet of separation from railings behind him, and probably close to a thousand feet to the O2 on the opposite side of the Thames. Additionally, he would be sat on a stool, meaning rather limited movement.

The answer was … so close yet so far. The overall look is good, but there are visible halos between CK’s legs and the railings, the O2 pylons come into focus some of the time when he moves his head in front of them, and the river occasionally comes into focus when he opens his arms:

To be fair, CK argues that the average person viewing the video isn’t going to see the problem. If they are neither a filmmaker nor a techie familiar with the way the feature works, they probably won’t even notice the issues, and it won’t bother them if they do. I suspect he may well be right.

But it does bother me, and I think anyone with even amateur filmmaking ambitions will share my frustration – and that’s precisely the target market for the feature.

As I said at the outset, my frustration isn’t because the feature is bad, but rather because I genuinely believe that it could be dramatically better if Apple took full advantage of the power of the current generation of iPhone chips and the neural processing capabilities they possess. Indeed, I would expect a properly updated version of Cinematic mode to be able to cope with significantly more challenging environments than this.

Do you agree with my assessment, and would you like Apple to show cinematic mode some love? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Android still dominates global smartphone sales; Google’s Pixel 10a shines in one country
snippet: Updated data shows that, yep, Android is still the dominant force in the global smartphone market, but country-by-country breakdowns would hint otherwise – and Google’s Pixel series really only breaks into the conversation in one country, too. more…
fullText:
Updated data shows that, yep, Android is still the dominant force in the global smartphone market, but country-by-country breakdowns would hint otherwise – and Google’s Pixel series really only breaks into the conversation in one country, too.

Counterpoint Research published a breakdown of global smartphone OS share, measured by sales, with Android taking the win by a mile. On the global scale, Android makes up about 75% of smartphone sales compared to iOS, which makes up 20%. The last 5% is Huawei’s HarmonyOS. Q2 2026’s numbers aren’t that different from the same time last year, with Android down from 79%, ceding 4% to Apple and 1% to Huawei.

Counterpoint Research

The report brings out that the popularity of the Galaxy S26 series, the Ultra in particular, helped in “mitigating” Android’s overall decline amid RAMageddon’s impact on the market. 

Android’s sales share fell 4% YoY in Q2 2026 to 75%, as competition from iOS and HarmonyOS intensified. The Samsung Galaxy S26 series performed better than its predecessor, mitigating the overall decline in Android’s share. Chinese Android OEMs are shifting their focus to higher-value devices and scaling back activity in the entry-level segment to navigate RAM shortages and rising costs.

Meanwhile, another Counterpoint report breaks down the top five best-selling smartphones in major markets across the globe in Q2 2025, with most markets seeing Apple’s iPhone 17 series up on top. That includes, Japan, which stands out on the list because right behind the iPhone 17 and iPhone 17E is Google’s Pixel 10a, the only place Google stands out in all of this talk about top-selling phones. The Pixel 10a made up 7% of Japan’s smartphone sales in Q2, continuing a trend of popularity among Google’s budget-conscious Pixel in the region. It’s also noteworthy as the Pixel 9a didn’t make the same list this time last year.

title: Apple cleared for the second time to pursue documents from federal agencies in antitrust case
snippet: Special Master Jose Linares has rejected the DOJ’s request to reconsider his decision allowing Apple to seek documents from 14 separate government agencies in the antitrust case against the company. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Special Master Jose Linares has rejected the DOJ’s request to reconsider his decision allowing Apple to seek documents from 14 separate government agencies in the antitrust case against the company. Here are the details.

A bit of background

One of Apple’s defense strategies in the antitrust lawsuit the DOJ brought against the company involves the US government’s own use of its products.

Apple’s basic argument is that some of the practices challenged by the DOJ are, in fact, legitimate security and privacy safeguards. Hoping to support that defense, Apple wants to examine how federal agencies evaluate security and privacy when setting smartphone policies and making purchasing decisions.

To that end, Apple has been seeking documents from the following 14 agencies:

Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)

Department of Commerce

Department of Homeland Security

Department of Defense

Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)

Federal Trade Commission (FTC)

General Services Administration

Department of Labor

National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)

National Security Agency (NSA)

Office of the Director of National Intelligence

Office of Management and Budget

Office of Personnel Management

Department of State

Following Apple’s initial request to force these agencies to turn over the documents, the DOJ objected. The dispute was then referred to Special Master Jose Linares for a ruling.

Last month, Linares granted Apple’s request, prompting the DOJ to file a motion for reconsideration. It argued that he had applied the wrong legal standard, that Apple’s requests were unduly burdensome and disproportionate, and that the documents sought had limited relevance to the case.

Apple then filed an opposition arguing that the DOJ’s motion “failed at every level” and refuting the department’s arguments point by point.

Linares has now issued his new decision, concluding that “none of [the DOJ’s] arguments in support of its application for reconsideration are persuasive,” and leaving his original ruling in place.

Apple cleared to seek documents

The new decision states:

The Special Master concludes that none of Plaintiff’s arguments in support of its application for reconsideration are persuasive.

It adds that Linares saw “no reason, persuasive or otherwise, to reverse course at this point,” adding that “Federal Agencies, in this case, (are) part of the United States for purposes of party discovery.”

From the decision:

Plaintiff tries to split hairs by asserting that, under Rule 45 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, “a non-party to litigation is afforded greater protection from discovery than a party.” […] Thus, Plaintiff concludes that the Special Master’s Order and Opinion rests on flawed reasoning since it did not reference or incorporate Rule 45 into the analysis.

The Special Master is familiar with Rule 45 and the different standards applicable to third-party discovery. A quick review of the Special Master’s Opinion and Order reveals that Plaintiff is simply incorrect. Indeed, the Special Master detailed how this dispute arose in detail. […]. A review of that portion of the Opinion and Order reveals that Plaintiff itself is the reason why Defendant had to issue the subpoenas in the first place.

The document goes on to explain that Linares considered the 14 federal agencies to be part of the United States, rather than third parties entitled to the additional protections that normally apply under Rule 45:

[…] the discovery sought here from the specific Federal Agencies is appropriate party discovery because “the definition of the ‘United States’ also includes agencies that inform the policies, rules, and regulations the executive branch sets.” (Order at 6 (emphasis in original and added)). Thus, Plaintiff is wrong that the Special Master needed to perform a Rule 45 third-party burden analysis here. […]

The document also says the DOJ “misunderstands the legal framework applicable to this dispute,” while criticizing its assertion that the requested information had “minimal” relevance as being made “without citation to any support.”

As a result, Apple is once again cleared to seek the documents from the 14 federal agencies.

“We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” Ternus also says, in reference to Apple’s forthcoming “Surprise and shine” special event.

Ternus also looks further ahead in message, teasing the “incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet.”

Here is the full memo from Ternus sent to Apple employees today. 

Team,

Today, on my first day as CEO, I just wanted to send a quick note to thank everyone for the warm wishes. I also want to extend my deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years. We’re so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity. We are all better for it, and I’m so grateful he’ll be our executive chairman.

I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.

I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together. There’s no team in the world I’d rather build the future with.

More to come. In the meantime, thanks for your excellent work!

John

title: Google’s Android update tackles motion sickness, accessibility, and more
snippet: While some of the features see Google playing catch-up to Apple, which already offers similar features for iPhone users, others specifically leverage Gemini to provide various improvements.
fullText:
On Tuesday, Google announced it’s rolling out five new updates designed to make Android phones more accessible, useful, and personalized. Announced in a blog post, the features include those aimed at reducing motion sickness, helping blind and low-vision users navigate their surroundings, remembering where users leave important items, and another that adds new ways to personalize Google Messages.

While some of the features see Google playing catch-up to Apple, which already offers similar features for iPhone users, others specifically leverage Gemini to provide various improvements. 

The most interesting update is “Motion Assist,” a feature designed to help people who experience motion sickness while using their phones in a moving vehicle. It adds a bubble overlay to the screen that moves in response to the vehicle’s motion, helping reduce the disconnect between what users see on their screens and what their bodies feel.

The concept isn’t entirely new, however. Apple introduced “Vehicle Motion Cues” in 2024, which uses animated dots around the edges of the display that move in response to a vehicle’s motion.

Users can set “Motion Assist” to turn on automatically, add it to Quick Settings, and customize the bubble’s shape, color, and transparency. Google says this feature is available to Android 17 users. 

Image Credits:Google

Google is also introducing “Guided Vision,” a feature designed with blind and low-vision users in mind. It combines the phone’s camera with Gemini to help with tasks such as reading small print on a food label, viewing a menu in a dark restaurant, or identifying objects around the house.

The feature can also provide voice guidance when the camera isn’t positioned correctly, telling users to move the phone, pan around, or center an object. Guided Vision is coming to phones running Android 9 and newer in countries where Gemini is available.

Image Credits:Google

Another update gives Gemini a new way to help users remember where they put important items. A “remembered items” section in Find Hub will allow users to tell Gemini where they’ve stored something. For example, a user could say they put their passport in a bedroom drawer, and Gemini can save that information in Find Hub. Users can also attach a photo to make the item easier to identify later.

Additionally, Google is adding a Google Keep integration to Google Messages, allowing people to share and edit grocery lists, vacation notes, and other information directly within a conversation.

Image Credits:Google

Plus, Google Messages is getting more personalization options. Users will be able to customize individual chats with backgrounds, photos, and colors, Google says. The text bubbles will automatically match. 

Apple added a similar custom background feature to Messages last year.

fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 is coming next week, launching at the September event alongside Apple Watch Ultra 4. Here are three new features rumored for Apple Watch Series 12.

#1: New S-class chip

Apple’s S-class chips don’t get meaningful updates very often. Even though Apple does change the number most years, actual CPU improvements are rare. And last year, the company skipped offering an S11 altogether and kept the S10 around.

But this year, rumors indicate an upgraded S-class chip is coming to Apple Watch Series 12. Likely named S12 or S11, it will be more powerful, faster, and also the first new Watch chip of the AI era.

Siri AI is a tentpole addition to watchOS 27, and it’s expected to run best on the new chip. But other everyday features should benefit from the new chip too.

Apple Watch Series 12 has long been rumored to add new health features. For example, the FDA reportedly reviewed an upgrade to hypertension notifications that’s expected to debut next week.

One other specific rumor is that the heart rate sensor will get always-on support. This would match functionality offered by competing products like WHOOP.

Per Mark Gurman, the new Series 12 sensor can “continuously collect data throughout the day — not just when it senses you’re doing intense activity or at other random intervals.”

#3: Ceramic case option, likely in white and dark gray

Joining the usual new watch bands and case options, Apple is expected to debut a Ceramic case for the first time since 2019’s Series 5 model. 

Apple will reportedly offer Series 12 in two Ceramic colors: white and dark gray. Per Bloomberg: “Apple has tested both white and dark gray configurations for the Series 12 ceramic cases.”

It’s unclear how much of a premium Ceramic will add to the Series 12 price, but the last time it was offered, it started at $1,299—far more than Apple Watch Ultra costs today.

Fix passwords with a tap. The Passwords app alerts you to weak or compromised passwords and can update them on your behalf without the hassle.

title: Galaxy S26 FE is $699 with last year’s specs, Android 17, and a few new features
snippet: Debuting with a higher price tag and effectively the same spec sheet, the Galaxy S26 FE might as well be a poster child for living through “RAMageddon.” more…
fullText:
Debuting with a higher price tag and effectively the same spec sheet, the Galaxy S26 FE might as well be a poster child for living through “RAMageddon.”

Samsung has just unveiled its new Galaxy S26 FE, with the “Fan Edition” device offering more or less an identical set of specs compared to last year’s Galaxy S25 FE – 6.7-inch FHD+ AMOLED display, Exynos 2500 chip, 8GB of RAM (128GB/256GB storage), a 4,900 mAh battery with 45W charging, and a triple camera setup on the back comprised of a 50MP main, 12MP ultrawide, and 8MP telephoto (3x). 

Outside of a chipset generation bump, the only new thing this year, at least on paper, is that the Galaxy S26 FE runs Android 17 (One UI 9) out of the box, an update only available otherwise on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series (and Flip 8). The software packs some added features, too, such as the “My FanCam” that tracks a subject in video for social sharing, new AI features powered by Gemini Omni, and more.

Samsung has also updated the design this year, with a new camera bump look that’s closer to the rest of the Galaxy S26 series. It also comes in “Blueberry,” “Graphite,” and “Pistachio” colorways.

	

It’s a tough sell, to say the least, given Galaxy S25 FE launched for $50 less last year, and currently sells for as little as $500 outright through some carriers and retailers. But that’s just life during “RAMageddon,” ain’t it?

Galaxy S26 FE will be available on September 4.

title: Roku Pro TV Now One of Cheapest OLEDs Starting at $999
snippet: The Roku Pro OLED TVs promise better picture quality at an affordable price.
fullText:
Roku has launched a significant upgrade to its Pro television lineup, the first Roku Pro OLEDs. The best bit? They’re some of the most affordable OLED TVs on the market with prices starting at $999.

Also read: Best Roku TV for 2026

The Roku Pro Series OLED TV and step-up Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV replace the existing Pro TV and are available exclusively on Amazon. Unlike the existing Pro, which uses LCD, the new OLED should boost picture quality with infinite contrast and better off-angle viewing.

The standard 4K Roku Pro Series TV features a 120Hz panel with support for Dolby Vision and Roku’s Smart Picture Max. The TV also includes an Automatic Game Mode with FreeSync Premium and VRR (Variable Refresh Rate) .

Meanwhile, the Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV upgrades include a brighter picture, a wider range of colors, a 144Hz variable refresh rate and an anti-reflective filter. 

Both TVs include a ultra-thin metal bezel but, as a result, can no longer include the great Soundstage audio port from the old Pro. Roku’s Chris Larson told CNET the feature would make the TV too thick, which is a blow to people who want better sound quality built in.

Like the existing Roku TVs, the Pro includes usability features like an adjustable tool-free stand and velcro cable straps. The TVs come with a push-to-talk voice remote with backlit buttons and you can pair your Bluetooth headphones directly with the TV.

The Roku Pro (2025) was the company’s best TV yet, and the promise of OLED should make the new TVs better than ever. The price is also ultra-competitive, and these could be the late 2026 TVs to beat for their combination of price and picture performance. Given the upgrades of the LX — brighter panel and anti-reflective coating — it appears to be the one to choose of the two.

The Roku Pro Series OLED is now available in 55-inch and 65-inch sizes starting at $999. The Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV will be available starting in October 2026 for $1,299.

fullText:
We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch.

On Tuesday afternoon, Pixel 11 series users received an OTA update to CD1A.260905.001.A1 (from CD1A.260714.001.A9). 

The Android security update level is “September 1, 2026.” (Note: Not September 5.) The install screen has the usual generic security message: “This update fixes critical bugs and improves the performance and stability of your device.”

This is not Android 17 QPR1. Several of the visual changes coming in that release are not yet present, so this is still the initial release of Android 17.

Rather, Google is likely rolling out this update as a hot patch for Pixel 11 issues discovered since last month’s launch. The fact Google did not wait for Android 17 QPR1 should be telling.

title: Google Maps has renamed ‘Lake America’ for users in the US
snippet: Following an executive order late last week, Google Maps has updated its label for “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America.” more…
fullText:
Following an executive order late last week, Google Maps has updated its label for “Lake Ontario” to “Lake America.”

If you are located within the United States, viewing “Lake Ontario” via Google Maps will now show the name “Lake America,” following last week’s executive order. 

Google, in a brief blog post, confirms that users in Canada will continue to see only “Lake Ontario” while users in other parts of the world will see “Lake Ontario (Lake America).” This can also be seen using a VPN.

From the United States
From Canada

Google continues to cite a policy in which it updates location names based on local government data; in this case, the US GNIS, where the name has been updated as of August 27 by the Department of the Interior following Trump’s order. Google referred to this same policy in February 2025 when it updated Maps to show “Gulf of America.”

	
	

Canada has confirmed that it will not be updating the name from “Lake Ontario,” with Prime Minister Mark Carney stating that “the name is more than 400 years ​old, predating ​both the Confederation of Canada ‌and ⁠the Declaration of Independence of the United States of ​America.” Carney added that the name comes “from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.'”

Notably, competitor MapQuest has directly said it will not change the name, instead building out a name generator that allows users to create their own new names for the lake, mocking the change. Apple Maps is not yet showing the name either. Apple changed “Gulf of America” within a day or two of Google back in February, though.

Steep backlash pushed Google to limit new reviews of “Gulf of America” in 2025, but the same limitation has yet to be placed on “Lake America,” we observed in testing.

title: AirPods 5: Here’s what rumors say will launch next week
snippet: Rumors indicate AirPods 5 are launching next week alongside iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12, and iPhone Ultra. Here’s what we know so far about the new AirPods. more…
fullText:
Rumors indicate AirPods 5 are launching next week alongside iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12, and iPhone Ultra. Here’s what we know so far about the new AirPods.

AirPods 5 expected to launch at September 9 event in two models, but no cameras

Apple’s biggest event of the year is happening next week on September 9. Alongside new iPhones, Apple Watch models, and likely Home products, AirPods 5 are also expected to debut. 

AirPods 4 launched in 2024, and historically Apple has had two- or three-year gaps between generations. AirPods launched in 2016, AirPods 2 in 2019, AirPods 3 in 2021, and AirPods 4 in 2024. So from a timing standpoint, a launch this year more or less fits the pattern.

What’s surprising about the new AirPods, however, is how few rumors and leaks there have been about them.

Most AirPods rumors of late have centered on new models with cameras. A recent video leaked in Apple software showed the camera-equipped model in action, sparking speculation it would launch soon.

However, Mark Gurman at Bloomberg says AirPods with cameras will not arrive until 2027. But he’s expecting AirPods 5—without cameras—to debut at Apple’s September event. He recently wrote:

[Apple is] planning to debut fresh AirPods as early as the September product launch event. The rollout will include new AirPods 5, an update to Apple’s entry-level earbuds, the people said. That model was last refreshed in 2024. A camera-equipped version of the AirPods, meanwhile, isn’t expected until next year.

In a post on X, Gurman added that AirPods 5 will come in two distinct models:

with Active Noise Cancellation

without ANC

Previously in his reporting, Gurman wrote that he doesn’t anticipate AirPods 5 getting the heart-rate sensor from AirPods Pro 3, but Apple “is looking to add several more health features to the AirPods over time, including a temperature reader.” He also noted separately that Apple is “working on an H3 chip designed for less lag time and better audio quality.”

It’s unclear whether AirPods 5 will get the H3 chip or not. When Apple launched H2, it was exclusive to the AirPods Pro line initially.

But new health sensors are possible for AirPods 5, and H3 is a possibility too. Otherwise, details on AirPods 5 are minimal at this point. Perhaps like it did with AirPods Max 2 earlier this year, Apple will be able to surprise us with its AirPods 5 reveal.

title: Galaxy S27 leaks reveal a design that Samsung just won’t kill
snippet: Whether you’re a fan of the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s new camera design or not, Samsung is ditching the cohesive design that has tied its Galaxy S models together last year. The Galaxy S27 looks nothing like the Galaxy S27 Ultra, according to these latest leaks. more…
fullText:
Whether you’re a fan of the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s new camera design or not, Samsung is ditching the cohesive design that has tied its Galaxy S models together last year. The Galaxy S27 looks nothing like the Galaxy S27 Ultra, according to these latest leaks.

What appear to be official-looking render images of the Galaxy S27’s design have appeared online, showing every nook and cranny of the new base model (via Android Headlines). The only part about this leak that might be off-putting is the fact that the Galaxy S27 looks nothing like the Galaxy S27 Ultra, which recently leaked in a similar fashion

The Ultra model has a new camera design similar to what Apple designed into the iPhone 17 Pro. The camera “pateau” expands the island we usually see around the lenses to span the entire rear width of the phone. For whatever reason, Samsung did it, whether it’s for Qi2.2 or less wobble when the phone lies face-up, the point is that it’s a major shift. Don’t get your hopes up for Qi2 magnets, though.

The Galaxy S27, however, won’t be much of a shift, or even a nudge.

	

The leak indicates Samsung’s Galaxy S27 will have nearly identical dimensions and design to the Galaxy S26, save for a fraction of a millimeter in each direction. It will bring another 6.3-inch display to users who want the smaller model of Samsung’s Galaxy S line.

Inside, there’s a question as to what the company plans on putting at the helm. It could be a top-tier Snapdragon SoC, or it could be Samsung’s own silicon. Storage configurations are also a mystery, for now. With the price of RAM jumping further and further, the possibility of another price hike and less RAM is on the table. The Galaxy S27 Ultra could come with a price increase, according to previous reports. The same is very possible for the Galaxy S26.

It’s interesting to see Samsung making such a big change to the Galaxy S27 Ultra while keeping the more affordable options essentially unchanged in design since the Galaxy S23, even. Even when the Galaxy S26 Edge was reportedly set for a debut as the middle-ground option, Samsung had to kill it in favor of – you guessed it – the same design that was leaked today. It just won’t die.

The Galaxy S27 is expected to launch at the beginning of next year.

Google has some interesting tests going on behind the scenes of Android Auto right now, but only one of them is likely to actually be released – a new quick settings menu.

About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. title: Apple reveals ‘shocking evidence’ from ex-employee’s MacBook in OpenAI suit
snippet: Apple has filed a new document in its ongoing lawsuit against OpenAI as it continues to push for expedited discovery. In today’s filing, Apple says that it has new “shocking evidence” based on early forensic inspection of a laptop used by former engineer Chang Liu. more…
fullText:
Apple has filed a new document in its ongoing lawsuit against OpenAI as it continues to push for expedited discovery. In today’s filing, Apple says that it has new “shocking evidence” based on early forensic inspection of a laptop used by former engineer Chang Liu.

Apple first filed the lawsuit in July, accusing ex-employees of stealing trade secrets for the benefit of OpenAI. It moved for a preliminary injunction a few weeks later, while also asking the court to expedite discovery, including early document production and depositions of key OpenAI employees and executives. Apple again emphasized the need for expedited discovery last week. OpenAI has called for dismissal. 

As covered before, Chang Liu is one of the parties named in Apple’s lawsuit. Liu was a senior system electrical engineer at Apple who left the company for OpenAI in January. The lawsuit alleges that Liu exploited a security bug to download confidential engineering files after leaving.

In today’s filing, Apple says that Liu’s lawyers recently handed over his MacBook that he used after leaving Apple. According to Apple, an “initial forensic analysis” of that MacBook revealed four things, quoted from Apple’s filing:

Mr. Liu not only downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic but also used it in his work at OpenAI;

Far from his unauthorized access to Apple’s third-party cloud storage being unknown to him, Mr. Liu and others at OpenAI were well-aware of that access;

Mr. Liu, upon learning of Apple’s internal investigation of him, sent instructions for destroying evidence to an OpenAI colleague who confirmed she would comply; and

Mr. Liu used a tool in his work at OpenAI that has the same name as an internal Apple engineering application used for Apple development work.

Apple alleges that Liu ran a simulation in March using the circuit schematic file in LTspice, an electrical engineering tool. In messages from around that time, Liu said his AI “agent” learned to run LTspice and review the results.

Apple argues that when trade secret information is fed into an AI agent or model that learns from it, that learning “may create irreversible and continually propagating uses of the trade secret.”

Apple says the defendants decided not to inspect the laptop and instead chose to “advance theories that the device’s data disproves.” 

Additionally, Apple learned about Liu’s use of the schematic because he used it on a Mac mini which later synced via iCloud to the MacBook he took from Apple. Apple now also wants access to that Mac mini. 

This “shocking evidence” is yet another point in favor of expedited discovery in the case, Apple says:

“This shocking evidence—which Defendants chose to ignore despite its availability—demonstrates why Apple urgently needs expedited discovery. The MacBook represents the very limited information Defendants provided so far (and only after weeks of delay), and shows Apple is not conducting ‘fishing expeditions’ but that its trade secrets are being used and evidence is being destroyed.”

title: The amazing USB-C gadgets that play old Nintendo cartridges
snippet: Last week, I powered on a 26-year-old copy of Pokémon Pinball, one of the best Game Boy games ever made. My save file was no more. fullText:
Last week, I powered on a 26-year-old copy of Pokémon Pinball, one of the best Game Boy games ever made. My save file was no more. The Charmander I’d caught for my daughter, the high scores we’d set together… gone. Before flash memory, Nintendo cartridges used tiny watch batteries to save their games, and those batteries were never meant to last this long.

But it’s not a huge deal, because I saved my family’s save file months ago. I backed it up with an Epilogue Operator, a device that connects your real Nintendo cartridges to Windows PCs, MacBooks, even a Steam Machine.

The $50 GB Operator is a transparent trapezoidal cartridge reader that reads and writes to real Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges over a USB-C cable; the company’s new $60 SN Operator does the same for Super Nintendo and Japanese Super Famicom titles. Epilogue’s also got a N64 version coming.

They’re not just for backups! As you can see in my embedded video, these gadgets can play your carts, too. My Xbox Ally now takes Super Nintendo cartridges, my Steam Deck plays Game Boy carts, and my phone is a Game Boy Camera, because I attached an Epilogue Operator to each one. (Double-sided magnet rings and Mechanism mounts helped.)

Technically, the SN Operator and GB Operator are just cartridge readers, there are no original Nintendo chips or FPGAs inside. When you play a game, your computer saves the ROM to your computer and plays it in an emulator.

But Epilogue’s Playback software makes that easy — just plug in the reader, plug in the cart, hit play — and it casts a convincing illusion that you’re playing your games on actual carts. Plug one in, and your game pops up on screen. Whenever you save in the game, Epilogue should automatically save back to your cartridge as well. Whenever you yank a cart, the game instantly winks out.

The SN Operator, with a big slot to fit an SNES or Super Famicom cartridge (and spring-loaded door covers up top).

The GB Operator, about a quarter of the size of the SN Operator.

That last one’s a bit of a double-edged sword, because Epilogue’s Operators can be touchy about cartridge detection. They aren’t as forgiving as an actual Super Nintendo or Game Boy if your carts are slightly dirty or damaged. I’ve got Japanese copies of Bahamut Lagoon and Sailor Moon R that’ll quit mid-session if I nudge them wrong.

But I love that I can write savegames to my cartridges: I can play a game on my PC, move the cartridge over to my Steam Deck, then pop it into an actual original Game Boy or Super Nintendo and pick up where I left off. If you don’t need to automatically write saves, you can even switch to an emulator core that offers RetroAchievements, plus optional creature comforts like saving anywhere in a game with save states, or the ability to rewind time and try that tricky jump once more.

Super Nintendo on an Xbox Ally? Yep.

Want to hear something especially nerdy? My family recently played Super Metroid on the Super Famicom Classic Edition that Nintendo released in 2017, and there’s actually a way to pull your savegames off of those emulator consoles, too. I converted and wrote that savegame to my actual Japanese Super Metroid cartridge, and now I’m playing that save on 30-year-old original Nintendo hardware. (Speaking of: did you know a Japanese copy of Super Metroid is downright affordable and entirely in English?)

(I attached the SN Operator with a Mechanism mount and some right-angle USB-C adapters.

I never had a Super Nintendo growing up, and I don’t have a working Super Scope light gun or SNES Mouse now. But the SN Operator is also helping me play amazing games like Metal Combat: Falcon’s Revenge and Mario Paint and share them with my kids, no crusty old peripherals necessary. There’s an option to let your PC mouse cursor emulate a light gun or mouse, and it was simple to map those to my Steam Controller’s gyroscope aiming.

While you can do most if not all of these things by pairing emulators with other hardware, including the Open Source Cartridge Reader and a variety of Game Boy readers, Epilogue’s hardware is surprisingly high-quality considering its low cost, with attractive minimalist circuit boards clearly visible through classy polycarbonate. You know how we love our transparent gadgets around here.

And Epilogue isn’t just riding on the coattails of emulator developers, either. While the hardware’s proprietary, the Romanian company contributes some money and some code to open source emulators. Co-founder Petru Sebastian Toader also tells me he built his software’s excellent new CRT filter himself, the company’s working on online multiplayer, and every single SN Operator has its clockspeed factory-calibrated using satellites so they can dump certain SNES games without errors.

Epilogue’s also teamed up with the developers of Delta Emulator so you can plug real carts into your phone, and even built its own Flashback app if you want to turn your phone into a Game Boy Camera.

The Operator’s 3D trapezoidal prism shape doesn’t exactly lend itself to portability, but I stuck a magnet ring to it just right.

With all these amazing features, I just think Epilogue should be a little bit more upfront on its product pages about the compromises you need to make.

You should know the limitations: the Operators don’t work with multi-game flashcarts, they don’t work with the Super Game Boy, and their heavily marketed “Counterfeit cartridge detection” has been very hit or miss in my tests, to the point I wouldn’t really trust it. The company advertises that it can turn your Game Boy Camera into a webcam, but it’s more of an OBS screen recording hack than I would have guessed.

The GB Operator.

And if you, like me, have original Game Boy cartridges with original batteries, it may be too late to save some of your saves by now. It’s far too late to pull Pokémon off second-gen games like Pokémon Gold, Silver and even Crystal, whose real-time clocks drained their backup batteries and might not have lasted more than a decade.

As for first-gen Game Boy games, I pulled a Charmander off an original Pokémon Red cart last year, but even those carts are reaching their battery’s end of life. I have a 30-year-old copy of The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening whose battery was working last month. Last week, I found its save, too, was gone. Thankfully, the GB Operator backed up my progress a few months ago.

Now I just need to install a new battery, flash my save, and I’ll be back in business.

title: Chrome’s Android navigation bar redesign has too much chrome
snippet: I quite like how Chrome for Android’s main interface has essentially remained the same since 2012. The consistency is refreshing as everything else on my phone changes. While I’m open to modernization, the latest attempt at a redesign suffers from too much chrome. more…
fullText:
I quite like how Chrome for Android’s main interface has essentially remained the same since 2012. The consistency is refreshing as everything else on my phone changes. While I’m open to modernization, the latest attempt at a redesign suffers from too much chrome.

When the browser launched in 2008, the name was meant to signify speed and a minimal graphical user interface, or chrome. On Android, that philosophy has persisted with just an address bar at the top or bottom of the screen. That text field can be flanked by various buttons, but the most minimal state consists of just the tab switcher and three-dot overflow menu. Over the years, Google has just refreshed these elements while keeping the placement unchanged.

Old vs. new

The upcoming redesign once again adds a secondary toolbar at the bottom of the screen that has buttons for your homepage (which can be disabled), Gemini, new tab, and the tab switcher. This lets Google add a dedicated back button to the left of the Omnibox, while the toolbar shortcut is now placed inside.

	

Google was close to launching a similar revamp in 2020, but ultimately abandoned it because “mainstream users” found it “disorienting.”

I don’t mind the Gemini shortcut, and think giving people a dedicated new tab button is a good idea. That was my toolbar shortcut of choice for ages, and Google is now showing a share button by default next to the URL. (Tip: Long-press on the address bar to quickly copy links.)

If you keep the address bar at the top, this interface is perfectly fine. However, as a bottom bar user, the stacked interface elements are just so thick. When you first scroll down a page and the interface auto-hides, it really hammers home how much web content Chrome is covering.

Things become downright ridiculous when viewing Tab Groups. Having three rows stacked on top of one another looks comical and makes your screen feel infinitely smaller. To me, this interface is not usable, and I’ve forced myself back to the top address bar. 

Simply making the bottom toolbar thinner would help a great deal. It would salvage this redesign and let Google stick to the browser’s namesake design.

This navigation bar redesign is slowly rolling out to the stable channel. It’s not clear whether Google has committed to this interface, but I hope it changes before launch. Ideally, Google would preserve the original interface as an option, but that seems unlikely.

title: iPhone Ultra release timing: Here’s what the latest reporting says
snippet: Apple will unveil its foldable iPhone Ultra next week at the September event, but it’s unclear exactly when the new model will ship to users. Here’s what to expect per the latest reporting. more…
fullText:
Apple will unveil its foldable iPhone Ultra next week at the September event, but it’s unclear exactly when the new model will ship to users. Here’s what to expect per the latest reporting.

iPhone Ultra is likely to ship in September, but with very limited availability per reporting

Next week, Apple will debut its first ever foldable iPhone model: the iPhone Ultra. 

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are coming too, expected to go on sale later that week ahead of wide availability September 18.

But even though iPhone Ultra will be announced at the same event, it’s still unclear if Apple’s foldable model will actually ship to users at the same time as iPhone 18 Pro.

There have been countless reports over the last several months regarding the launch timing for iPhone Ultra. Fortunately, the most recent reporting is optimistic that we’ll see the device ship in September—albeit with limited supply.

Earlier this month, Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital said supply will be “extremely limited” at launch, but per his sources in the supply chain, there’s no evidence of a delay past September.

Similarly, a July report in Cailian News Agency referenced conversations with Apple supply chain sources. “They said that there was no change in the delivery time date in September, denying rumors of product postponement.” ChannelNews Australia was another recent source saying the device would be available in September, at least in the US.

Looking further back though, the story changes. 

Ming Chi-Kuo predicted earlier in the summer that iPhone Ultra will follow a similar strategy to the iPhone X in 2017. Meaning it could be announced in September but ship later in the fall. Macworld heard a similar plan from its sources.

And back in April, Nikkei Asia stirred a lot of buzz by reporting the foldable could be delayed several months into 2027. Mark Gurman at Bloomberg refuted that report though, saying the device was still “on track” for September.

iPhone Ultra release timing: wrap-up

In summary, the more recent reporting indicates that iPhone Ultra will indeed ship in September. It might be available in very limited territories and quantities, but early adopters should be able to buy it soon.

title: Google’s hyper-personalized ‘Dreambeans’ feed is now free to test
snippet: Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test. more…
fullText:
Dreambeans is an experimental app from Google Labs that will “proactively dream up personalized daily stories.” After previously requiring a subscription, Dreambeans is now available for free Google Accounts in the US to test.

Dreambeans is very much like a hyper-personalized Google Now or Discover feed. Like the Gemini app and AI Mode, it uses Google’s Personal Intelligence system to learn your interests by looking at your Gmail, Google Photos, Calendar, Workspace, Search history, and YouTube. During setup, you can choose which apps Dreambeans can access.

Workspace supplies ground-truth transaction data like receipts and upcoming flights

Photos provides the visual memories and insights about you and the people in your life

YouTube identifies your active hobbies

Search detects your budding interests

By combining all these unique signals, Dreambeans can proactively generate rich and highly customized daily visual stories.

The app suggests topics to explore, things to try, places to visit, and interesting events. New stories arrive every morning.

Instead of using stock imagery, each Dreambeans story is accompanied by Nano Banana 2-generated artwork that uses an illustrated style. For example, if Dreambeans recommends a hike, you might see yourself and a group of friends at that location.

	

Tapping on a story lets you see a longer description. In the same example, you’ll get trail details, specific places to stop, what to wear, and timing recommendations. Dreambeans will link to trail guide content on the web. There’s also an “Ask anything” chat experience to get more information.

You can leave feedback by tapping the heart or downvoting, while the chat interface allows you to provide more details. “Tune your feed” lets you tell Dreambeans what you “want more stories about” and what it should never show.

The name combines two ideas at the heart of the app. The “dream” is how the app works overnight to find meaning in the content overload across your connected apps. It then distills what it finds into “beans” – a fresh collection of stories brewed for you each morning.

In June, it was just available for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with Google expanding to AI Pro earlier this month. The setup process “requires up to a day to build your first set of stories.” 

It remains to be seen how Dreambeans will graduate from Google Labs. The experience it offers today is largely standalone, with Daily Brief in the Gemini app possibly benefiting from a more visual experience. 

Dreambeans is available on Android and iOS in the US.

title: Acer Shows Off a Transformer-ish Concept for a Windows Gaming Handheld
snippet: If it’s going to do double duty as a computer, it might as well have a keyboard, right?
fullText:
Project DualPlay MiniAcer/CNET

While we tend to think of Windows gaming handhelds as primarily gaming devices, they really have more in common with ultralight laptops: They run Windows, have a built-in screen and perform like them thanks to mobile processors with integrated graphics. And though some people have always used them as a primary computer, today’s high prices for both handhelds and traditional computers make handhelds seem like an even more attractive general-purpose option for gamers. 

But if you want to play a game with a keyboard and mouse, much less nongaming uses, you frequently experience the cumbersome process of connecting to the input devices or being restricted to wherever you’ve got a dock set up.

Project DualPlay MiniAcer

Acer’s Project DualPlay Mini concept takes a Transformers-like approach to making a handheld more suitable for general computing and KBM gaming: It’s a clamshell laptop design with the speakers on either side of the display, but the 8-inch screen flips up, and the grips are on the back of the speakers, so it turns into a traditional handheld when closed. 

You’d still have to connect a mouse, but the built-in keyboard remedies the most awkward design issue. As with any of these devices, you can connect to an external monitor as well as other peripherals as well.

The closest I’ve seen to a multipurpose design in a Windows gaming handheld is Lenovo’s Legion Go series (not the Legion Go Fold, though). But “close” in this case just comes down to a built-in kickstand that makes it a little easier to use on a desktop.

Predator Atlas 7

There aren’t any specs for it — it’s not a real product, at least at the moment — but Acer says it will use the same Intel G3 chips as in its Predator Atlas 8, announced at Computex 2026 in May and slated to ship later this month for an as-yet-unannounced price. The company has followed that with another launch this week for the Predator Atlas 7, a slightly smaller, lighter — and presumably cheaper — 7-inch model. It’s expected to ship around October or later in 2026.

title: The robot butler dream doesn’t have legs
snippet: LG’s CLOiD is a robot housekeeper on wheels, not legs. The company says it’s developing a robot foundation model by training hundreds of CLOiDs in home environments. | Image: LG The idea of humanoid robots running our homes has been the stuff of science fiction for years. But unlike hoverboards and self-tying sneakers, a robot housekeeper has never felt close to rolling into our homes. Until now. This has been the year of the humanoid robot. At CES, there were dozens of human-shaped bots on the show floor, a handful designed for homes. US-based robotics company 1X has already put its $20,000 Neo robot into homes to do housework (with a lot of remote assistance); and this week at the IFA tech show in Berlin, around half a dozen humanoids, mostly from China, will take to a catwalk to show off the alarming (?) accele … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
The idea of humanoid robots running our homes has been the stuff of science fiction for years. But unlike hoverboards and self-tying sneakers, a robot housekeeper has never felt close to rolling into our homes. Until now.

This has been the year of the humanoid robot. At CES, there were dozens of human-shaped bots on the show floor, a handful designed for homes. US-based robotics company 1X has already put its $20,000 Neo robot into homes to do housework (with a lot of remote assistance); and this week at the IFA tech show in Berlin, around half a dozen humanoids, mostly from China, will take to a catwalk to show off the alarming (?) acceleration of their skills as they plan to backflip into our lives.

But do we really need mechanical, multimodal robots that do our housework, or is there a smarter path that doesn’t involve 170-pound hunks of metal that could accidentally kill your dog with one misstep?

I’ve spent the last few years testing robots in my home; from robotic vacuums that can sweep and mop, to bots that mow my lawn, scoop cat poop, and cook dinner for me (all different bots, to be clear). I’ve also invited in Amazon’s Astro robot and several companion robots, including Ecovacs’ LilMilo, SwitchBot’s Kata, and Intuition Robotics’ ElliQ.

During my time with these robots, two things have become clear.

A fully humanoid robot housekeeper just isn’t practical

First, despite my tech-reviewer fascination with humanoid robots, a fully humanoid robot housekeeper isn’t practical. Unlike factories, where humanoids have seen some success, homes are messy, unpredictable environments. Also, most people have stairs. Solving that problem requires a robot that can either fly or have a pair of legs that can exert substantial force — neither of which is a good fit for a home. (Just ask Ring where its much-touted Always Home flying camera is).

Second, tech history has proven that precious few gadgets do multiple things well. We don’t need an expensive jack of all trades and master of none. At CES, I walked around the Las Vegas show floor with a bottle of laundry detergent, challenging every humanoid robot I met to open it. Not a single one could. I was repeatedly told it had to learn how to do it first.

What I think is more practical is a robot brain: an AI-powered smart home controller that can orchestrate the autonomous devices we already own based on the needs of the house and its occupants. Instead of one expensive machine trying to do everything, imagine a smart home that can proactively manage itself and adjust to the occupants: send the robot vacuum out when the dog spills his kibble, start the washing machine when energy is cheap, or dispatch the lawnmower when the edges need trimming.

Today, smart homes are mostly command-and-control or based on routines you create that require triggers. A robot brain could run your home autonomously and use reasoning to adapt when the home’s unpredictabilities arise. This appeared to be the idea behind Samsung’s Ballie robot (which never launched), and LG’s CLOiD humanoid (which looks more promising). It’s also the long-term vision of Amazon’s Alexa Plus and Google’s Gemini for Home smart assistants. No one is close.

At IFA this week, Tuya, a global AI cloud platform service provider, will launch a similar concept but with a tighter focus. Doova is an AI home companion designed to help seniors living alone. It is a short, round robot on wheels with no arms, but it does have “dynamic facial expressions.”

Tuya says Doova can track its owner in the house and be ready to assist in an emergency. It can open a live video call with family if they don’t respond. It will also provide “conversational companionship” and work as a smart home hub to control lights, curtains, and kitchen and bathroom appliances. The company hasn’t announced a price or release date, but says it will come to market.

The future of home robotics isn’t one machine that can do everything

Doova doesn’t need to fold laundry or load a dishwasher to be useful; it can understand what’s happening in the home, connect people to the home, and control machines already there. It does, however, present the other huge challenge for robots in our homes: They need cameras to navigate and interact, and cameras in our homes raise major privacy concerns.

Still, there is appeal in the idea of a robot brain that can do some manual chores — pick up clutter, load and unload a washing machine and dishwasher, and other tasks that require hands. I tested a robot vacuum with an arm that was supposed to pick up shoes and socks, and it mostly failed, but the idea is solid.

The middle ground between an imposing full-sized humanoid with legs and an armless robot companion is a wheeled bot with arms. That’s the direction LG took with CLOiD, a wheeled bot/smart home controller with arms boasting 7 degrees of freedom and five individually actuated fingers per hand.

I saw a live demo of CLOiD at CES this year using these appendages to perform simple tasks like folding clothes, taking items out of the fridge, and loading a washing machine, but not unscrewing a detergent bottle (I guess it uses pods?). Along with (very slow) physical actions, it also connected to and controlled smart appliances, including a washer, dryer, and oven.

This week, LG announced it is training hundreds of CLOiDs at a new data factory in Seoul, where they will practice a range of cleaning tasks in a home environment. By the end of this year, the company says this training data will feed roughly 100,000 hours of training data — equivalent to 12 years — into its own robot foundation model, built using Nvidia Cosmos open-world models.

It’s clear home robots are coming. But I don’t believe we need a robot butler that caters to our every need — very few people could afford one anyway. The future of home robotics isn’t one machine that can do everything, but a team of robotic machines, coordinated by a robot brain. And if that brain happens to come with a pair of hands that can open my laundry detergent, even better.

title: Apple Maps still shows Lake Ontario as Google Maps changes name
snippet: The latest development in the trade war Trump started with Canada is an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. Google Maps has updated the name, though what you see depends on which country you are in, with only US users seeing Lake America. Apple Maps has so far stuck to the real name … more…
fullText:
The latest development in the trade war Trump started with Canada is an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. Google Maps has updated the name, though what you see depends on which country you are in, with only US users seeing Lake America. Apple Maps has so far stuck to the real name … 

Lake Ontario is this year’s rerun of the Gulf of Mexico. Trump last year signed an executive order stating that the latter would be renamed to Gulf of America, and has now signed another saying that the smallest of the Great Lakes will be renamed Lake America.

Canada and most of the rest of the world has responded with amusement and mockery. Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a new billboard on the shoreline of the lake reading “Lake Ontario. Now and always.”

Google Maps has updated its naming, with the label depending on where you are based:

US users: Lake America

Canadian users: Lake Ontario

Rest of the world: Lake Ontario (Lake America)

This mirrors the approach the company took with the Gulf of Mexico. Associated Press cites a Google blog post stating that its policy is to use the names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (GNIS).

So far, however, Apple Maps has stuck to Lake Ontario, including for US users. Whether it too will compromise as it did for the Gulf of Mexico remains to be seen. The company normally tries to avoid political flak, and has often taken the decision to appease the Trump administration, but with a new CEO, this may or may not change.

Apple has a lot in store for this fall, headlined by the iPhone Ultra and iPhone 18 Pro launching next month. Apple is also working on a new iPad mini, and a new report today suggests it’s coming in October. 

A new iPad mini is coming soon

In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Mark Gurman reports that the new iPad mini with an OLED screen “should go on sale by the end of October.”

This suggests the new iPad mini won’t be announced at next month’s “Surprise and shine” special event. Instead, Apple will likely announce it separately in October, either via a press release or another event.

I think one of the biggest questions right now is how the foldable iPhone Ultra will impact the market for the iPad mini. title: Apple reportedly considered launching a new Apple Pencil for iPhone Ultra
snippet: Apple’s first foldable iPhone should be making its debut in just over a week. In the development process, Apple was reportedly mulling the idea of launching a new Apple Pencil to use alongside the iPhone Ultra – though it probably won’t make it to market. more…
fullText:
Apple’s first foldable iPhone should be making its debut in just over a week. In the development process, Apple was reportedly mulling the idea of launching a new Apple Pencil to use alongside the iPhone Ultra – though it probably won’t make it to market.

This news comes from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who wants to make it very clear that this pencil probably won’t be announced next month. That said, he does detail exactly how it would’ve looked and worked.

It wouldn’t have been the same as Apple Pencils that currently exist for the iPad lineup. It was “stubbier,” to align with the shorter height of the iPhone Ultra. However, similar to Apple Pencils on the iPad, it would’ve magnetically attached to the side for storage and charging.

He notes that it would’ve been awkward to hold while you were using the iPhone Ultra, since it’d stick on the side, versus the iPad where it sticks at the top when you’re in landscape.

He also notes that it likely would’ve made “unsightly marks” on the much more delicate inside screen of the iPhone Ultra.

Ultimately, he reckons that Apple probably isn’t launching this to not conflict with Steve Jobs’ position when launching the original iPhone: “Who wants a stylus?”

I’d still say an Apple Pencil on iPhone Ultra would be rather useful, but it sounds like we won’t have one – at least for the time being.

title: Who is John Ternus, the new Apple CEO?
snippet: Starting on September 1, Ternus will lead one of the world's most valuable companies, but if you're not a dedicated Apple enthusiast, you've probably never heard of this man, who has largely remained out of the spotlight until now.
fullText:
After 15 years, Tim Cook has handed off the Apple CEO role to John Ternus, the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering. As of Tuesday, Ternus now leads one of the world’s most valuable companies. But if you’re not a dedicated Apple enthusiast, you’ve probably never heard of this man, who has largely remained out of the spotlight until he was announced as Cook’s successor in April.

Ternus is assuming the CEO role at a crucial time for Apple. Next week, the company will host its iPhone launch event, ushering in its newest line of hardware. Apple will also soon roll out its new-and-improved Siri AI experience, which is powered by Google’s Gemini.

“I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” Tim Cook wrote to staff on his last day as CEO. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”

Cook will remain at Apple as executive chairman.

How long has John Ternus worked at Apple?

Ternus has worked at Apple for nearly half of his life — now 51 years old, he has been with the company for 25 years.

He joined Apple’s product design team in 2001 as only his second job out of college (his first was at a small maker of virtual-reality devices called Virtual Research Systems). By 2013, Ternus was a VP of hardware engineering and was promoted to the SVP role in 2021. 

Ternus — who is 15 years younger than Cook — was among the youngest of top Apple executives who had been rumored as a possible successor, implying that Apple could be looking for someone to lead the company for a long time. After all, Apple has only had two CEOs in this millennium, so it seems that leadership continuity is important to the company.

Ternus previously reported to Cook, who he considers a mentor, and led all of hardware engineering at Apple. That’s a pretty big deal for a company that’s known for ubiquitous hardware like the iPhone and the MacBook.

In his 2024 commencement speech at his alma mater, the University of Pennsylvania’s engineering school, Ternus reflected on the lessons he learned at Apple, which perhaps can tell us a bit about his character — or at least a sanitized version of it. 

“Always assume you’re as smart as anyone else in the room, but never assume that you know as much as they do,” Ternus said in the speech. “With this mindset, you’ll find the confidence you need to push forward, but more importantly, the humility to ask questions.”

In a tech ecosystem populated with abrasive egos, it’s refreshing to hear Ternus utter the word “humility.” Better yet, he only just joined X!

Image Credits:Apple

What projects did John Ternus lead at Apple?

Ternus’ earliest project at Apple involved scrutinizing parts for the Apple Cinema Display, an early desktop monitor.

“At some point in my first year, I found myself at a supplier facility. I was far away from home. Well past midnight, I was using a magnifying glass to count the number of grooves on the head of a screw … and I was arguing with the supplier because these parts had 35 grooves. They were supposed to have 25,” Ternus recalled in his commencement speech. “I distinctly remember stepping back for a minute and thinking, ‘What the hell am I doing? Is this normal?’”

As Ternus climbed the corporate ladder, his responsibilities grew. He may no longer spend as much time analyzing screws, but he still seems to take pride in getting the little details right. In a recent interview, when Ternus was asked about his favorite memory of Steve Jobs, he mentioned the former Apple co-founder’s attention to craftsmanship.

“[Jobs] was moving a piece of furniture, a chest of drawers, and pulled it away from the wall and looked at the back and was just reflecting on, you know, that the carpenter who made it had made it beautiful,” Ternus said. “It finished the back as beautifully as the rest of it, even though nobody was going to see it, right? And I think about that all the time because I think that perfectly exemplifies what we do here.”

From there, he went on to lead the hardware development behind products across the Apple ecosystem, overseeing launches like AirPods, Apple Watch, and the Vision Pro. He also had a hand in major technical upgrades at Apple, like Apple’s transition from Intel chips to its own proprietary Apple silicon.

Most recently, Ternus was involved in the production of the MacBook Neo, Apple’s new, more affordable laptop model that lowers costs through some clever trade-offs in hardware design, like using an iPhone chip to power the device.

“We never want to ship junk. We want to ship great products that have that Apple experience, that Apple quality. To do that with the Neo required building something completely new from the ground up … leveraging both the technologies we’d been developing like Apple silicon, but also the kind of expertise that we’ve developed over many, many years of building Macs, and building phones, and building iPads, and all of these things,” Ternus told Tom’s Guide.

As CEO, Ternus will have to steer Apple through its challenge to catch up in the AI race and figure out what to do with the underlying tech behind the Vision Pro.

What else do we know about John Ternus?

Ternus was on the swim team at Penn. For his senior project, he built a feeding arm that people with quadriplegia could control with head movements.

According to public records of political donations, Ternus donated $2,900 to Senator Chuck Schumer (D-NY) in 2021.

Otherwise, Ternus has maintained a relatively low profile.

This article was originally published on April 20, 2026, and has been updated to reflect that Ternus has now assumed the CEO role.
