title: Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: More similar than ever before [Video]
snippet: More of the same isn’t always a bad thing, but in some cases it could be. Does that ring true with the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro? Find out here. more…
fullText:
More of the same isn’t always a bad thing, but in some cases it could be. Does that ring true with the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro? Find out here.

Pixel 10 vs. Pixel 10 Pro: Closer together than ever? [Video]

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

Hardware

We’re looking at some very similar designs again for 2026 and 2027. Yes, the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro look like the Pixel 10, which in turn looked like the Pixel 9. That’s not to say some changes haven’t been made, the most important is to the camera bar.

The outer frame is metal, but the “bar” is glass. Google also slimmed down the thickness of the Pixel 11 camera bar. It’s thinner and doesn’t stick out quite as much. The Pixel 11 Pro camera bar still protrudes. This is something to consider, as although supported cases work on both phones, the Pixel 11 Pro camera sticks out more and could be in harm’s way. You should check that any third-party case is fully compatible with both models before picking one up.

	

The Pixel 11 Pro has a higher-resolution 1280 x 2856 panel, while the base Pixel 11 stays at 1080 x 2424. The cheaper phone has thicker bezels, and because it’s not LTPO — supporting a 60–120Hz refresh rate instead — it lacks some of the hyper-dynamic refresh rate changes that the Pro’s 1–120Hz LTPO display offers. 

They are both super bright panels, though, reaching up to 3,000 nits of peak brightness on the base Pixel 11 and an illuminating 3,600 nits on the Pixel 11 Pro. For protection, the base model still uses standard Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2, but the Pro adds a specialized anti-scratch coating on top of its Victus 2 glass, delivering more than double the scratch resistance compared to previous models. Even so, a screen protector might still feel necessary in our experience if you’re going to use the HiLight feature, which requires your phone to be face down.

There are a few things to be aware of spec-wise. The base Pixel 11 comes standard with 12GB of RAM and storage options of 256GB or 512GB. The Pixel 11 Pro runs similarly at the entry-level, shipping with 12GB of RAM for its 256GB storage option. 

That is down from 16GB on the Pixel 10 Pro, and if you want Google’s top-tier performance configuration, only the 512 GB and 1 TB models of the Pro step up to 16 GB of RAM. One bonus is that all models now have UFS 4.0 storage by default on the entry-level tier of either phone. Google has locked even faster storage performance to higher tiers, meaning you must upgrade to at least the 512 GB tier on either model to get the benefit of Zoned UFS.

Other little things to be aware of are that the Pixel 11 has Wi-Fi 6E connectivity, while the Pixel 11 Pro has Wi-Fi 7 connectivity, and it also has UWB support for better Bluetooth connectivity and some benefits when using digital car keys.

The Pixel 11 Pro also has HiLight. To be frank, this is just a colorful LED integrated into the flash. It serves as an indicator for Gemini and calls when face down in Flip to Shh mode. A basic, limited notification LED. That’s all it does at launch.

Software

There is zero change between how the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro look and feel. Android 17 is identical, even down to all of the core features and functions. The Pro doesn’t get anything extra. There may be some benefits with the addition of Zoned UFS with the 512GB and 1TB models, or long-term performance gains if you pick the 16GB RAM version.

HiLight gives you some extra controls for the color tuning of the rear notification LED. This is limited, but it works only in the Contacts application as of today. Further compatibility is expected in the coming months.

There’s the default promise of seven years of OS, security, and Pixel Drop updates. So, at least in theory, expect these phones to get OTAs until August 2033. Whether the hardware will last that long is another question entirely.

Brand-new AI features introduced on the Pixel 11 series include Gemini Intelligence for proactive task offloading, allowing you to delegate routine tasks like restaurant reservations or compare shared apartment and hotel links directly inside your text chats. 

Gboard’s Rambler voice-to-text tool cleans up spoken filler words, alongside Gboard’s Sign-to-Text input, which translates sign language in real time using the front-facing Pixel Camera.

For photo and video creation, both models benefit from the new conversational, Gemini-powered Edit with Ask Photos, sensor-level film aesthetics with fully customizable Camera Looks, and the comprehensive video production tools of the Creator Suite.

Lastly, they both feature the brand-new Magic Capture mode to automatically extract the five best HDR+ frames from a short video clip and real-time 4K Portrait bokeh video, ensuring you don’t miss out on these cutting-edge flagship innovations by choosing the base model

Battery

A couple of things stand out right away with the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro. Firstly, the base model has a bigger battery at 4,985 mAh compared to the Pixel 11 Pro’s 4,850 mAh. We don’t even know the reason for this change because they retain identical physical footprints (both measuring 6.0 x 2.8 x 0.3 inches).

Both support fast charging up to 55% in about 30 minutes with a 30W USB-C PPS charger or higher, which, let’s be honest, is still somewhat slow by modern Android smartphone standards.

The upgraded Qi2.2-certified Pixelsnap wireless charging means you now get up to the full 25W rate on both models. This delivers up to 25% faster wireless charging on the base Pixel 11 and up to 29% faster on the Pixel 11 Pro compared to their predecessors. That doesn’t seem like much, but is great for Pixelsnap charger owners.

Camera

For a lot of people, the camera is where you’ll likely decide which Pixel 11 or 11 Pro phone is going to be what you want or need. The Pixel 11 has a new 48MP main sensor, but retains the same 13MP ultrawide and 10.8MP 5x telephoto from the Pixel 10. The new main is a big jump back up from the disappointing 10MP main from the base model a year prior. It offers 56% increase in light sensitivity, so it is just a better sensor all around.

The telephoto hasn’t changed, but Super Zoom is now supported up to 30x on the base Pixel 11, which is a nice bump up from the 20x limit on the previous generation. Google says this is thanks to the Tensor G6 chip.

While software tuning and the improved primary sensor help the phone, you will still get a vastly superior camera experience on the Pixel 11 Pro over the standard Pixel 11, no matter how you cut it.

On the Pixel 11 Pro, Google has packed a much more advanced triple array, including a redesigned 48 MP telephoto camera that pulls in 32% more light. This improved lens enables up to 120x Pro Zoom, combining Tensor G6 hardware with the latest AI imaging models to improve blocky, long-distance photos with a level of clarity that is impressive if a little artificial. 

Fortunately, you don’t lose out on some of Google’s best shooting guidance on the cheaper option, as Camera Looks are still here, Magic Camera, Portrait Blur video, and the Creator Mode are available. It misses out on the Instant Night Sight, Video Boost, Super Res Zoom Video, 

If you want the best Pixel photos and videos, the choice remains simple: the Pixel 11 Pro is far more capable than the standard Pixel 11.

Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro: Which should I choose?

About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.

It’s a tough year to be a smartphone buyer. There are some difficult decisions you will have to make where an upgrade is concerned, and the Pixel 11 lineup signifies this much more than almost any other recent release.

The Pixel 11 doesn’t feel like it has been held back this year like the Pixel 10 was. You get enough functionality to get within touching distance of the Pixel 11 Pro. Most people will be really well-suited to the base model, because it has some important upgrades.

Being able to stomach the price jumps is another problem entirely. The Pixel 11 Pro is now well over $1,000. The Pixel 11 starts at an eye-watering $899 in the US, which is very high for what you get. There is a lot of settling within either price bracket this time.

Last year’s phones might provide you with substantially more bang for your buck because you’re still getting 90% of the Pixel 11 at under 70% of the cost. If you must have Google’s latest phones, wait a little while until we see sales and further discounts. Some trade-in deals have softened the blow of the RAM downgrades and price increases, so be sure to shop around for a deal that works for you – or check out the best current deals below.

title: Review: The Pixel 11 Pro XL is great, but a little too early for Google’s futuristic vision
snippet: At this point, phones have been boring for long enough that even calling them boring feels a little passé. The days of smartphones feeling like the cutting edge of technology are long gone, replaced with iterative updates and a big focus on software-as-a-service. Disconnecting from your smartphone might not seem too difficult on its face, but from rideshare apps to mobile payments, today’s solutions tend to leave a lot more gaps in your life than you might otherwise expect. more…
fullText:
At this point, phones have been boring for long enough that even calling them boring feels a little passé. The days of smartphones feeling like the cutting edge of technology are long gone, replaced with iterative updates and a big focus on software-as-a-service. Disconnecting from your smartphone might not seem too difficult on its face, but from rideshare apps to mobile payments, today’s solutions tend to leave a lot more gaps in your life than you might otherwise expect. 

I say all of this because, in some ways, Google appears to be the one smartphone maker seriously thinking about this divide. Sure, the Pixel 11 Pro XL — and its various siblings — all fall into the exact “boring” archetype I’m describing. We’re on the third generation of this design, after all, which itself is an evolved take on the camera bar style initially launched with the Pixel 6 in 2021. Nearly everything new here feels like a software trick that, it’s easy to assume, could be backported to at least some previous Pixels, and the handful of hardware changes you’ll find aren’t all positive.

And yet, Google appears to be attempting to bridge the gap between our always-connected world and the one we left behind. HiLight wants you to turn your phone over, relying on a modernized notification LED in lieu of an always-on display. Magic Capture wants you to take your eyes off the viewfinder so you can get the shot without missing the actual moment. Even the pitch of Gemini Intelligence is designed to anticipate tasks before you actually reach for your phone to begin with.

Whether Google actually pulled this off with the Pixel 11 Pro XL is another story, but there’s certainly something to be said for trying.

	

Hardware and design

We begin, however, with a design that, no doubt, anyone reading this review is all too familiar with. Once again, Google is recycling its Pixel 9 design from 2024, with just a handful of refinements that feel more like change for the sake of change than real stylistic decisions. It’s a few grams lighter than its direct predecessor, but still not as light as the magnet-less Pixel 9 Pro XL — or, for that matter, its closest competitor in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Its chassis is nearly identical to both of Google’s last two swings, though a revised camera bar means you’ll want a new case anyway. Whatever comes next for Pixel, I’m hoping for something a little slimmer and lighter; as it stands, Google’s XL model very much still feels like a brick. A very pretty, very elegant brick, but a brick nonetheless.

I’m a little mixed on my review unit’s Canyon color. As is often the case with Pixels in particular, this shade is less saturated in person than it appears in Google’s online renders, giving the impression of Coral more than anything truly fresh. Yet again, the metal frame on both Pro models remains perfectly polished, designed for attracting smudges, sweat, fingerprints, and scratches. Google is one of the few companies that has yet to fully embrace matte finishes across a flagship portfolio, even as the existence of an all-matte Obsidian model appears to suggest it’s aware of the perks.

Really, aside from an updated slate of colors, it’s the camera bar that gives the game away. Google’s decision to bring back its first uncovered camera bar since the Pixel 6 series can be read as a big swing, considering that model faced some big lens flare issues at the time. I can’t say I’ve seen any more lens flares than usual, thankfully, and all-black look is, admittedly, pretty striking. There’s a reason Google initially chased this look back in 2021, after all, and I think it really works here in a refined, full-circle kind of way.

HiLight

What doesn’t work, though, is the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s new camera flash. Google has seen fit to try to revive notification lights, only modernized for the AI era. The result is HiLight, a terrible name for a terrible product that will make you nostalgic for the freshly-removed temperature sensor you never actually used.

HiLight, at least in its current state, is a waste. It’s a waste of time, space, money, resources, R&D, labor, and LEDs. Only Google, deep in its Gemini mindset, could overcomplicate a notification light — a concept that feels as old as computers themselves — and reduce it to something that can alert you to phone calls from specific contacts. You might be saying, but Will, it also syncs up with Gemini. Not only does that add nothing to the overall experience of actually using Gemini, but by forcing you to turn your phone over, using HiLight means you’ll need to abandon any on-screen context. Zero out of ten, Google. Get an API out the door ASAP, or ditch it on the Pixel 12.

But wait — it gets worse. Google’s new notification light is diffused via a white cover that helps those color LEDs blend and blur together whenever Gemini is active. That’s all well and good, but it comes at the cost of a more usable flashlight. I’ve long thought Google’s LED flashes, particularly in recent years, are pretty mediocre as quick utility flashlights; I don’t mind their warmth, but in comparison to some of its rivals, the throw of the beam was frequently too far to pinpoint specific objects. Worse: prior to Google finally adding a slider to adjust the flashlight brightness, you’d be locked into half of the maximum setting without turning to a third-party app.

So, of course, less than a year after this slider even debuted in a Canary build, Google has seen fit to permanently cut its brightness levels thanks, I assume, to this diffusion layer. It’s possible something else is at play here, such as a smaller LED to make space for the surrounding color lights. Either way, the end result is the same: a frustrating downgrade for anyone who chucked their old flashlight in a drawer back in the 2010s to be preserved for particularly bad storms and power outages. In my view, Pixel 11 Pro buyers should probably throw one more accessory in their shopping cart: a USB-C keychain light.

Am I harping too much on something that, for most users, will simply be a forgotten piece of the phone within a couple of weeks? Perhaps. But I’m also willing to bet that, in 2026, the vast majority of people will use their camera’s flash in lieu of a flashlight far, far more than they do for actual photo-taking. And I have no doubt that some of those people are going to be pretty frustrated by what they find following their upgrade.

Display, specs, and performance

Here’s the good news: the Pixel 11 Pro XL’s display is so good, you’ll probably never want to turn it over to use HiLight anyway. Google’s come a long way since the terrible panel I did my best to ignore nearly a decade ago on the Pixel 2 XL. It’s now rocking a maximum peak brightness of 3,600 nits, along with a more realistic rating of 2,400 nits in high-brightness mode. I’ve carried this thing through no shortage of sunshine-filled late summer walks, and unsurprisingly, had absolutely no issues making out what was on my display at any given time. The bar for flagship screens in direct sunlight was cleared ages ago; everything since has simply been icing on the cake. But what delicious icing it is.

A word of caution, though. Google’s talking a big game about a new display coating that apparently brings “2x scratch resistance” to the device. I’m not trying to call that claim into question, but after a year’s worth of hearing iPhone 17 users talk about the strength of Apple’s Ceramic Shield 2, I might’ve gotten a little cocky. It took less than a week for my unit to pick up a fairly deep scratch in the top-right corner of the display, something I think was caused by it sharing a pocket with a mini USB-C flashlight while doing some home renovations. Would I have had this flashlight in my pocket were HiLight not dimming the camera flash beyond my personal use case? Who’s to say, but at least I brought it full circle.

As usual, Google’s getting some flak for the Pixel 11 Pro’s spec sheet this year, though this time, it’s not just about Tensor. Sure, Tensor G6 — like truly all of its predecessors — leaves something to be desired on sheer raw horsepower if nothing else. I think Google’s basically fixed all of the efficiency hiccups that plagued previous generations; like with the Pixel 10, I didn’t feel this device get more than a little warm during initial setup, and only extended use in direct sunlight has made the chassis feel noticeably warm in my hand since. But I won’t try to pretend there isn’t a group of potential buyers who will once again be let down by this year’s GPU performance.

While I’m sure Google gets plenty of advantage out of controlling as much of its hardware stack as possible — especially as it tries more and more to compete directly against the iPhone — the Tensor experiment continues to feel like it’s failing to achieve true greatness. For whatever advantages Tensor held in the early days on AI performance over Snapdragon, Qualcomm has certainly caught up, all while outperforming Tensor in practically every other metric. And it comes as local AI models seem to have even less to do on mobile than they did just a couple of generations ago. I’m hoping Google eventually gets the message on this; as 9to5’s Damien Wilde said in a recent episode of The Sideload, it’s time for Tensor to have its own Ryzen moment.

Adding fuel to the “who cares about local AI” fire is Google’s decision to drop the base 256GB Pixel 11 Pro models to 12GB of RAM. The company issued 512GB variants to reviewers, which still sport a full 16GB of memory, so it’s tough for me to say how the performance on these downgraded versions match up. However, I’m coming from nearly a full year on the base Pixel 10, so I feel mostly comfortable in saying it shouldn’t make too much of a difference in everyday use for the time being. In seven years though? Your guess is as good as mine.

Software and battery

As I said up top, the Pixel 11 series feels like the start of a big swing from Google to find ways to get people to live in the moment a little more without actually ditching their phone (or, you know, swapping to a minimalist device like Light Phone). Obviously, if this is Google’s strategy moving forward, it’s very early days, and I don’t just say that to kick sand at HiLight again. It really just feels like this is the beginning of a new chapter the company is chasing, and combined with new enhancements to Digital Wellbeing coming… eventually, it’s an agenda I’m all about.

That said, I’m hard-pressed to find anything in this space I’d call a complete success. I’ve seen Proactive Assistance — Google’s update to last year’s middling Magic Cue — activate just once on my Pixel 11 Pro XL, over a list of potential birthday dessert recipes stored in Keep. Gemini prompted me to “Shop groceries,” but tapping that action simply created a prompt to order the desserts as if they were, you know, actual ingredients and not “Banoffee Pudding.” Were I more of a Google Messages user, I’m sure I’d have more to say about this tool, but unfortunately, my reliance on third-party chat apps is one of the more European things about me. Some of the non-messaging tools, like location-based suggestions within At a Glance, also have yet to show up on my device.

I continue to be more or less underwhelmed by Gemini in general. It’s perfectly fine for really run-of-the-mill searches or prompts — you know, spaces in which it can mostly paraphrase Wikipedia — but venture off a relatively narrow path and I inevitably find myself getting frustrated. A search for a specific brand of craft root beer in the greater Western New York area, which I thought would be a relatively simple task, drove me in circles until I finally just texted a friend who’d been to the actual store in person. Really, Gemini’s big advantage right now is just how baked in it is to the Pixel experience, but I’d be lying if I said it doesn’t feel like all of this would be at least a little better if Gemini 3.5 Pro wasn’t months late.

Basically, today, Google’s idea of saving you time or keeping you connected to the physical world around you mostly exists in advertisements and hypothetical situations. There are spaces where this isn’t true — check out Daniel Bader’s extended thoughts on Magic Capture for a perfect example — but if, like me, you were sold by the pitch of a device you can easily ignore without having to create an entirely new minimalist experience for yourself, just know that reality hasn’t arrived quite yet.

These sorts of features on Niagara are exactly the strategies Google should be looking towards to refresh its launcher.

I’d also argue Google could take more steps in this direction without having to wait for future models with improved AI performance simply by giving its launcher a (in my opinion) much-needed makeover. For all of the Pixel’s promises towards being “proactive” or “predictive,” I’m genuinely surprised we haven’t seen a rethinking of the traditional grid of icons and widgets on your home screen. I look at something like Niagara, which has intelligent media widgets or in-line notifications for your most-used apps, and I wonder why Google hasn’t thought to build similar experiences into the Pixel’s launcher. The closest tool is probably Gemini’s Daily Brief, which mostly exists to try and pull contextual data from places like Gmail into a single list. It’s… fine, but it’s not quite the leap into the future I’d be hoping for — nor is it actually built into the launcher.

While the Pixel 11 Pro XL is undoubtedly behind today’s true battery champs — I wouldn’t say I had difficulty in killing this device the way I did, say, the OnePlus 15 — I never found myself stressing about whether I’d make it to the end of the day. Usually, I was heading to bed with about 40% left in the tank. Keep in mind I spend most of my day on Wi-Fi, but even on days where I was out of the house for longer stretches, I never really felt the need to make sure I was charged up. As unscientific as it may sound, if you’re an average mixed-use smartphone user like myself, you’ll likely experience very minimal battery anxiety.

Camera

If there’s one space where I think even those with relatively recent Pixel devices might be tempted to upgrade, it’s the camera. Google has packed the Pixel 11 Pro XL with a refreshed main sensor and an upgraded 5x telephoto lens that now supports 120x Super Res Zoom. While it’s still absolutely susceptible to creating images that look like AI-generated slop, Super Res Zoom is also capable of capturing a shockingly accurate image of a bird that barely appears within the same shot taken at 1x. It’s impressive, even if you probably won’t want to max it out super often.

That main 1/1.3″ sensor sounds familiar on paper, but it’s allowed Google to bring forth Instant Night Sight, a long-awaited upgrade to the Pixel’s low-light mode that, believe it or not, has been around for nearly a decade now. I can’t speak to whether Google’s quoted 4.5x speed improvement is fully accurate or not, but in practice, it’s certainly faster.

If there’s one thing I’d love to see Google work on for the Pixel 12, it’s a more accurate Night Sight. While the speed in which the Pixel 11 Pro XL can capture and enhance a low-light image into something easily viewable is no doubt impressive, it still frequently defaults to an photo that goes way too far in brightening scenes that probably should, you know, look like nighttime. In one example, a fairly dim image of my cat Linus hanging out in our living room ended up looking like the overhead kitchen light was on behind him, which… it wasn’t. The second shot, which forced me to dial back the exposure manually, is much closer to reality without being too dim.

I could probably go on for 1,000 words about Camera Looks, my favorite Pixel 11 feature and my favorite addition to the Pixel’s camera in quite some time, except I already did. Here’s the short version: Despite some relatively-minor UX decisions that left me scratching my head, this is exactly what I’ve been hoping Google would build into the Pixel’s camera app since at least the Pixel 7. The customizable defaults are great starting points, and shooting with the more personality-driven modes like Editorial or Digi is so fun.

Actually, fun might be the best word to describe Camera Looks. It’s really brought a sense of joy and experimentation to the Pixel 11’s camera system that I’ve sorely missed through the Tensor era, and I hope Google keeps adding to this experience for generations to come. But man, what a bummer this isn’t getting backported to older hardware.

Some minor complaints aside, though, this really is the happiest I’ve been with a Pixel camera in ages. I haven’t felt the need to tweak a shot in Photos after the fact in the two weeks I’ve been using this device, and I don’t expect that to change any time soon. It’s nice to see Google giving more freedom to its photographer fans after half a decade of safe, sterile, contrast-free images.

Conclusion

Google’s Pixel 11 pitch as a more intelligent evolution of the smartphone experience you already know might’ve been a little too early for its own good, but I can see the vision forming. While I remain a skeptic of agentic AI applications ever radically shifting my interactions with Android, I’d be lying if I said it wasn’t a little refreshing — or sobering, even? — to see a tech giant like Google at least acknowledging the growing cry for a break, even if leaning into AI is likely exactly what that audience doesn’t want. It’s an interesting dilemma, and I’m excited to see how the Pixel series continues to tackle it, both through software updates and future hardware refreshes.

Today, though, the Pixel 11 Pro XL mostly exists as yet another phone. Its big aspirations towards a more peaceful future — HiLight, Proactive Assistant — mostly fall flat in practice, all while revealing all sorts of missed opportunities to really rethink the modern approach to smartphones. Then again, there’s very little here that can’t be improved in the months and years to come; slow and steady usually wins the race, after all.

Potential aside, the Pixel 11 Pro XL you can actually buy right now is quite good for all but the most demanding of users. It’s a big, bold, bright display paired with solid battery life, excellent quality-of-life improvements like stronger Pixelsnap magnets (a feature you still won’t find on most other Android phones, Samsung), and — from my perspective — a definitive claim to the camera throne, at least here in the US. As has become tradition with Google’s hardware refreshes, there’s very little to truly dislike here, especially from a core experience perspective.

While we’re expecting a much bigger swing next year with the Pixel 12 — assuming RAMageddon hasn’t derailed Google’s confirmed design cycle — if you’re ready for a new smartphone right now, I wouldn’t hold back from picking up the Pixel 11 Pro XL. It might not be a total success in pulling off its vision for the future of mobile, but that can’t prevent it from being a reliable daily driver in the present. And if this is a cap on the era of Pixel that began with the Pixel 6, it’s certainly an ending to be celebrated.

The Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and is available now.

The days of smartphones feeling like the cutting edge of technology are long gone, replaced with iterative updates and a big focus on software-as-a-service. Disconnecting from your smartphone might not seem too difficult on its face, but from rideshare apps to mobile payments, today’s solutions tend to leave a lot more gaps in your life than you might otherwise expect.

I say all of this because, in some ways, Google appears to be the one smartphone maker seriously thinking about this divide. fullText:
Dominic Preston

 

is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

For the last few years, PC gamers on the go have had a choice: Buy a gaming laptop, or pick up one of the many Steam Deck–inspired handhelds that are a fraction of the size but a lot less versatile. Acer’s latest concept device, Project DualPlay Mini, is an attempt to upend that dichotomy by sticking a keyboard in a handheld.

The DualPlay Mini is first and foremost a Windows gaming handheld, cut from the same cloth as Acer’s existing Predator Atlas 8 (which is being joined this week by a new 7-inch model). In its default configuration, the handheld’s screen is flanked by analog sticks, a D-pad, and Xbox-style ABXY face buttons, plus two triggers on each shoulder. But the DualPlay Mini’s “flip-and-swivel design” allows you to flip the device open and swivel the screen round to instead line it up with a compact, backlit mini keyboard.

With a dinky little 8-inch screen, I’m not sure the DualPlay Mini would ever become anyone’s primary work device, unless they intended to make heavy use of its ability to connect to an external screen. But it might be just enough to make it a useful backup option while traveling, letting you bring one device instead of two. The option to play keyboard-friendly PC games on a device the size of a Steam Deck is an obvious appeal too.

Since the DualPlay Mini is strictly a concept, with no plans for a retail release, Acer hasn’t gone into much detail on the specs inside it so far. It’s powered by an Intel chip and uses a similar dual-fan cooling design to the Predator Atlas 8 — with one metal fan and one plastic — though the blades on the metal element are thinner than before. A pair of USB-C ports sit on the back, with Thunderbolt support on one.

1/3Acer is pitching this as a device that can be a regular gaming handheld. Image: Acer

It’s unclear if Acer will ever release a real product with anything like the DualPlay Mini’s design, but I’ll be seeing all of Acer’s new IFA hardware this week, and I’m hoping for a chance to get my hands on the DualPlay Mini to see if the concept has legs.

title: Sept. 2026 Android Drop: Find Hub ‘Remembered’ list, Motion Assist, & Keep in Google Messages
snippet: Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features. more…
fullText:
Google today is rolling out the September 2026 Android Drop with a number of major features.

Find Hub Remembered

Find Hub and Gemini can now keep track of things that don’t have a tracker tag on them. You can now tell “Gemini to remember where you placed important items.” For example, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer,” with the ability to add a photo. 

The location will be saved to a new “Remembered” tab in the Find Hub app. You can also ask Gemini for its location with a voice command. This is rolling out on Android 16+.

Motion Assist

Motion Assist on Android 17+ will help reduce motion sickness with a subtle bubble overlay on your screen that moves with the vehicle. This is “designed to help bridge the gap between what your eyes see and the movement of your ride.”

	

You can customize the color, shape, and opacity. There’s also an option to have the color and shape change every few seconds.

Android can enable Motion Assist automatically when movement in a car, bus, or train is detected, while there’s also a Quick Settings Tile shortcut.

Gemini Live Guided Vision

Gemini Live is adding Guided Vision to offer verbal “descriptions of what’s in front of you.” Use cases include “reading fine print on a food label, ordering from a menu in a low-lit restaurant, or locating household objects.”

If your camera isn’t lined up, voice feedback will guide you to reframe, pan across a space, or center an object so you get the answers you need. 

Guided Vision is available as an Accessibility shortcut or via the TalkBack menu. This is “coming soon to phones running Android 9+ in countries where Gemini is available.”

Google Messages Keep integration

Following the wide rollout of Chat themes, Google Messages is adding Google Keep integration. This lets you “share and update grocery lists or vacation notes right inside your chat.”

A “Create list” suggestion and ‘plus’ menu shortcut will bring up a sheet that lets you start creating. Once done, the list will appear inline as a shared note. This integration is rolling out starting today.

title: The Cheap Kitchen Tool I Bring to Every Rental House or Airbnb
snippet: Cooking without this inexpensive acccessory is a nonstarter.
fullText:
You don’t need chef training to be picky about the tools you use in the kitchen. That goes doubly for when you might be called to someone else’s kitchen, whether that’s a family holiday situation or a rental property. If you’re cooking for the group — by coercion or self-nomination — you have every right to want to use whatever tools and gadgets make you most confident about the outcome. Especially when feeding a crowd.

I’m known to travel with cooking supplies and have even taken my cake pans across the Atlantic. In my defense, I was A) making a multi-tiered birthday cake and B) making it for my future siblings-in-law, whom I was meeting for the first time. My then-boyfriend, now-husband, is a great cook, it must be said, but cake wasn’t a regular part of his repertoire, and I didn’t want to take my chances with whatever might have been lurking in the darkest corners of his kitchen cabinets. 

I used to travel to summer beach rentals with all manner of basic tools: tongs, a whisk, a rubber spatula, you name it, plus a fleet of knives, a good bottle of olive oil and bagged-up samples of my entire spice rack. 

After a couple of years, I realized that most beach rentals, at least on the East Coast, were pretty well-equipped, and I was happier not having to schlep my entire kitchen to feel empowered to make dinner. I might stash a chef’s knife, just in case, but more often than not, even that would stay tucked in my bag. 

Kitchen gear at a rental house is always hit-or-miss.Connect Images/Getty

There is only one tool, however, whose utility is so singular that it can’t be substituted, that, in my experience, is the key between a good dinner and a great dinner (and dessert) and that, surprisingly, you can’t always reliably find in other people’s kitchens.

My Microplane, myself

The Microplane is an essential tool I can’t count on finding in the drawers of an Airbnb.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Yes, it’s a Microplane. If you’re now puzzling over how a handheld zester of all things is that important a tool, well, some of you have never enjoyed scraped-together key lime pie for breakfast at the beach, and it shows.

But seriously. There is no other tool that does what a Microplane does to the same degree. Using a paring knife to gingerly cut the rind off citrus fruits without taking the pith with you and then mincing that up? I’ve done it. Hard pass.

A box grater is not likely to do the trick.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Don’t start with me about some cheap grocery store zester that manages to be both ergonomically overcomplicated and entirely ineffective. A box grater that you would typically use for cheese or carrots that has that one plane dedicated for zesting? Have you tried it lately? (Actually, has anyone ever? It just looks like a recipe for pulpy zest and bloody knuckles.)

	

			

	

			

									

						Microplane Zester					

							

		

Why the zester is an essential kitchen tool

Maybe your dubiousness isn’t so much the quality of the tool itself, but why any kind of zester is that critical? To which I challenge you: the next time you make salad dressing or pasta, enchiladas or pad thai, or anything at all that calls for citrus juice, add a hit of zest and see what that does to the outcome. Citrus zest adds several times the flavor, minus the sharp acidity. In a word, it adds vibrancy to whatever you’re doing, without the pucker. It’s a wow factor with the simplest execution. Not to mention: key lime pie for breakfast.

A hit of zest is like fairy dust for food.Pamela Vachon/CNET

And the economics are inarguable. Even in today’s economy, a lemon or lime can only set you back so far, but it contributes so much. And the Microplane itself? Is all of about $18.

Here I am waxing all poetic about citrus, but let’s also talk about two other cooking champions whose processing is made infinitely easier by a Microplane. Garlic and ginger — also cheap yet dynamic ingredients. A garlic press is a fine thing, but if yours is as difficult to clean after use as most I’ve owned have been, ditch it. The microplane can do that work for you, and basically rinses clean afterward.

A zester will inspire you to grate cheese over, well, everything.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Or if you’ve been buying pre-shredded Parm or another hard cheese, here’s another taste test challenge for you. It’s so quick to just grab a hunk and shave directly into or onto whatever you’re making or eating, with the added bonus of leaving out the additional starches that act as anti-clumping agents in the pre-shredded stuff. I could also make a point here about freshly grated nutmeg, but that would be extra. Suffice to say, I never make béchamel without it.

Microplanes of a different color

My go-to zester comes in more than a dozen colors.

If you’re convinced, I am partial to the Microplane brand here, whose handles are especially comfortable and which includes a protective sleeve for storage. Incidentally, you can also get a Microplane in over a dozen colors, and they are made in the US, if buying locally is a compelling argument.

If you’re already a Microplane evangelist and have made it this far, here’s an invitation to maybe upgrade yours. They don’t last forever, as the blades will dull over time. I recently switched out my 15-year-old model, and it has brought new life to my kitchen.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

For argument’s sake, I also checked out one of Amazon’s best-selling and least expensive models, the MasterChef version, which retails for only $10. It’s a little more generous in width, and its protective cover is admittedly a little easier to maneuver. Functionally, it works just like the Microplane, but is made in China for those keeping score.

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 is so popular that Samsung is stealing parts from next year’s phones just to make more
snippet: Samsung has a hit on its hands with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, to the point where the company is taking parts production from its 2027 smartphones just to meet demand for the foldable. more…
fullText:
Samsung has a hit on its hands with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, to the point where the company is taking parts production from its 2027 smartphones just to meet demand for the foldable.

ZDNet Korea reports that Samsung has run into a wall when it comes to boosting Galaxy Z Fold 8 production, with demand for the foldable far outpacing initial supply. Shipping delays were seen immediately after launch, and Samsung even set out to produce one million more units. 

The problem Samsung has run into, the report brings out, is around Display Driver ICs (DDIs). This specific part is built by a Taiwan-based semiconductor foundry, UMC, on a 22nm process with the partner having “reached its limit” around building these parts. As a result, Samsung is prioritizing DDI volume that was already secured for 2027 products and shifting that to boosting production of the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

Samsung isn’t directly using parts designed for other devices here, though, as the DDI is built specifically for each individual phone model. It’s the production of these parts that is being shifted around, which is still a major change on Samsung’s part. Samsung has also requested a “super hot run” – i.e. “express service” – for the Fold 8’s DDIs in order to meet demand. 

	

This comes as the Fold 8 is partially out of stock on Samsung.com in the US, and the foldable continues to contribute to a rapidly growing foldable market. Omdia this week reports that foldable shipments will double by 2028 to the tune of around 36 million units.

In recent weeks, Google Messages has mostly reverted to the two-circle read receipts underneath the message design after trying a single circle within the bubble.

Messages for web removing QR code pairing

title: Acer Recommits to Repairability With New Vero 16 Laptop
snippet: The company also unveils the sleekest Swift yet and a Swift Air update at IFA 2026.
fullText:
Acer is a brand closely associated with budget workhorse machines — the company largely manufactures laptops for entry-level gamers, students and office workers. It’s an admirable (and tough) niche to fill at a time when RAMageddon is inflating hardware component prices and even sub-$700 laptops feel like a dying breed.

Maybe that’s why the company is continuing to throw its weight behind the right-to-repair movement with the fourth-generation Vero 16 revealed at IFA 2026. If you’re going to be shelling out more cash for a so-called “budget laptop,” it makes sense that you’d want it to stand the test of time. The repairable and upgradable Vero 16 is one way for the company to adapt to changing market conditions.

While that more modular Vero design is one of the laptops Acer is positioning front-and-center at the show, its other clamshells certainly aren’t being ignored: Two new lightweight Swift laptops are making their debut at IFA 2026.

The latest Vero 16 doesn’t look quite as distinguishable as its predecessor. Whether that’s a good thing is up to you.Acer/CNET

When Acer revitalized its Vero laptop line last year, sustainability was the name of the game. The 2025 version of the Vero 16 had a chassis composed primarily of recycled post-consumer plastic waste and oyster shells. It was a gritty, textured clamshell shot through with gray-blue specks — a spectacle piece, to be sure. And while vague commitments to sustainability and repairability are great, there wasn’t anything especially interesting going on aside from the computer’s oceanic aesthetic.

The next-generation Vero 16 brings the sustainability theme to one of its natural conclusions, and the company ended up with a more interesting computer in the process. The 2026 Vero 16 is an even more repairable laptop, allowing you to swap out or upgrade parts. That could cut back on some waste — and additional expenses for you, the laptop owner.

Parts of the chassis (including the bottom cover, hinge and I/O port covers) are removable, granting Vero 16 owners access to the laptop internals for quick repairs. You’ll be able to swap out a bad battery or SSD on your own, and the device is designed to support processor upgrades for the next two generations. You still might need to bring the computer into a repair shop for more serious maintenance, but there’s a lot here that you can service completely on your own.

While Acer isn’t the only computer manufacturer hopping on the repairability trend, the Vero 16 feels like it fills a niche for folks who might not feel technically savvy enough to benefit from, say, one of Framework’s fully modular computers. This laptop even has a visual repair guide engraved on the chassis to help owners feel more confident about completing simple swapouts. Hey, who knows, maybe that’s what it’ll take for your dad to phone you for computer help a little less frequently?

Every fourth-generation Vero 16 configuration has an OLED panel, with 2.8K (2,880×1,800-pixel) and 2K (1,920×1,200-pixel) resolution options available. The 1,920×1,200-pixel panel will support an optional touchscreen. This clamshell will house up to an Intel Core Ultra X9 388H processor with integrated Intel Arc B390 graphics, up to 32GB of LPDDR5x memory and 512GB of storage.

The diminutive Swift Blade is a durable 14-inch laptop.Acer/CNET

Swift Blade 14

Acer’s Swift laptops might not be quite as funky-looking as the Vero 16, but the two new additions to the company’s more premium lineup are some of the sleekest laptops ever from Acer.

The Swift Blade is the more compact entry. This 14-inch laptop weighs just 1.76 pounds and is half an inch thick, making it appreciably lighter than the Swift Edge 14 AI. The Swift Blade 14 can be configured with up to a 2.8K OLED panel, an Intel Core 7 350 Wildcat Lake processor, 12GB of LPDDR5 RAM and 1TB of storage.

With Acer laptops, you’re usually making build quality compromises, as many of the company’s computers have plastic chassis. That’s not the case with the Swift Blade 14, which will be built from a magnesium-aluminum alloy and carbon fiber. These lightweight metallic build materials are crucial for a thin laptop to withstand accidental stress, so I think the Swift Blade could carve out a meaningful place in the brand’s lineup, depending on its price.

The Swift Air 16 is a refresh of one of Acer’s more premium lightweight clamshells.Acer/CNET

Swift Air 16

Unlike the Swift Blade 16, the Swift Air isn’t an entirely new entry into Acer’s sleek laptop lineup. In fact, this 16-inch laptop refresh is rather beefy compared to the rest of the Swift lineup, weighing in at 3.3 pounds. Perhaps that can be attributed to the all-aluminum build, since Acer ditched its magnesium alloy for this particular clamshell.

Like its predecessor, the Swift Air 16 features an up to 2.8K display with OLED and IPS options — certain IPS panels will offer touchscreen support. This laptop houses up to Intel Core 7 350 silicon, 16GB of LPDDR5x memory and 512GB of system storage.

Acer has neither confirmed when its new laptops will be available for purchase nor the prices for the Vero 16, Swift Blade 14 and Swift Air 16. Stay tuned for that information in the coming days.

title: This Robot Vacuum Aims to Compete With the Suction Power of a Stick Vacuum
snippet: Robot vacuums aren’t very good at deep cleaning carpets. Roomba is about to show me how it’s fixed this problem.
fullText:
Robot vacuums are a great way to do some general cleaning, but most lack the power of a dedicated vacuum cleaner because you can’t pack enough suction into a small design. iRobot may have an interesting solution for that with its new Roomba Max 875 Combo, which it describes as the “most powerful robot ever” because it uses a proprietary vacuum seal technology that concentrates suction power on the floor. 

“With the Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot, we not only increased overall suction power, but also changed how that suction gets applied to the carpet,” Adam Pope, vice president and chief engineer at iRobot, said in a statement. “With SealForce, we’re able to seal the chassis against the carpet fibers, so the airflow, which has the greatest impact on pickup performance, has somewhere to go instead of escaping around the edges. More suction helps, but the seal is what takes it to a level beyond what’s previously been possible.”

I cover vacuums and home tech for CNET. While I’m here at IFA Berlin 2026, I’m determined to seek out the most interesting tech that solves your most common cleaning problems. I’m excited to see the Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot in person on Wednesday. I’ll report back with my impressions later.

iRobot

In a video call with me prior to IFA Berlin 2026, Pope described the technology as being similar to pressing down harder on the carpet when you’re vacuuming with a regular vacuum, to increase the seal and focus the suction on a particular spot. In the case of the Max 875, rather than pressing down, the robot vacuum’s chassis lowers a “skirt” that forms a tight seal against carpet fibers.

Once the seal is established, it can use 35,000 pascals of suction to clean the floor, which iRobot describes as “tornado-like airflow.” The company also says that it has three times deeper carpet cleaning and the best pickup performance to date among its models. Essentially, rather than just boosting suction power, the robot vac is making its suction more targeted and efficient on the surfaces it cleans. It’s a good idea if it works as promised. In our testing, we’ve generally found that cordless vacuums have better suction than robot vacuums, but this type of tech could help robots catch up. 

There’s also some other interesting cleaning technology under the hood. To handle dried-on stains on hard floors, the Max 875 Combo continuously sprays heated mist as it mops, loosening and softening older stains so the mop roller can remove them. Pope told me that the new roller mop is also the industry’s largest, has 300 rotations per minute and 18 newtons of downward pressure. The company claims that all this gives the robot vacuum twice the stain removal, 3.75 times deeper scrubbing and 1.2 times wider coverage per pass. 

iRobot

Available on other robot vacuums, the 875 Combo has an AI-powered carpet-detection feature that automatically raises the mop when it detects carpet and lowers a protective shield to prevent dripping. It also comes with the other high-end features we’ve come to expect from flagship robot vacuums, including antitangle and hair-cutting main brushes, side brushes, lidar navigation and AI object recognition for more than 300 household objects. 

The 875 Combo also has a docking station that washes the mop with water heated to 176 degree Fahrenheit and dries it with air heated to 131 F; it also auto refills cleaning fluid and self-empties into a debris bag that should last up to 90 days.  

iRobot

The Roomba Max 875 Combo will cost $1,199 and launch alongside the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo. The 678 Combo falls more into a midrange price segment, but it has plenty going for it. It comes with its own unique feature that iRobot calls SprayForce AI. 

It uses 40,000 pascals of high-pressure water (not heated) to break up dried messes and improve mopping efficiency by 40%. The mop rollers come with 15 newtons of downward pressure and 30,000 pascals of suction for vacuuming, as well as the SealForce tech. Other capabilities are pretty similar, including automatic mop lifting (without the protector), antitangle and hair-cutting brushes, edge cleaning, lidar navigation and AI obstacle avoidance as well as a self-emptying and self-cleaning docking station.

Both the $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo Robot and AutoWash Dock and the $899 Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot and AutoWash dock models are available now at iRobot.com. 

Editor ’s note: Ajay Kumar’s travel costs for the IFA conference were covered by Roborock. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: New Apple TV 4K is coming: Four features launching soon
snippet: A new Apple TV 4K is long overdue, and was originally expected to launch last fall. But now that Siri AI is finally ready, all signs point to the new Apple TV 4K being unveiled soon—possibly at the September 9 event. Here’s what’s rumored. more…
fullText:
A new Apple TV 4K is long overdue, and was originally expected to launch last fall. But now that Siri AI is finally ready, all signs point to the new Apple TV 4K being unveiled soon—possibly at the September 9 event. Here’s what’s rumored.

#1: Siri Remote update

Though no details have been revealed, Apple reportedly has an updated Siri Remote coming with its new Apple TV 4K.

Code leaked in a build of macOS 26.7 seemingly confirms the existence of the new Siri Remote. And before that leak, Mark Gurman had reported that a “tweaked Apple TV remote” was possible for the new hardware.

It doesn’t sound like any big changes are coming. But hopefully we’ll at least get a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding.

#2: Siri AI and more Apple Intelligence features

Siri AI is expected to be a major part of the marketing push for the new Apple TV, as well as other new Home products.

So far, Apple has said nothing about the new assistant coming to either Apple TV 4K or HomePod. But evidence keeps mounting that tvOS 27 will include Siri AI—and likely only on new hardware.

It’s very possible we’ll get some additional Apple Intelligence features too, such as an improved search experience.

#3: New A-class chip

The current Apple TV has an A15 Bionic chip that first debuted in 2021. Fortunately, the new model should come with a big upgrade in the performance department.

A new A-class chip is coming that’s more powerful and enables AI features. 

Rumors have indicated it could be an A17 Pro or A18 chip. But that reporting was largely from the pre-Siri AI era. It wouldn’t be surprising if Apple gave the new hardware a more powerful A19 or A20 chip instead.

#4: N1 wireless chip

	

The N1 wireless chip that first debuted in iPhone 17 is rumored to come to the new Apple TV 4K too.

By adding N1, Apple will give the Apple TV Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, as well as support for Thread networking.

The current, four-year-old Apple TV hardware only offers Wi‑Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5, by comparison.

title: Galaxy S27 Pro has Ultra’s design as leak reveals just how much smaller it is [Gallery]

fullText:
Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 Pro is an Ultra-tier phone in a smaller package, and a new leak reveals both what it looks like, as well as just how much smaller it is compared to the standard device.

CAD-based renders and details from @OnLeaks (published via Android Headlines) claim that the Galaxy S27 Pro will have the same new redesign as the Galaxy S27 Ultra. That is, a new iPhone-like camera bar with reorganized lenses and a plateau across the entire width of the device.

Galaxy S27 Pro: 154.06 x 73.77 x 7.95mm

Galaxy S27 Ultra: 163.76 x 78.25 x 7.97mm

Pixel 11 Pro: 152.7 x 71.9 x 8.4 mm

Pixel 11 Pro XL: 162.7 x 76.5 x 8.5 mm

The leak claims that the Pro will have a 6.6-inch display, which seems a bit large given the dimensions. Pixel 11 Pro, by comparison, has a 6.3-inch display, but it all depends on how Samsung measures, bezel size, and other factors. In any case, it’s going to be meaningfully smaller than the Galaxy S27 Ultra’s 6.9-inch panel.

	

A mockup, above, shows the difference in size, though it’s hard to tell if this is fully reflective of reality.

Rumor has it that the Galaxy S27 Pro will fit into the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s existing $1,299 price point, with the Ultra getting its own price hike. All four of Samsung’s new flagships should arrive sometime around January or February of next year.

title: Google announces new Fitbit Air Special Edition with Pokémon Sleep [Hands-on]
snippet: The first follow-up to the Fitbit Air is a new Special Edition that integrates with Pokémon Sleep. Available in the US and Japan, it’s meant to make sleep tracking feel like a “daily adventure,” while celebrating Pokémon’s 30th anniversary this year. more…
fullText:
The first follow-up to the Fitbit Air is a new Special Edition that integrates with Pokémon Sleep. Available in the US and Japan, it’s meant to make sleep tracking feel like a “daily adventure,” while celebrating Pokémon’s 30th anniversary this year.

On the hardware front, this is the same Fitbit Air that launched in May with a special Performance Loop Band. The Sleepy Blue colorway is quite nice and different from Google’s existing lineup, while there’s a “custom silk print label of Sleeping Pikachu right on the strap.”

Meanwhile, the retail packaging features some rather nice touches.

The software integration lets you connect this Fitbit Air — along with all other Pixel and Fitbit wearables — to the Pokémon Sleep app on Android and iOS. The game takes your overnight sleep and any naps during the day to unlock “interactive rewards.” This covers Google Health sleep duration and stages.

	

Gather Pokémon around Snorlax: When you wake up, Pokémon with sleep types similar to yours gather around Snorlax. Research their sleeping styles to complete your Sleep Style Dex and befriend new helper Pokémon to your team.

Calculate your Drowsy Power: The Pokémon you befriend collect Berries to raise Snorlax’s Strength. When you wake up, your Sleep Score, calculated from sleep duration tracked from Google Health, multiplies Snorlax’s Strength to generate “Drowsy Power.”

Discover rare sleep styles: The higher your Drowsy Power, the more Pokémon — and rare sleep styles — will appear around Snorlax the next day.

In some ways, this is another take on Fitbit’s Sleep Animals in the old app. Behind the scenes, Health Connect on Android and Apple Health on iOS are leveraged. The sync occurs automatically every morning. 

Pre-orders begin today at the Google Store and Target (with in-store availability). The $129.99 Fitbit Air Special Edition Pokémon Sleep starts shipping on September 15.

5.5-inch cover display and 7.8-inch inner display

“Latest Apple Pro chip and latest Apple modem”

He also talks about two key features: the rumored “crease-less” display and liquid metal hinge. He says the crease isn’t entirely gone, but it’s comparable to the new Samsung foldables and might be even better thanks to the more durable hinge.

On the note of the hinge and durability, he adds:

The spec for Apple was to make the foldable phone as durable or at least close to it as any other iPhone. And that’s one of the things that they’ve spent a lot of time working on is the durability.

Multitasking was another key area addressed in the interview. Gurman previously reported that iOS 27 will enable iPad-like app layouts and side-by-side app multitasking. Today he adds that drag and drop will be supported between multiple on-screen apps, so you can quickly move data from one app to another.

Gurman also comments on launch timing, with encouraging news on that front:

I would be very surprised if the foldable phone did not come out at the same time as the new Pro phones, or very close to it. title: Apple Photos in iOS 27 upgrades one of my favorite features in a big way
snippet: Apple Photos is full of exciting updates in iOS 27, including for one of my favorite features in the app: iCloud Shared Albums. more…
fullText:
Apple Photos is full of exciting updates in iOS 27, including for one of my favorite features in the app: iCloud Shared Albums.

Apple’s Photos app is one of my most-used apps, as I suspect it is for many iPhone users. It’s where all of the photos and videos I capture live, plus screenshots, pictures shared by friends, and more.

But did you know that the Photos app also has a social media-style feature?

I’m not big on social media, but I do enjoy having a private, social-lite way to share memories with loved ones. And iCloud Shared Albums offers exactly that.

With iCloud Shared Albums, you can create an album that’s shared with only the people you choose. Anyone invited can add their own photos and videos, and you’ll get notified when they do. You can also ‘like’ shared photos and comment on them—just like a proper social network.

I’ve used and enjoyed Shared Albums for a long time, but the feature has felt in need of some upgrades. Fortunately, iOS 27 provides them.

In iOS 27, Shared Albums now support full-resolution photos and videos. That’s a huge item checked off my wish list.

Additionally, iOS 27 expands how you can react to a photo or video. Now you can use any emoji of your choosing as a reaction—you’re not limited to just ‘likes.’

For the first time, Android and Windows users can contribute to the album via the web. Previously, they could only view content shared by Apple users.

Apple is also making it easier to save shared photos with a tap. And you can set new participant permissions and optionally have your album expire at a later date.

These upgrades address all of the complaints I’ve previously had about Shared Albums. Combined with the other improvements in iOS 27, it’s a big year for Apple Photos.

title: ChatGPT and Codex now support multiple Gmail and Google Calendar accounts
snippet: OpenAI confirmed today that ChatGPT and Codex users can now add multiple Gmail and Google Cal accounts. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
OpenAI confirmed today that ChatGPT and Codex users can now add multiple Gmail and Google Cal accounts. Here are the details.

‘Add your second (or third!) account’

Depending on how your personal and work lives are organized, you likely have more than one Gmail or Google Calendar account.

For many users who rely on ChatGPT’s plugins for those platforms, there has been one limitation until now. Each plugin could only be connected to a single Google account, making it harder to use ChatGPT Codex across separate personal and work inboxes or calendars.

Today, as confirmed by OpenAI DX engineer Gabriel Chua, the company rolled out multi-account support for Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Contacts.

1. In the left side bar, select “Plugins” and search for Gmail/Google Calendar/Google Contacts

2. If you’ve already connected on account, click on the gear icon to add your second (or third!) account pic.twitter.com/5G6Z7YPXGK

— Gabriel Chua (@gabrielchua) August 28, 2026

To add another account, users can open the Plugins section in the sidebar, find Gmail, Google Calendar, or Google Contacts, and click the gear icon for a plugin they have already connected. From there, they can add a second or third account and complete the usual Google authorization process.

In practice, the change means users can have one ChatGPT conversation working with information or taking actions through a personal Gmail account, while another relies on a work account, contacts, and calendar to handle professional tasks.

ChatGPT can also pull relevant information from multiple connected accounts when needed, giving it a broader picture of the user’s communications, relationships, and schedule, enabling it to provide more useful and contextual responses.

Importantly, OpenAI’s plugins documentation notes that connected accounts are subject to their respective app permissions and workspace controls, meaning availability can vary depending on the user’s plan, organization, and administrator settings.

Our thoughts are with all those affected by the tragic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal and Tibet. Apple is making a donation to support relief and rebuilding efforts on the ground.

title: Google Health 5.07 rolling out with better manual logging, maps, & more
snippet: Google Health 5.07 is rolling out on Android and iOS with meaningful updates to manual workout logging and a handful of bug fixes. more…
fullText:
Google Health 5.07 is rolling out on Android and iOS with meaningful updates to manual workout logging and a handful of bug fixes.

Version 5.07 lets you manually enter more metrics, with additions appearing in “workout summaries more quickly once you’ve made them.” There’s also a sizable update to map performance. The update is still rolling out on Android and widely available on iOS today.

The full list of improvements and fixes is organized into three categories:

Activity and Fitness Updates

	

Improved Manual Workout Logging: We’ve made three updates for users who log exercises manually. First, you can now add and adjust more metrics when logging an exercise manually. Your edits will also show up in the workout summaries more quickly once you’ve made them. And finally, you can now log more metrics when switching from a pool to open swim exercise.

Maps: We’ve continued to improve the maps experience, with faster loading times, and smoother rendering and adjustments. We’ve also fixed an issue where maps were occasionally missing when using your phone to track a running, biking, or walking session.

Running Distance Totals: Trail runs and incline runs now count toward your Running Distance totals.

Weight Tracking Updates

Weight Graph: We’ve recalibrated the graph’s dynamic minimum and maximum range so your weight trends and changes are easier to view at a glance. 

Health Connect Updates

We’ve fixed an issue that caused some Android users to lose their connection with Health Connect. If you were impacted, you’ll now see Health Connect listed in the Partner Apps section of the Connections screen.

title: Sony’s new ULT Tower party speakers start at $450
snippet: Sony has announced new additions to its ULT Tower party speaker lineup, now offering options that are much more affordable. more…
fullText:
Sony has announced new additions to its ULT Tower party speaker lineup, now offering options that are much more affordable.

The Sony ULT Tower collection kicked off back in 2024 with a pricey but powerful $1,200 speaker. The ULT Tower 9 launched earlier this year with a smaller, but still pricey $900 package. These speakers are designed with parties in mind, delivering music on a much larger scale than a traditional Bluetooth speaker.

Now, Sony is expanding the lineup.

Three new Sony ULT Tower party speakers are launching in September, starting with the most affordable of the bunch, the ULT Tower 5. This is the most compact of the bunch – it’s not exactly small – but Sony says it still delivers “impressive bass and sound pressure.” Like the rest of the lineup, it also features four sound profiles, including: 

	

ULT1: Enhances deep bass for a rich, low-frequency sound that makes your heart tremble.

ULT2: Boosts even greater power, delivering body-shaking bass and strong sound pressure.

FLAT: Reproduces music exactly as intended, delivering a true-to-source listening experience.

LIVE: Recreates the spacious feel of a live performance while preserving vocal clarity.

ULT Tower 5 starts at $450, with the whole lineup on Sony’s website, Amazon, and more.

The whole lineup also supports wireless audio alongside XLR, USB, and Line inputs, as well as having a microphone input too. Multiple speakers can also be set up in a stereo pair.

Meanwhile, ULT Tower 7 offers more power and volume, as well as adding 360-degree audio at $650.

ULT Tower Max is the last option debuting this month, jumping up to the top of the lineup at $1,500. This monstrous party speaker has three woofers (two front and one back-facing) as well as four tweeters, 360-degree sound, and “a high-powered amplifier.”

title: Afterglow brings classic After Dark screen savers to modern Macs
snippet: This interesting project by Jeff Halter (via Daring Fireball) lets users run the original 68k After Dark screen saver modules on modern Macs. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
This interesting project by Jeff Halter (via Daring Fireball) lets users run the original 68k After Dark screen saver modules on modern Macs. Here are the details.

’Run classic After Dark screen savers on modern macOS’

Depending on how long ago you started using or getting interested in Macs, you likely remember After Dark, a collection of screen savers that became a fixture on Macintosh computers throughout the 1990s. At the very least, you’re possibly familiar with the famous Flying Toasters screen saver.

Over the years, running these classic screen savers has generally required vintage hardware or a classic Mac OS emulator, which can be finicky. However, a new project called Afterglow makes the process much easier on modern Macs.

As John Gruber noted on Daring Fireball, the project comes from Jeff Halter, who previously created Lunacy, a native Swift app that lets users play the classic Lunatic Fringe game from More After Dark on modern Macs.”

With Afterglow, the original After Dark modules run through an emulator built specifically for them, without requiring a complete classic Mac OS environment. Notably, Afterglow also includes a modern macOS screen saver module, allowing users to set any imported After Dark module as their Mac’s screen saver.

Here’s Halter on the motivation behind the project:

In the ’90s, Berkeley Systems’ After Dark screen savers brought Flying Toasters, Fish, and Starry Skylines to Macintosh screens everywhere. They served a practical purpose in preventing burn-in on CRT monitors, but also entertained, with animations that could be funny, surreal, beautiful — sometimes gross.

They are works of art worth preserving.

Running After Dark modules in the present day has involved fussy configuration of Mac OS emulators or vintage hardware. Even then, no single emulator or vintage computer can faithfully run every module: some animate too fast, some too slow.

Afterglow is an emulator built specifically for running After Dark modules — the original 68k module code, not a remake or port — with no dependencies on ROMs or classic Mac OS. Created in the spirit of software preservation, it makes After Dark easy to enjoy today and for years to come.

The project’s website notes that After Dark modules aren’t included, but provides instructions for finding and importing them into Afterglow.

Halter also notes that Afterglow includes features such as module controls, full-screen mode, a randomizer, multimodule support, 3D box art, a CRT shader, a resource inspector, and a DrawMorph editor.

title: Google Maps is finally going to bring turn-by-turn navigation to Korea
snippet: Google Maps is filling a gap in its operations by working on bringing turn-by-turn navigation to Korea. more…
fullText:
Google Maps is filling a gap in its operations by working on bringing turn-by-turn navigation to Korea.

Reported by The Korea Herald, Google has recruited a new “Strategic Partnerships Development Manager” who will be working with the Google Maps team to bring full service to South Korea. This includes working with private companies and public entities to get things up and running.

While Google Maps works in South Korea, it only serves as a hub for locations, reviews, and directions for public transit. Turn-by-turn navigation, the functionality that makes Google Maps so popular across the world, is simply not available in the country as of today. That also results in Maps having fewer users in the country, with local options Naver Map and Kakao Map having as many as 3x more users than Google’s app.

Google, in a brief statement, says that will change:

	

The plan is to bring full-functioning Google Maps capabilities to Korea, which includes turn-by-turn directions…

This comes after the South Korean government approved Google’s ability to use high-precision map data on overseas servers earlier this year, with the condition that military and similar sensitive facilities are blurred. Latitude and longitude coordinates will also be disabled in the country, Reuters notes.

title: Today is Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO, John Ternus takes over tomorrow
snippet: After 15 years at the helm, today is officially Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO. In April, Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO on September 1, with John Ternus set to take the reins. Cook, of course, isn’t going away completely. Instead, he’s set to become executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors. more…
fullText:
After 15 years at the helm, today is officially Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO. In April, Apple announced that Cook would step down as CEO on September 1, with John Ternus set to take the reins.

Cook, of course, isn’t going away completely. Instead, he’s set to become executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors.

Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO 

Cook became Apple’s CEO in 2011, two months before Steve Jobs passed away. Ternus, meanwhile, joined Apple in 2001 as a member of the company’s Product Design team. He moved up the ranks quickly and was formally promoted to senior vice president of Hardware Engineering in January of 2021.

In a report over the weekend, Bloomberg reiterated that Cook’s focus as executive chairman will see him managing Apple’s relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government.

Cook will serve as Apple’s executive chairman. He’s told Ternus that he’ll keep managing the company’s relationships with President Donald Trump and the Chinese government, and that he’s eager to handle any other tasks his successor deems necessary. While Cook has talked about plans to take up more outdoor activities and spend time at his vacation home in Palm Springs, he’s also told staffers the company will remain his No. 1 priority, because he “can’t imagine it any other way.”

When he becomes CEO, Ternus is expected to take Tim Cook’s current office, Bloomberg says. The Information has reported that Cook’s executive assistant will stay on and work for Ternus.

Apple held a farewell dinner for Cook at Apple Park last week, according to reports. This included “hours of tributes from Ternus, Laurene Powell Jobs, and other current and former Apple executives.” OneRepublic, one of Cook’s favorite bands, also performed at the event.

The transition comes ahead of Apple’s “Surprise and shine” special event, which will take place on Wednesday, September 9. Cook will not be featured in the event. Instead, it will be spearheaded by Ternus. During the event, Apple is expected to unveil the foldable iPhone Ultra, iPhone 18 Pro, new Apple Watch models, and more.

In recent weeks, Apple has made a wave of unpopular announcements, including raising prices on most of its hardware products (but not iPhone), as well as subscription services including Apple TV, Apple Music, and Apple One. This should set the stage for Ternus to take over and focus on kicking off what’s been described as Apple’s most ambitious product cycle ever.

title: People are sticking the Fitbit Air to their bodies, literally, and it works [Gallery]
snippet: The Fitbit Air might be one of Google’s most versatile products in a while not just because it’s so simple, but because buyers are finding very unique ways of using it. That includes quite literally sticking the Fitbit Air to your body with tape which, apparently, actually works quite well. more…
fullText:
The Fitbit Air might be one of Google’s most versatile products in a while not just because it’s so simple, but because buyers are finding very unique ways of using it. That includes quite literally sticking the Fitbit Air to your body with tape which, apparently, actually works quite well.

Google designed the Fitbit Air to be worn around your wrist, where most health trackers sit, and that’s where most buyers probably do use it. Early on, many figured out that the included band was a good way to dual-wield both the Air and a traditional watch on the same wrist, and there are dedicated products that have since come out to do that a bit more elegantly.

But another way to use the Fitbit Air? Stick it to your body, literally, with tape.

A recent thread on Reddit showed a Fitbit Air owner who started using kinesiology tape – also known as athletic tape, usually used to support sore/strained muscles – to attach the tracker to their upper arm. The subtle location is out of sight and, at least according to this user, offers “more accurate data.” That checks out, as bicep trackers can often provide slightly more accurate data by cutting out motion from the wrist, among other things. Whoop offers an official bicep band for its tracker, and there are a host of bicep bands for Fitbit Air around the web.

	

But this trend of just using some tape has been around for a little while, actually. We found a few more threads of users who have been sticking the tracker to their upper arm, and it sounds like it works out pretty well. And it’s not the only other place people are putting the tracker, as some mention putting it in their sock and elsewhere.

fullText:
Google morning. How many times have you written that before? I hope you had a lovely final weekend before Labor Day. This morning, I’m reading about tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of pristine Duck Hunt cartridges found in a box in Wisconsin, vigorously nodding my head along to John Oliver’s takedown of subscription bloat (but remember to subscribe to 9to5Google Pro anyway!), and wishing I had a 3D printer to create my dream storage and organization system.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

I think it’s safe to say that Google’s decision over the weekend to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America has been met with a bit of pushback.

	

In a blog post, Google says that it generally abides by the Geographic Names Information System when it comes to how it presents names on maps, and since Executive Order 14420 “directs the Board on Geographic Names (‘BGN’) to immediately rename Lake Ontario to Lake America and to update the Geographic Names Information System to appropriately reflect the change,” it was merely following its own protocols. Google went through the same rigmarole when it renamed Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America in February 2025.

One beneficiary of the drama has been MapQuest, the company whose rise and subsequent fall can be directly traced to Google Maps’ ascent over the past two decades. In social media posts on Friday, the company showed a cropped map of Lake Ontario with the caption, “We’re not changing it,” inspiring widespread support alongside understandable questions of “MapQuest still exists?!”

Over the weekend, the company’s Android and iOS downloads shot up 128%, bringing it to the top of their respective “maps & navigation apps” categories on both platforms, and app usage was up 50x, according to owner System1. 

As of writing, Apple has yet to make the same change to its Maps app, but it’ll likely happen any day now, particularly because the President is applying pressure, according to reports. 

Though the name change itself amounts to a minor scuffle within the larger trade war between the US and Canada, Google Maps’ enormous reach — and companies’ reliance on its APIs — means that long after the heat has died down, its effects will be felt indefinitely.

✉️ Inbox

Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 rolling out with many Pixel bug fixes. Google’s relentless Android release cycle continues unabated, and Beta 4 appears more feature-filled than most.
